The burgeoning volume of online user-generated content, particularly in the form of text reviews, presents a unique opportunity to enhance recommendation systems. Traditional recommendation approaches, such as collaborative filtering and matrix factorization, have achieved considerable success, but they primarily rely on user-item interaction data – ratings, purchases, clicks – while largely ignoring the rich semantic information embedded within associated textual reviews. While various opinion mining techniques exist to extract sentiments and aspects from reviews, these often fail to provide a seamless integration with the recommendation process, requiring separate feature engineering steps and potentially losing valuable contextual information. This disconnect limits the potential for leveraging the full power of user reviews to improve recommendation accuracy. In this paper, we address this limitation by proposing a novel approach that learns distributed representations—also known as word embeddings—of both users and items directly from the textual content of reviews, explicitly tailored for recommendation tasks. Our method aims to bridge the gap between opinion mining and recommendation by formulating a unified framework that maximizes the likelihood of observing words within the review corpus. This allows us to construct vector representations that capture the nuanced preferences expressed by users and the characteristics of items in a continuous, low-dimensional space. Crucially, our approach moves beyond simply extracting opinions to building comprehensive profiles that can be used to predict user-item interactions on previously unobserved pairs – a core challenge in recommendation. Unlike existing systems that treat text analysis and recommendation as separate stages, our framework integrates both processes into a single, end-to-end learning pipeline. This holistic approach ensures that the learned representations are optimized for the specific task of recommendation, rather than being solely focused on sentiment extraction or topic modeling. Furthermore, we develop efficient and scalable algorithms to handle the large-scale text archives commonly encountered in real-world recommendation scenarios. By leveraging distributed representation learning and a recommendation-aware objective function, our system aims to capture a richer and more accurate understanding of user preferences and item characteristics than traditional methods. We validate the effectiveness of our approach through extensive experiments on real-world datasets, demonstrating significant improvements over state-of-the-art baseline recommendation systems. Our findings underscore the potential of distributed representations to unlock the full value of text reviews for more personalized and effective recommendations. Anaphora resolution, the task of identifying the antecedent of a pronoun or other referring expression, is a cornerstone of natural language understanding. While much research has focused on coreference resolution – determining when two expressions refer to the same entity – a significant class of phenomena, particularly prevalent in languages like Japanese, resists straightforward coreference analysis. These are known as associative anaphora, a bridging phenomenon where the anaphor and antecedent, though related, do not directly co-refer but rather share an associative relationship, often based on shared context or thematic roles. For instance, consider the sentence “John went to the store and then bought milk.” Here, “then” acts as an anaphor referring not to John, but to the action of going to the store. Handling associative anaphora is crucial for accurate discourse interpretation and has posed a considerable challenge to traditional anaphora resolution systems. Existing approaches to anaphora resolution often struggle with associative anaphora due to their reliance on coreference detection mechanisms. Standard coreference resolution techniques effectively identify expressions that denote the same entity, but fail to capture the more nuanced relationships involved in associative linking. Recent work has explored bridging anaphora resolution, but many approaches remain task-specific or rely on hand-crafted rules lacking generalizability. Furthermore, many languages exhibit zero anaphora, where an antecedent is implied rather than explicitly expressed. The interplay between zero anaphora and associative anaphora represents a particularly complex area requiring sophisticated modeling. This paper introduces a novel probabilistic model tailored for resolving associative anaphora specifically within the Japanese language. Our approach frames associative anaphora as a form of zero anaphora, allowing us to leverage existing techniques for zero anaphora resolution while incorporating crucial lexical knowledge to capture the characteristic associative relationships. We automatically acquire this lexical knowledge, significantly reducing the need for extensive manual annotation and improving the model’s adaptability. By simultaneously resolving zero anaphora and associative anaphora, we aim to capitalize on the shared underlying mechanisms and improve overall resolution accuracy. Experimental results on a Japanese corpus demonstrate that our proposed model effectively resolves associative anaphora with competitive performance, and that integrating associative anaphora resolution into a joint zero anaphora resolution framework leads to notable gains, highlighting the synergistic benefits of this combined approach. We believe this work represents a significant step toward a more complete and flexible anaphora resolution system capable of handling the nuances of bridging phenomena in Japanese and potentially other languages. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

The automatic construction of taxonomies, or hierarchical relationships between concepts, has long been a central challenge in natural language processing and knowledge representation. Such taxonomies are invaluable for various downstream tasks, including information retrieval, question answering, and semantic web applications. Traditional approaches to taxonomy induction often rely on manually curated lexical resources or heuristic methods, which are time-consuming and scale poorly. Recent efforts have explored machine learning techniques to automate this process, but many struggle to effectively incorporate diverse sources of relational evidence and efficiently explore the vast space of possible taxonomic structures. In this paper, we address these limitations by presenting a structured learning approach to hypernym taxonomy induction, leveraging a probabilistic graphical model and efficient inference techniques. Our core innovation lies in formulating the taxonomy induction problem as a structured learning task, where the goal is to jointly infer the entire taxonomic hierarchy from multiple heterogeneous sources of evidence. Specifically, we model hypernymy and siblinghood relations within a probabilistic graphical model, incorporating semantic features derived from Web n-grams and Wikipedia abstracts. These features capture various patterns and statistical regularities that suggest hierarchical relationships, providing a rich signal for learning. A key challenge in structured learning is efficient inference, especially when dealing with complex, loopy graphical models. To tackle this, we employ loopy belief propagation (LBP) for approximate inference over the taxonomy structure. Furthermore, we introduce a novel directed spanning tree algorithm tailored for the core hypernymy factor, enabling more efficient propagation of information. To train our model, we adopt a discriminative learning approach, utilizing subgradient stochastic optimization to learn parameters that accurately reproduce sub-structures of WordNet, a widely used lexical resource. This evaluation strategy allows us to assess the model’s ability to capture complex hierarchical relationships. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. Compared to a chance baseline, our model achieves a significant 51% error reduction in reproducing WordNet sub-hierarchies. Notably, incorporating non-hypernym-factored sibling features contributes to a 15% error reduction, highlighting the importance of siblinghood information for taxonomy induction. Finally, in a direct comparison to previous state-of-the-art methods, our approach achieves up to a 29% relative error reduction in ancestor F1 score, showcasing its superior performance. This work represents a significant step towards building robust and scalable systems for automatic taxonomy induction. In this work, we propose a structured learning approach to induce hypernym taxonomies using a probabilistic graphical model formulation.

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has rapidly emerged as the dominant paradigm in machine translation, demonstrating substantial improvements over traditional Phrase-Based Statistical Machine Translation (PBSMT) approaches (Bahdanau et al., 2014;Sutskever et al., 2014;Cho et al., 2014). Attention mechanisms, in particular, have proven crucial in enabling NMT models to focus on relevant parts of the source sequence when generating the target sequence, significantly improving translation quality (Bahdanau et al., 2014). However, most NMT research has focused on translating between textual sources, neglecting the rich information that can be conveyed through visual data. The advent of large datasets incorporating both text and images, such as Multi30k (Yu et al., 2016), provides a unique opportunity to explore multi-modal NMT, where visual features are integrated into the translation process. This is particularly relevant in scenarios where images provide vital context for accurate translation, such as describing scenes, objects, or actions. Existing approaches to multi-modal NMT primarily concentrate on fusing visual information with the textual input at a single point, often concatenating image features to word embeddings in the encoder (Lu et al., 2016;Hakkani-Türksavaş et al., 2016). While these methods demonstrate encouraging results, they often overlook the potential of incorporating visual information into different stages of the translation pipeline. Furthermore, many approaches rely on relatively simple fusion techniques, neglecting the complex interplay between textual and visual cues. A more nuanced strategy would involve exploring different integration points and assessing their individual and combined impact on translation quality. The idea that global image features could be leveraged in various ways, beyond simple concatenation, is largely unexplored in the context of attention-based NMT. This paper addresses these limitations by introducing a novel framework for incorporating global visual features into attention-based NMT models. Our approach explores three distinct strategies for integrating image features: (i) augmentation of the source sentence with image features represented as discrete tokens, (ii) initialization of the encoder's hidden state with global image features, and (iii) initialization of the decoder's hidden state with global image features. We conduct extensive experiments on the Multi30k dataset, translating from English to German and English to English, comparing the effectiveness of these strategies and evaluating their impact on model performance. Moreover, we investigate the benefits of augmenting the training data with synthetic multi-modal, multilingual data to further enhance the model’s ability to handle visual information. Our results demonstrate that incorporating global visual features into multiple components of the NMT model significantly improves translation quality, and, importantly, that our best models achieve state-of-the-art results, surpassing even strong Phrase-Based Statistical Machine Translation baselines across all evaluated metrics.

The burgeoning field of deep learning has revolutionized numerous natural language processing (NLP) tasks, with neural network architectures demonstrating remarkable capabilities in understanding and processing human language. A crucial component of these models is the use of word embeddings, dense vector representations of words that capture semantic and syntactic relationships. Pre-trained word embeddings, such as Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) and GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014), offer a significant advantage by leveraging vast amounts of unlabeled textual data to learn these representations, thereby injecting valuable prior knowledge into task-specific models. While these embeddings are frequently employed as either initializations or fixed features within downstream classification models, a growing body of research suggests that fine-tuning these embeddings during task-specific training can further enhance performance. However, directly optimizing pre-trained embeddings solely with the task-specific loss function can lead to a specialization of those embeddings that may sacrifice their broader, more general semantic understanding. This specialization can be detrimental when the task domain differs significantly from the domain of the original pre-training data, or when the task requires a nuanced understanding of word meanings. In this paper, we address this challenge by introducing a novel approach to training neural network models for text classification that combines task-specific and unsupervised objectives at the word-embedding level. Specifically, we extend our classification model's loss function with an auxiliary, unsupervised loss component that encourages the learned word representations to retain both task-specific features, acquired through supervised training, and more general features, inherited from the initial pre-training. Our core hypothesis is that incorporating an unsupervised objective during task-specific fine-tuning can help prevent overfitting to the task-specific data and promote the development of more robust and generalizable word embeddings. We evaluate our proposed method within the context of temporal relation extraction, a challenging NLP task that involves identifying and classifying temporal relationships between events mentioned in text. We focus on narrative containment relations—determining whether one event occurs before, after, or during another—extracted from clinical records, a domain characterized by specialized terminology and complex sentence structures. Our experiments on the widely-used THYME dataset demonstrate that continued training of the word embeddings using our combined loss function, alongside the standard task loss, significantly improves performance. Notably, we achieve state-of-the-art results while relying solely on a general-domain part-of-speech tagger as our linguistic resource, highlighting the effectiveness of our unsupervised loss extension in compensating for the lack of domain-specific linguistic knowledge.

The burgeoning field of Natural Language Processing (NLP) has witnessed remarkable advances in recent years, particularly concerning semantic understanding. Tasks ranging from machine translation to question answering necessitate a deep comprehension of language, moving beyond mere syntactic structure towards representing meaning. Among these semantic tasks, Sentence Similarity (SS) has emerged as a critical benchmark for evaluating a model’s ability to grasp the nuances of language, engaging with the challenge of comparing the semantic content of two sentences. SS differs significantly from document-level semantic tasks, posing unique considerations for model design. Unlike longer documents, sentences are characterized by their inherent sparsity; each individual word contributes to the overall meaning, and capturing this subtle interplay is paramount for achieving accurate similarity assessments (Mitra and Gilbert, 2007). Consequently, robust modeling of individual words within a sentence is absolutely critical to construct a comprehensive semantic representation. Traditional approaches often rely on simple bag-of-words models or distributional semantics, which can struggle to adequately represent the intricacies of word meaning in context. Recent research has explored various strategies to improve semantic representations, including incorporating contextual information like word embeddings (Mikolov et al., 2013) and attention mechanisms (Bahdanau et al., 2014). However, a fundamental question remains: can enhancing our understanding of individual word meanings directly translate to improved sentence-level semantic understanding? This question forms the core motivation of our work. We posit that improving the modeling of lexical semantics – the meaning of individual words – is indeed a key avenue for achieving more accurate and robust sentential semantics. Specifically, we hypothesize that augmenting semantic representations with readily available lexical information, beyond simply co-occurrence patterns, can significantly bolster performance on SS tasks. To this end, we focus on two crucial aspects of lexical semantics: selectional preference and semantic similarity. Selectional preference, as defined by Levin and colleagues (1993), describes the tendency of verbs to co-occur with certain types of arguments. For example, “eat” typically takes animate objects, while “build” takes inanimate objects. Modeling this preference can provide valuable constraints on how words function within a sentence. Similarly, incorporating information about words that are semantically similar, often readily available in lexical resources like WordNet, can help to bridge the gap when sentences use different words with overlapping meanings. In this paper, we propose a novel approach that combines these two aspects of lexical semantics within a latent variable model. By integrating corpus-based information (selectional preference extracted from large text corpora) and knowledge-based information (semantic similarity derived from dictionaries), we aim to create a richer and more nuanced representation of word meaning, ultimately leading to improved performance on SS tasks.

The burgeoning volume of Electronic Health Record (EHR) data presents unprecedented opportunities for advancing healthcare through data-driven insights. However, realizing this potential hinges on our ability to effectively extract meaningful information from the unstructured text within EHR notes—clinical narratives detailing patient encounters, diagnoses, procedures, and treatments. A crucial step in this process is the identification and categorization of medical events, such as diagnoses, medications, allergies, and procedures, along with their associated attributes (e.g., dosage, frequency, date). Accurate medical event detection is fundamental to a plethora of health informatics applications, including pharmacovigilance, drug surveillance, clinical decision support, and patient risk stratification. It enables automated tracking of patient health history, facilitates cohort analysis for research, and ultimately contributes to improved patient care. Traditional approaches to medical event detection have largely relied on supervised machine learning models, particularly Conditional Random Fields (CRFs). These models, while effective, typically depend on hand-crafted features derived from fixed-size context windows surrounding potential event mentions. This approach is inherently limited by the difficulty of anticipating all relevant contextual cues and often necessitates extensive feature engineering efforts. Furthermore, fixed context windows fail to capture long-range dependencies within the text, which can be critical for disambiguating event mentions and accurately determining their attributes. The reliance on manually defined features also restricts the model's adaptability to variations in clinical language and different EHR note formats. Recent advances in deep learning, particularly in Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), have demonstrated significant promise for sequence labeling tasks in other NLP domains. RNNs, with their ability to model sequential dependencies, offer a compelling alternative to CRF-based approaches for medical event detection. Unlike CRFs, RNNs learn task-specific representations directly from the data, eliminating the need for hand-crafted features. Moreover, their inherent capability to process variable-length sequences and capture long-range contextual information makes them well-suited to the complexities of clinical narratives. In this work, we investigate the application of recurrent neural network frameworks, specifically Bidirectional RNNs (BiRNNs), for medical event detection in EHR notes. BiRNNs process the input sequence in both forward and backward directions, allowing the model to leverage information from both preceding and succeeding contexts—a crucial advantage for resolving ambiguities and accurately identifying event attributes. We demonstrate that our BiRNN-based approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art CRF models in this domain, highlighting the potential of deep learning techniques to advance medical event detection and unlock the full value of EHR data.

The task of entity linking (EL), also known as named entity disambiguation, seeks to connect mentions of entities within text to their corresponding entries in a knowledge base (KB). Accurate EL is crucial for a wide array of downstream natural language understanding tasks, including question answering, information retrieval, and knowledge graph completion. While significant progress has been made in EL, current approaches often struggle to effectively utilize the diverse sources of information available for each entity and mention. Traditional approaches often rely on hand-engineered features and domain-specific training data, limiting their generalizability and scalability. Moreover, many systems fail to adequately incorporate rich contextual information surrounding mentions or to effectively represent the multifaceted nature of entities themselves, encompassing their descriptions, types, and relationships within a KB. The growing need for systems that can process text from diverse domains without expensive domain adaptation necessitates a more robust and flexible approach. Existing EL systems frequently treat various aspects of entities – their descriptions within the KB, the textual contexts in which they appear, and their hierarchical type information – as largely independent signals. This often results in suboptimal linking decisions, as the synergy between these information sources is not fully exploited. Furthermore, many systems struggle to handle novel entities – those that are not yet present in the KB – and require specialized techniques for out-of-KB linking. The reliance on hand-engineered features introduces a significant engineering bottleneck, limiting the adaptability of these systems to new domains and knowledge bases. The need for domain-specific training data adds another layer of complexity and cost, particularly when dealing with specialized corpora. To address these limitations, we propose a novel neural, modular entity linking system that learns a unified and dense representation for each entity by jointly encoding its type information, textual descriptions from the KB, and the surrounding context in which it is mentioned. Our approach moves beyond the traditional separation of these information sources, instead leveraging a neural network architecture to learn how they interact and contribute to accurate entity linking. This allows our system to capture nuanced relationships between entities and their contexts, leading to more precise linking decisions. By design, our model avoids the reliance on hand-engineered features and domain-specific training data, enabling it to achieve high performance across a diverse range of datasets. Moreover, we demonstrate the ability of our model to effectively link mentions of previously unseen entities, extending its applicability to open-domain and evolving knowledge bases.

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has achieved remarkable progress in recent years, demonstrating impressive translation quality across various language pairs (Sutskever et al., 2014;Bahdanau et al., 2015;Wu et al., 2016). However, conventional NMT models typically focus on translating individual sentences in isolation, neglecting the valuable document-level contextual information that is crucial for generating coherent and contextually appropriate translations. Sentences within a document are not independent; they exhibit dependencies and relationships that contribute to the overall meaning and flow of the text. Failing to incorporate these dependencies can lead to inconsistencies, repetitions, and a lack of fluency in the translated output. Several approaches have been proposed to address this limitation, including incorporating discourse markers, memory networks, and using hierarchical sequence-to-sequence models. However, effectively capturing and utilizing document-level context within the NMT framework remains a challenging problem. Existing methods often struggle with maintaining a dynamic representation of the entire document history and integrating it effectively with the sentence-level translation process. Addressing these challenges requires a mechanism that can selectively attend to relevant contextual information from the document, while also allowing the model to adapt its attention based on the current sentence being translated. To this end, we propose a novel document-level NMT model that utilizes a hierarchical attention network to capture context in a structured and dynamic way. Our approach builds upon the standard NMT architecture, introducing an additional level of abstraction that conditions the translation process on the NMT model’s own prior hidden states. This hierarchical attention mechanism allows the model to selectively attend to and incorporate relevant context from previously translated sentences, enabling it to generate more coherent and contextually accurate translations. The encoder and decoder both benefit from context in complementary ways. Through extensive experiments on a benchmark dataset, we demonstrate that our proposed hierarchical attention model significantly improves the BLEU score compared to a strong NMT baseline and surpasses the state-of-the-art in existing context-aware NMT methods. Our results highlight the effectiveness of hierarchical attention networks for capturing document-level context and enhancing the overall quality of neural machine translation. The contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows: (1) We introduce a novel hierarchical attention network for document-level NMT. (2) We demonstrate that the model significantly improves translation quality compared to existing approaches. (3) We provide insights into how both the encoder and decoder benefit from incorporating document-level context.

The burgeoning field of opinion mining has traditionally focused on identifying sentiment expressed towards entities—detecting whether a review or text expresses a positive or negative opinion about a product, person, or organization. However, a growing body of research recognizes the importance of considering the  context  of opinions. Specifically, opinions frequently arise in relation to events that have consequences, either positive or negative, for the entities involved. We refer to these as “+/-effect events”—events associated with an effect, which can be beneficial (+) or detrimental (-). Consider the sentence “The company’s decision to raise prices angered consumers.” Here, the “decision to raise prices” is the event, and it has a negative effect on “consumers.” Understanding these +/-effect events is crucial for robust opinion inference; simply knowing that consumers are angry is not as informative as knowing  why  they are angry – because of a price increase. Recent work has begun to explore this dimension of opinion analysis, demonstrating its potential for more nuanced understanding of subjective text. However, a key challenge in this area is the lack of readily available resources, particularly a lexicon of words representing +/-effect events at a fine-grained, sense level. Existing sentiment lexicons are primarily word-level and lack the necessary granularity to distinguish between different nuances of event-related sentiment. For example, the word "bankruptcy" clearly indicates a negative effect, while the word "promotion" clearly denotes a positive effect. However, many other words can express effects depending on context and specific sense. Our work addresses this gap by presenting a novel method for acquiring a sense-level lexicon of +/-effect events, which we term “+/-EffectWordNet.” We hypothesize that leveraging both the structured knowledge of WordNet and the descriptive power of word glosses can lead to a significantly improved lexicon compared to approaches relying on either method alone. Our approach combines a graph-based method that propagates information through WordNet’s semantic relationships with a supervised classifier that utilizes word glosses. Critically, we move beyond purely word-level annotation, aiming to identify specific senses of words that carry +/-effect connotations. Furthermore, we investigate the potential of our model to guide manual annotation efforts, identifying senses that are less readily apparent from existing seed sets, thereby expanding the coverage of our lexicon. We provide empirical evidence demonstrating the effectiveness of our hybrid approach and its utility in guiding annotation, showcasing its potential to significantly advance research in +/-effect opinion inference.

The demand for simplified text has rapidly grown alongside advancements in natural language processing (NLP), driven by applications such as text summarization, accessibility for individuals with cognitive disabilities, and educational tools. Sentence compression, a particularly effective form of text simplification, focuses on reducing the length of a sentence while preserving its core meaning. Traditionally, sentence compression has been approached within a monolingual framework, where the task is to shorten sentences in a single language. However, the increasing interconnectedness of the world and the rise of multilingual NLP applications necessitate exploring cross-lingual extensions of these techniques. In this paper, we address this need by investigating parallel sentence compression, a novel task wherein we aim to generate parallel compressions of parallel sentences—that is, shorter versions of sentences in two or more languages that maintain semantic equivalence. The ability to create parallel sentence compressions holds significant potential for a variety of multilingual NLP tasks, including cross-lingual information retrieval, machine translation quality estimation, and the development of simplified multilingual educational materials. Consider, for example, the scenario of translating a simplified document. Generating parallel sentence compressions before translation can potentially improve the fluency and naturalness of the translated output by reducing the complexity of the source sentences. Moreover, parallel sentence compressions can act as a bridge between languages, facilitating cross-lingual transfer learning for NLP tasks. While parallel sentence simplification has seen some prior research, parallel sentence compression is a relatively unexplored area. Existing approaches to sentence compression generally rely on monolingual training data and models, and directly extending these methods to a parallel setting can prove challenging due to issues of language divergence and the need to maintain cross-lingual alignment. In this work, we examine two distinct approaches to incorporating bilingual information into the sentence compression task. The first approach leverages shared latent representations learned from parallel data, while the second explicitly models cross-lingual constraints during the compression process. We then evaluate the effectiveness of these methods on a parallel corpus of news articles, contrasting their performance with respect to compression rate, semantic preservation, and cross-lingual alignment. Our analysis provides valuable insights into the challenges and opportunities of parallel sentence compression and sheds light on the potential of this approach for advancing multilingual NLP. We believe that the development of robust and efficient parallel sentence compression techniques will play a crucial role in enabling a wider range of cross-lingual NLP applications.

The task of syntactic analysis – determining the grammatical structure of a sentence – is fundamental to many natural language processing applications, ranging from machine translation to information extraction. In Chinese, syntactic analysis presents unique challenges due to the lack of explicit word boundaries and relatively free word order. Traditional Chinese syntactic analysis systems typically employ a pipeline approach, first performing word segmentation, then part-of-speech (POS) tagging, and finally dependency parsing. While effective, these pipeline systems suffer from a well-known “error propagation” problem: errors made in earlier stages propagate to subsequent stages, negatively impacting overall accuracy. This inherent limitation has motivated research into joint models, which perform all three tasks simultaneously, mitigating error propagation by leveraging dependencies between the sub-tasks. Transition-based dependency parsing, a popular approach, operates by iteratively applying grammatical transitions to build the syntactic tree, making it a natural fit for a joint modeling framework. While joint models for Chinese have been developed, they have largely relied on hand-engineered features, limiting their ability to leverage the power of neural networks. Recent advances in neural networks, particularly the development of powerful word embeddings, have revolutionized many NLP tasks. However, these embeddings, while effective for dependency parsing, have been difficult to integrate effectively into joint models due to the complexities of the Chinese language and the intricacies of transition-based parsing. This paper introduces a novel neural joint model for Chinese syntactic analysis, specifically designed to address these challenges. Our work represents the first fully joint neural approach for Chinese word segmentation, POS tagging, and dependency parsing, effectively preventing error propagation and achieving state-of-the-art results. A key innovation lies in our use of character string embeddings alongside traditional word embeddings. While previous approaches have primarily focused on word embeddings for dependency parsing, we observe that character-level information is crucial in Chinese due to the lack of explicit word boundaries. This allows our joint model to better handle ambiguous word segmentations and improve overall accuracy. Furthermore, we explore the application of bi-directional Long Short-Term Memory (bi-LSTM) networks, demonstrating that they can achieve competitive performance with fewer hand-engineered features, simplifying model development and improving generalizability. We systematically evaluate our model on standard Chinese syntactic analysis benchmarks, demonstrating significant improvements over existing systems in both word segmentation and POS tagging, and competitive accuracies in dependency parsing. Our findings highlight the efficacy of neural joint models with character string embeddings for comprehensive Chinese syntactic analysis.

The ability to organize knowledge into structured representations like ontologies is crucial for a wide range of applications, including knowledge graph construction, data integration, and semantic search. Ontologies define concepts (entities) and the relationships between them within a specific domain, providing a semantic framework for understanding and reasoning about information. A common challenge arises when multiple ontologies are developed independently, often covering similar domains, but utilizing different vocabularies and structures. The need to reconcile these ontologies—to establish correspondences between their entities—is paramount for unifying knowledge and enabling interoperability. The process of aligning ontologies, or finding mappings between entities in different ontologies, is a long-standing and actively researched area within the broader field of knowledge representation and reasoning. Existing approaches often rely on manually-defined rules or require labeled training data, limiting their scalability and applicability in real-world scenarios. Furthermore, traditional ontology matching methods tend to operate on lexical similarity, often overlooking the deeper semantic relationships between entities. In this work, we address the limitations of existing ontology matching techniques by proposing a novel unsupervised approach, which we term DeepAlignment. Our method leverages recent advances in representation learning, specifically the use of pre-trained word embeddings, to derive improved entity descriptions tailored for the ontology matching task. Word embeddings, often generated through distributional semantic modeling, capture semantic relationships between words based on their co-occurrence patterns in large corpora. While powerful, these pre-trained embeddings are generally not optimized for the specific requirements of ontology matching, which necessitates a focus on capturing nuanced entity relationships and domain-specific semantics. DeepAlignment tackles this challenge by refining these pre-trained word vectors in an unsupervised manner. Crucially, our refinement process doesn’t require any explicit labels or guidance related to ontology matching; it operates solely on the structure and content of the ontologies themselves. This unsupervised nature significantly enhances the practicality and scalability of our approach, making it suitable for aligning large and diverse ontologies without human intervention. We perform extensive experimental evaluations on standard ontology matching benchmarks, demonstrating that DeepAlignment achieves substantial performance improvements over state-of-the-art methods. These results highlight the considerable advantages of representation learning techniques for tackling the complexities of ontology matching and pave the way for more effective and scalable knowledge integration strategies. Clinical documentation serves as the cornerstone of patient care, capturing a wealth of information about diagnoses, treatments, and patient history. Central to this documentation is the assignment of medical codes, such as ICD (International Classification of Diseases) and CPT (Current Procedural Terminology) codes, which are standardized representations of these clinical concepts. These codes are crucial for billing, insurance claims, quality reporting, and clinical research. However, the process of manually assigning these codes is notoriously laborious, time-consuming, and prone to human error. Moreover, current systems often lack transparency, failing to explicitly articulate the connection between the clinical text and the assigned codes, thereby hindering understanding and trust in the system’s decisions. This lack of explainability poses a significant barrier to widespread adoption and integration into clinical workflows. In this paper, we address the challenge of automating the prediction of medical codes from clinical text while simultaneously providing interpretable explanations for those predictions. Existing approaches often prioritize accuracy over explainability, treating medical code prediction as a “black box” problem. While achieving high accuracy is essential, the ability to understand  why  a particular code was assigned is equally important for clinicians. Such understanding fosters trust, allows for error detection, and potentially reveals novel insights from the clinical data. We propose a novel approach that combines the power of deep learning with an attention mechanism to achieve both high predictive accuracy and meaningful explanations. Our method utilizes an attentional convolutional neural network (CNN) to process clinical text and predict a set of relevant medical codes. CNNs are well-suited for capturing local patterns and features within text, while the attention mechanism allows the model to focus on the most relevant segments of the document for each code. This provides a degree of interpretability, as the attention weights can be visualized to highlight the parts of the text that contributed most significantly to the final prediction. We demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on a benchmark dataset, surpassing previous approaches in terms of precision at 8 (P@8) and Micro-F1 score. Critically, we also conduct a rigorous interpretability evaluation involving a physician, who assesses the relevance and meaningfulness of the attention-based explanations. The results of this evaluation demonstrate that our model effectively identifies clinically relevant segments of text that justify the assigned codes, thereby providing valuable insights and enhancing the trustworthiness of the system. Our work represents a significant step toward building intelligent and transparent medical coding systems that can support clinicians and improve healthcare outcomes.

The proliferation of smartphones and the increasing adoption of voice assistants have dramatically altered how users interact with information. A significant portion of this voice-driven interaction revolves around local business discovery – users seeking nearby restaurants, shops, or services through voice commands. Consequently, local business directory assistance via voice search has become a crucial application, experiencing rapid growth. However, a persistent challenge hindering the seamlessness of this experience is the relatively low accuracy of speech recognition systems when processing business listing names. These names are often idiosyncratic, containing uncommon words, abbreviations, or variations in spelling, leading to recognition errors and frustrating user experiences. Traditional speech recognition systems often rely on nationwide language models, which lack the granularity to effectively handle the diverse and localized nature of business names. Such models treat all businesses as equally likely, failing to account for the significant variations in business types and naming conventions across different geographic areas. This paper addresses this limitation by introducing a novel approach to language model generation specifically tailored for local business voice search on mobile devices. We propose a geo-centric language model (GeoLM) generation algorithm that dynamically adapts to the user's location, providing a highly localized language model capable of accurately recognizing business names within a specific geographic area. Our core insight is that the linguistic landscape surrounding local businesses—the prevalence of certain business types, preferred naming conventions, and common abbreviations—varies considerably from one location to another. By incorporating this geographic context into the language modeling process, we can significantly improve recognition accuracy for voice search queries related to local businesses. Our algorithm boasts several key advantages. First, it allows for the creation of language models for any user, regardless of their location. Second, it dynamically adjusts the geographic scope of the language model based on local business density, ensuring that areas with high concentrations of businesses receive more granular and accurate models. Finally, the GeoLMs can be pre-compiled and efficiently deployed, resulting in fast recognition times—a critical requirement for responsive voice search applications. Through rigorous experimentation using real-world spoken business listing name queries from a business directory assistance service, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our GeoLM approach. Our results show a substantial 16.8% absolute improvement in recognition accuracy and a remarkable 3-fold speedup in recognition time compared to a traditional nationwide language model. These findings underscore the potential of geo-centric language modeling to significantly enhance the user experience in local business voice search.

The sheer scale of modern numbers—billions of dollars in corporate deals, trillions in government budgets—can be overwhelming and difficult to grasp. While raw numeric values provide information, they often lack context, leaving readers struggling to understand their true significance. Consider the question: how much is 131 million US dollars? The number itself is difficult to internalize without a relatable frame of reference. Existing methods for providing this context, such as comparing a number to a static benchmark (e.g., “$131 million is more than the GDP of country X”) often lack dynamism and can be disconnected from the reader’s existing knowledge. This paper addresses this challenge by introducing a novel task: automatically generating brief, compositional descriptions, or "perspectives," that put numbers into context. For example, "$131 million is about the cost to employ everyone in Texas over a lunch period." These perspectives aim to provide intuitive and accessible understandings of large numbers by relating them to everyday experiences or well-known facts. To effectively tackle this problem, we propose a system built around two key steps: formula construction and description generation. The formula construction phase aims to identify and combine relevant numeric facts from a knowledge base to create a numerical "formula" that represents a reasonable perspective. This formulation process is not simply a lookup; instead, it involves composing multiple facts—for example, the average annual salary in Texas and the total number of employed Texans—to arrive at the desired comparison. Crucially, we rank these formulas based on a combination of factors: familiarity (how commonly the comparison is made), numeric proximity (how closely the computed value matches the target number), and semantic compatibility (how logically sound the comparison is). The description generation phase then takes the best-scoring formula and translates it into a fluent and natural language description using a sequence-to-sequence recurrent neural network (RNN). This allows for generating a variety of descriptions for the same formula, catering to different stylistic preferences. To facilitate our research, we created a new dataset of numeric mentions extracted from news articles, augmented with human-provided perspectives. Each mention is labeled with a set of rated perspectives, providing valuable training data for both the formula construction and description generation components of our system. We then conducted extensive experiments comparing our compositional approach against a non-compositional baseline and observed significant improvements. Specifically, our system achieves a 15.2% F1 improvement in formula construction and a 12.5 BLEU point improvement in description generation, demonstrating the efficacy of our approach to produce more relevant and human-like perspectives.

The burgeoning field of word embeddings has revolutionized numerous natural language processing tasks, enabling models to capture semantic relationships between words in a distributed vector space (Mikolov et al., 2013; Pennington et al., 2014). Early work largely focused on learning embeddings from monolingual data, often struggling to represent the full complexity of word meaning due to polysemy — the phenomenon where a single word can have multiple distinct meanings depending on context. Consequently, the development of multi-sense word embeddings, which aim to capture these different meanings in separate vector representations, has become a central area of research. While various techniques have been proposed, many either rely on pre-defined sense inventories (e.g., WordNet-based approaches) or struggle to effectively integrate both monolingual and bilingual information. Bilingual word embeddings, those learned from parallel corpora, offer a promising avenue for capturing cross-lingual semantic similarity, but can also be leveraged to improve the representation of polysemous words in a single language. Current methods often treat monolingual and bilingual learning as separate processes, failing to exploit the synergistic potential of combining both sources of information. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel approach to learning multi-sense word embeddings that leverages both monolingual and bilingual data in a unified framework. Our model employs a discrete autoencoder architecture, allowing it to learn a latent sense representation for each word based on its surrounding context in both the target and source languages. Specifically, we structure our model around an encoder-decoder framework where the encoder contextualizes a given word using both monolingual and bilingual context (i.e. a parallel sentence), and then chooses a discrete sense representation. The decoder then uses the chosen sense to predict the surrounding context words. Crucially, we jointly estimate both the encoder and decoder, allowing the model to learn a coherent mapping between context, sense, and prediction. We hypothesize that by forcing the model to reconcile semantic differences across languages, it will develop more robust and nuanced multi-sense representations, even in the absence of direct cross-lingual supervision. Our experimental results demonstrate that the word representations induced from bilingual data consistently outperform those derived from monolingual corpora across a wide range of evaluation tasks, highlighting the effectiveness of our approach in capturing and leveraging cross-lingual semantic information. This paper makes the following contributions: (1) A novel framework for jointly learning multi-sense word embeddings from both monolingual and bilingual data using a discrete autoencoder architecture.

Linguistic alignment – the tendency for individuals to converge on linguistic features during conversation – has long been considered a cornerstone of social interaction. It’s believed to facilitate rapport, foster understanding, and signal affiliation (Giles et al., 1991;Levenson, 1983). A frequently cited line of research suggests that social power dynamics influence this alignment process, with the hypothesis that individuals of higher power exert greater influence on their interlocutors, thereby receiving more linguistic alignment (e.g., Holmes, 1991;Yan & Miller, 2001). This perspective posits that those with greater social standing are more likely to be imitated, adopted, and generally mirrored in their language use by those of lower standing. Consequently, power imbalances are believed to manifest linguistically, with the higher-status individual experiencing a greater degree of convergence from their conversational partner. While intuitively appealing and supported by numerous studies, this perspective may overemphasize the role of social power in shaping alignment patterns and overlooks potentially more salient linguistic factors. A critical oversight in many of these investigations is the systematic consideration of low-level linguistic features—such as utterance length, lexical choice, and syntactic complexity—which independently affect alignment without necessarily being driven by social power dynamics. Previous work has largely treated power as an independent variable, often without fully accounting for the potential confounding influence of these more basic linguistic properties. This creates a risk of attributing alignment patterns to social power when, in reality, they are primarily driven by more readily observable linguistic characteristics. In this work, we challenge the prevailing assumption that social power is a primary driver of linguistic alignment. We investigate the relationship between power and alignment in two distinct datasets, meticulously controlling for a range of low-level linguistic features. Using logistic regression models, we systematically decompose the effect of power, revealing that its influence diminishes significantly, or even reverses, once these features are incorporated into the analysis. Our findings strongly suggest that alignment is more accurately explained by these fundamental linguistic properties than by social power considerations. We argue that future research on observational data investigating social factors in language use must broaden the scope of factors considered, specifically incorporating cognitive processes and more detailed linguistic analyses to avoid spurious correlations and provide a more nuanced understanding of alignment phenomena. By highlighting the overlooked importance of low-level features, we aim to stimulate a re-evaluation of the role of social power in shaping the intricacies of human conversation.

The accurate identification of predicate-argument structures—dependencies between verbs and their associated nouns—is a cornerstone of many natural language understanding tasks. These tasks range from complex information extraction pipelines to sophisticated question answering systems, where correctly parsing the relationships between words is crucial for extracting meaning. While many dependency parsing approaches focus on recovering local, “bounded” dependencies, a substantial portion of the semantic relationships within natural language often manifest as “unbounded” dependencies – non-adjacent words linked by intervening material. Failing to accurately recover these unbounded dependencies can severely compromise the overall performance of downstream NLP systems, leading to incomplete or inaccurate interpretations. Existing approaches to unbounded dependency recovery have shown promise, but often grapple with challenges relating to computational complexity, grammar expressiveness, and the ability to generalize across diverse linguistic constructions. This paper introduces a novel approach to accurate unbounded dependency recovery, leveraging the principles of Generalized Categorial Grammars (GCG). Categorial grammars (CG) offer a compelling alternative to traditional phrase-structure grammars by directly encoding syntactic categories as functions that combine words into larger phrases. This functional approach, unlike the layered structure of phrase-structure grammars, provides a more direct mapping between syntactic structure and semantic composition. A key advantage of CG is its inherent simplicity and uniformity—a small, fixed set of semantic composition operations (functors and arguments) are applied across the entire grammar, making it readily learnable from data. However, traditional CGs can struggle with enforcing grammatical constraints such as agreement or case marking. To address this limitation, we adopt a generalized approach, drawing inspiration from Head-driven Phrase Structure Grammar (HPSG) and its strategy of limiting the number of categories used to only those necessary for enforcing grammatical constraints. This combination yields a framework that retains the elegance and learnability of CG while gaining the expressive power needed to capture a wide range of grammatical phenomena. Furthermore, we present a novel reannotation system designed to efficiently transform existing syntactic resources, such as the Penn Treebank, into our GCG representation. This addresses a crucial practical concern—the scarcity of directly annotated data in this particular formalism. By leveraging established resources, we enable a broader applicability and faster development cycle for our system. Finally, we rigorously evaluate our proposed grammar and reannotation system on a standard unbounded dependency recovery task (as established by Rimell et al., 2009; Nivre et al., 2010), demonstrating its effectiveness and competitiveness against existing state-of-the-art approaches.

The explosion of digital text data presents an unprecedented opportunity to systematically extract structured knowledge from the web. Traditional Information Extraction (IE) systems rely on hand-crafted rules and pre-defined relation schemas, limiting their scalability and applicability to new domains. Open Information Extraction (Open IE) emerged as a promising paradigm to address these limitations, aiming to automatically extract assertions from text without requiring a fixed vocabulary of relations (Banko et al., 2006; Surdeanu et al., 2010). Instead of predicting a pre-defined relation type, Open IE systems identify potential relationships expressed by verbs and extract the corresponding entities, resulting in triples of the form (entity1, relation, entity2). While Open IE offers significant advantages in terms of flexibility and scalability, existing approaches often struggle to produce high-quality extractions. Current state-of-the-art systems frequently generate a large number of noisy and incoherent assertions, making it difficult to leverage the extracted knowledge effectively. These issues stem from the lack of constraints guiding the extraction process, leading to the inclusion of trivial or meaningless relationships. For instance, a system might extract triples like (Paris, is-located-in, France) or (John, speaks, English), which, while technically correct, offer little new or valuable information. Furthermore, many extractions lack coherence due to poor handling of syntactic structure and semantic context, resulting in nonsensical connections between entities. Addressing these challenges is crucial for realizing the full potential of Open IE and enabling downstream applications such as knowledge base construction, question answering, and text summarization. This paper introduces REVERB, a novel Open IE system designed to mitigate these issues by incorporating simple yet effective syntactic and lexical constraints on binary relations. We argue that by leveraging readily available linguistic information, we can significantly improve the quality of extracted assertions, leading to a more coherent and informative knowledge representation. Specifically, we focus on constraints related to the syntactic roles of the entities involved in the relation and the lexical properties of the verb mediating the relationship. Our experiments demonstrate that REVERB substantially outperforms previous Open IE systems, achieving a more than two-fold improvement in the area under the precision-recall curve relative to systems like TEXTRUNNER and WOE pos. Moreover, a significant portion (over 30%) of REVERB's extractions achieve a precision of 0.8 or higher, a level rarely attained by earlier approaches. Finally, we conduct a detailed error analysis to identify the remaining limitations of REVERB and outline promising avenues for future research in Open IE.       References   Banko, P., Surdeanu, M. A., Collins, M., & Marcus, S. (2006).

The burgeoning field of natural language processing has seen remarkable advances fueled by the rise of neural word embeddings. Techniques like Skip-grams (Mikolov et al., 2013) and GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014) have demonstrated the power of representing words as dense, low-dimensional vectors, capturing semantic and syntactic relationships that underpin language understanding. These embeddings have become a cornerstone of numerous NLP tasks, from sentiment analysis and machine translation to question answering and beyond. However, a common limitation of these established methods lies in their fixed dimensionality. Once an embedding vector is trained to a specific size (e.g., 300 dimensions), it's difficult to adapt it to different use cases that might require varying embedding sizes without retraining the entire model from scratch. Applications like transfer learning, resource-constrained environments, and dynamic adaptation of embedding granularity pose particular challenges to this rigidity. Existing solutions often involve significant computational cost, requiring either retraining or sophisticated interpolation techniques that may not fully capture the underlying semantic information. This paper addresses this critical limitation by proposing a novel and efficient incremental learning strategy for neural word embedding methods. Our approach, termed Right-truncatable Neural Word Embeddings, leverages an iterative dimensionality growth process. Specifically, we train embedding vectors one dimension at a time, progressively building up the complete vector representation. This seemingly simple modification yields an unexpected and highly valuable characteristic: any right-truncated version of the fully trained embedding vector precisely corresponds to the optimal solution of the corresponding lower-dimensional embedding. This means a single, large embedding vector can effectively serve as a repository of increasingly granular representations, catering to a diverse range of dimensionality requirements without retraining. The implications are far-reaching, allowing for seamless adaptation to different task demands, reduced computational overhead for transfer learning scenarios, and the ability to dynamically adjust the embedding granularity based on resource availability. We rigorously demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through experiments, showcasing its ability to generate right-truncatable embeddings that maintain high-quality representations across various dimensionality levels and outperform traditional methods in downstream tasks where varying embedding sizes are beneficial. Our method provides a practical and theoretically sound solution for managing the ever-evolving demands for word embeddings in modern NLP applications. Num. of words: 464. Cross-lingual lexical substitution – the task of replacing words in one language with equivalent words in another – is a crucial step in many natural language processing applications, including machine translation, cross-lingual summarization, and multilingual information retrieval. While numerous approaches have been proposed, many rely on distributional similarity or translation probabilities without explicitly considering semantic nuances like word sense and sentiment. The challenge lies in identifying substitutions that not only preserve meaning but also maintain the contextual tone, particularly when dealing with words possessing both subjective and objective senses. For instance, the English word "interesting" can denote genuine curiosity (subjective) or merely factual relevance (objective). A naive substitution based purely on semantic similarity might fail to capture this crucial distinction, potentially altering the intended sentiment of the original text. The assumption that sentiment transfer is a key indicator of a successful substitution forms the basis of our work. We posit that a good cross-lingual lexical substitution should preserve, or at least not distort, the word’s inherent subjectivity in its context. A word’s subjectivity, in this context, refers to its tendency to express, or elicit, an emotional or personal viewpoint. Words with strong subjective connotations tend to carry sentiment, whereas those with objective connotations are more neutral. Intuitively, replacing “amazing” with an equivalent that lacks a similar degree of positive sentiment would likely result in a less faithful translation, particularly when the original text’s overall sentiment is important. Recognizing this, we investigate the relationship between word sense subjectivity and the quality of cross-lingual lexical substitutions. Prior research in cross-lingual lexical substitution predominantly focuses on distributional semantics and translation probabilities (Vilain et al., 2005;Mikolov et al., 2013). These methods excel at identifying words with similar contextual usage patterns but often neglect the crucial aspect of sentiment preservation. While leveraging Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) has shown promise in other NLP tasks (Tej et al., 2011), integrating fine-grained WSD into cross-lingual lexical substitution can be computationally expensive and require large amounts of labeled data – a significant bottleneck in many language pairs. Our research aims to explore a more lightweight approach that captures the essential aspects of sentiment transfer without relying on complex WSD systems. Specifically, we propose leveraging word sense subjectivity – a coarser-grained measure than full WSD – to guide the substitution process. By focusing on whether a word tends to be subjective or objective, rather than pinpointing its exact sense, we aim to achieve a pragmatic balance between accuracy and efficiency.

Domain adaptation has emerged as a critical challenge in statistical machine translation (SMT), particularly as the demand for specialized translation systems grows. Training robust SMT models typically requires vast amounts of parallel data, a resource that is often scarce for specific domains like legal, medical, or technical texts. While various domain adaptation techniques exist, many involve complex model modifications or require substantial amounts of labeled in-domain data, which is frequently unavailable. This paper investigates a simpler, yet effective, approach to domain adaptation: the strategic selection of relevant sentences from a large, general-domain parallel corpus to create what we term "pseudo in-domain subcorpora." The core idea is that a small, carefully curated subset of a general corpus can offer significantly more benefit than the entire corpus when adapted to a target domain. The traditional assumption in SMT is that more data invariably leads to better performance. However, as demonstrated by Cherry et al. (2012) and others, including irrelevant or noisy data can actually degrade translation quality. Our work directly addresses this issue by focusing on identifying and extracting only those samples from a general-domain corpus that possess characteristics most similar to the target domain. We hypothesize that by prioritizing domain-relevant data, we can achieve comparable or even superior translation performance with substantially reduced training data. To explore this hypothesis, we present three straightforward data selection methods based on cross-entropy, a common and efficient metric for evaluating the likelihood of a sentence given a language model. These methods, while conceptually simple, demonstrate surprising effectiveness in identifying pseudo in-domain data. Once selected, these pseudo in-domain subcorpora, often comprising as little as 1% of the original general-domain corpus, are used to train small, domain-adapted SMT models. Remarkably, these models consistently outperform systems trained on the entire, much larger, general-domain corpus. Furthermore, we demonstrate that combining these domain-adapted models with a baseline, general-domain model during decoding yields even greater improvements, highlighting the synergistic benefit of integrating both domain-specific and general knowledge. Our findings challenge the conventional wisdom that "more data is always better" and underscore the importance of data selection strategies tailored to the domain adaptation problem. This work contributes a practical and efficient approach to domain adaptation for SMT that minimizes the need for large amounts of labeled in-domain data. --- References Cherry, M., Micallef, A., Pulido, R., & Lengarica, I. In natural language processing, identifying entities and their spans within text is a fundamental task with applications ranging from information extraction to question answering. Traditional entity recognition approaches often treat mentions as non-overlapping, failing to account for the common phenomenon where entity mentions can contain other mentions recursively – a concept known as nested mentions (e.g., “the CEO of Microsoft” contains “Microsoft”). Recognizing these nested structures is crucial for accurate entity linking, relation extraction, and downstream reasoning tasks. Existing approaches to nested mention recognition often suffer from scalability issues or rely on complex parsing techniques that struggle to handle variability in natural language. This paper addresses these limitations by introducing a novel, scalable, and transition-based neural model specifically designed for nested mention recognition. Our approach leverages the efficiency of transition-based parsing frameworks while incorporating powerful neural representations to capture both the syntactic and semantic nuances of nested mentions. The core of our method lies in a bottom-up construction of a designated "forest" structure. We first map each sentence containing nested mentions into a forest representation, where each mention corresponds to a distinct constituent within the forest. This allows us to represent the hierarchical relationships between nested mentions in a structured manner. Building upon this forest representation, we employ a shift-reduce parsing system, a well-established technique in computational linguistics, to learn the forest structure through a sequence of actions. Critically, we guarantee an upper bound on the maximal length of the action sequence to ensure computational efficiency, restricting it to three times the length of the input sentence. To effectively model the system’s state and guide the transition-based parsing process, we utilize a Stack-LSTM architecture. This allows our model to efficiently and effectively represent the states of the parser in a continuous vector space. Furthermore, we enhance our model with a character-based component, enabling it to capture fine-grained letter-level patterns often indicative of mention boundaries and nested structures. This combination of syntactic transition-based parsing, semantic Stack-LSTM representations, and lexical character-level features provides a robust and scalable framework for nested mention recognition. We evaluate our model on the widely used ACE datasets, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance and highlighting the effectiveness of our proposed approach in accurately detecting and classifying nested mentions. Our results showcase a significant advancement in effectively modeling and recognizing the complex nested structures present in natural language text. . . .

The field of statistical machine translation (SMT) has long relied on carefully engineered features to capture linguistic and domain-specific information. Traditionally, feature engineering for SMT models, particularly phrase-based systems, has been a labor-intensive process that requires considerable intuition, linguistic expertise, and detailed domain knowledge (Koehn et al., 2003). While these handcrafted features have proven effective, their design is often constrained by the limitations of human understanding and can be difficult to generalize across different language pairs or domains. Recently, there has been growing interest in leveraging unsupervised and semi-supervised learning techniques to automatically discover relevant features for SMT. Deep learning models, in particular, offer a powerful means to learn hierarchical representations from raw data, potentially uncovering latent patterns that would be difficult to identify manually. Deep Belief Networks (DBNs), a type of generative deep neural network, have gained traction as feature extractors for SMT, demonstrating the ability to capture complex dependencies between input phrases (Huang et al., 2010;Chen et al., 2011). However, DBN features tend to be relatively unstable and may not always generalize well to unseen data. This motivates us to explore alternative deep learning architectures and training methodologies that can lead to more robust and effective feature representations. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to learning new features for phrase-based SMT models using a semi-supervised deep auto-encoder (DAE) paradigm. Unlike traditional feature engineering, our method aims to automatically discover relevant features from the training data, leveraging the power of deep learning to capture subtle relationships between phrases. Our approach builds on previous work with DBNs but introduces several key innovations: We initialize the DAE's parameters using a pre-trained DBN, benefiting from the DBN's ability to capture general-purpose features. We employ a semi-supervised fine-tuning strategy, where the original phrase features serve as a “teacher” to guide the DAE’s learning process. This allows the DAE to refine its representations while maintaining consistency with existing features. Furthermore, to learn high-dimensional feature representations suitable for complex SMT models, we introduce a novel horizontal composition of multiple DAEs to construct large hidden layer feature representations. By combining these techniques, we aim to learn semi-supervised DAE features that are both effective and stable, outperforming traditional unsupervised DBN features and handcrafted baseline features. We evaluate our approach on two Chinese-English translation tasks, demonstrating statistically significant improvements in BLEU score over both the unsupervised DBN features and the baseline features.

The task of generating coherent and engaging responses in conversational AI has garnered significant attention in recent years. Traditional approaches to neural response generation often rely on sequence-to-sequence (Seq2Seq) models (Sutskever et al., 2014; Cho et al., 2014) trained to map input contexts to appropriate responses. However, these models frequently suffer from a crucial drawback: the generation of "safe" or non-informative responses, such as generic greetings or acknowledgments (Li et al., 2016). Such responses, while grammatically correct, fail to contribute meaningfully to the conversation and lead to a frustrating user experience. This issue arises from the training objective, which primarily focuses on maximizing the likelihood of the target response, neglecting the crucial aspect of generating diverse and engaging text. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach to neural response generation leveraging the power of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) (Goodfellow et al., 2014). GANs have demonstrated remarkable success in various generation tasks, including image synthesis and text generation, by framing the process as a two-player game between a generator and a discriminator. In our setting, the generator is a Seq2Seq network responsible for generating responses, while the discriminator aims to distinguish between human-produced responses and those generated by the network. This adversarial training setup incentivizes the generator to produce responses that are indistinguishable from human-generated ones, effectively mitigating the problem of non-informative responses. However, a significant obstacle in training a GAN with a Seq2Seq generator lies in the non-differentiability of the output decoding procedure. Seq2Seq models typically employ sampling-based decoding methods, such as beam search, which are inherently discrete and not amenable to gradient-based optimization. To circumvent this limitation, we introduce an  approximate embedding layer  that transforms the discrete output tokens into a continuous vector space, enabling the GAN framework to be effectively trained. This approximation allows for gradient flow through the discrete decoding process, facilitating the optimization of the generator. The benefits of this approach are twofold. First, the GAN framework encourages more diverse and engaging responses, moving beyond the “safe” outputs prevalent in standard Seq2Seq models. Second, the approximate embedding layer resolves a key technical challenge and enables the seamless integration of GANs with Seq2Seq architectures for response generation. We validate our approach on both Mandarin and English datasets, demonstrating significant improvements in response diversity compared to existing neural response generation models, with palatable gains in relevance as well.

The automatic induction of dependency grammars has emerged as a critical area within computational linguistics, offering a pathway towards parsing languages for which annotated resources are scarce or non-existent. Traditional approaches to dependency grammar induction grapple with either exploiting bilingual resources via projection methods or relying solely on unsupervised learning techniques to uncover syntactic structure from monolingual data. Projection-based methods, while leveraging readily available parsed corpora in related languages, often struggle to accurately represent the intricacies of the target language’s grammar, particularly when linguistic structures diverge significantly between languages. Conversely, unsupervised induction methods, though capable of capturing language-specific patterns, frequently fall short due to the inherent ambiguity and complexity of natural language syntax without any external guidance. Recent advances in neural machine translation and cross-lingual transfer learning have fueled interest in leveraging readily available bilingual resources to enhance monolingual tasks. However, the application of such techniques to dependency grammar induction remains relatively unexplored. This work addresses this gap by presenting a novel strategy for automatic induction of monolingual dependency grammars, elegantly integrating the strengths of both bilingual projection and unsupervised induction. Our core idea is to "moderately" leverage dependency information projected from a parsed counterpart language, while simultaneously mining the underlying syntactic structure of the target language. This hybrid approach aims to overcome the limitations of existing methods by providing valuable structural constraints derived from bilingual alignments, whilst retaining the ability to adapt to language-specific peculiarities through unsupervised learning. We argue that a balanced combination of both approaches leads to a more robust and accurate monolingual dependency grammar compared to methods solely relying on bilingual projection or unsupervised induction. To validate our approach, we induced dependency grammars for five diverse languages—German, French, Spanish, Italian, and Chinese—all guided by dependency information projected from their respective English translations. Empirical evaluation demonstrates the significant benefits of our bilingually-guided method, achieving an average improvement of 28.5% over an unsupervised baseline and 3.0% over the best existing projection baseline. These results confirm the potential of our strategy to substantially advance the state-of-the-art in monolingual dependency grammar induction, particularly for resource-poor languages. The remainder of this paper details our methodology, presents the experimental setup and results, and concludes with a discussion of future directions and potential applications.
