The burgeoning field of human-computer conversation systems has garnered significant attention in recent years, driven by advancements in natural language processing and deep learning. Amongst the various approaches to building these conversational agents, generative models based on the sequence-to-sequence (Seq2Seq) framework, implemented using neural networks, have emerged as a dominant paradigm. These models, trained to map input sequences (user questions or statements) to output sequences (system responses), offer a promising avenue for creating engaging and adaptive dialogue partners. However, despite their successes, standard Seq2Seq models frequently struggle to generate responses that exhibit sufficient depth and informativeness. A common pitfall is the tendency to produce trivial or generic replies – a phenomenon that significantly detracts from the overall conversational quality and perceived intelligence of the system. This issue highlights a crucial need for methods that equip generative conversation models with the ability to incorporate external knowledge and context, enabling them to craft more meaningful and insightful responses. The current research landscape largely focuses on explicit knowledge injection techniques, such as retrieving knowledge from external databases or incorporating pre-defined knowledge graphs. While these methods have shown promise, they often introduce complexities related to knowledge management, retrieval efficiency, and integration into the decoding process. This paper takes a different approach, exploring a more flexible and implicit method for content introduction into generative short-text conversation systems. Our core insight is that responses often benefit from subtle cues or hints – “auxiliary information” – that guide the generation towards more relevant and informative content. Rather than explicitly providing this information, we aim to equip the model with the ability to implicitly leverage it during the decoding process. To achieve this, we propose a novel implicit content-introducing method, which seamlessly incorporates additional information into the Seq2Seq framework. The key innovation lies in our proposed hierarchical gated fusion unit, designed to intelligently fuse both the general decoding process and auxiliary cue word information. This architecture allows the model to selectively incorporate relevant external signals without overwhelming the primary generation task. We evaluate our approach on real-life conversational data, demonstrating its effectiveness through a comprehensive analysis of both automatic metrics (BLEU scores) and human evaluation. Our results consistently demonstrate that our model outperforms a range of competitive baseline models, underscoring the potential of implicit content introduction for improving the quality and informativeness of generative short-text conversation systems. . 200 words. 375 words 417 words. 418 words.

The ability to infer relationships between verbs—to determine, for example, whether "bake" entails "heat"—is a cornerstone of robust semantic understanding. Such inference capabilities are vital for a wide range of natural language processing (NLP) applications, including question answering, textual entailment recognition, and commonsense reasoning. While significant progress has been made in recent years, much of the existing research on learning verb inference rules has relied on relatively limited sources of information. Traditionally, methods have focused heavily on distributional similarity – the assumption that verbs appearing in similar contexts are semantically related – and, to a lesser extent, on manually constructed verb co-occurrence patterns. However, we argue that these approaches are insufficient to capture the full complexity of verb semantics and the nuanced relationships that govern verb inference. The inherent limitations of reliance on distributional similarity alone are well-documented. While it can capture some aspects of semantic relatedness, distributional information can be easily misled by spurious correlations and fail to detect subtle inference relations. Furthermore, many manually created knowledge bases are expensive to maintain and may not be fully comprehensive. To address these shortcomings, this paper proposes a fundamentally different approach to learning verb inference rules, grounded in a belief that a richer, more multifaceted view of linguistic evidence is essential. We contend that effective verb inference requires leveraging information from multiple textual scopes: immediate verb co-occurrence within a single sentence, broader co-occurrence patterns across an entire document, and general corpus-level statistics about verb usage. Our work introduces a novel framework that incorporates a much broader and linguistically motivated set of cues for detecting entailment relationships between verbs. Instead of relying solely on distributional overlap, our framework integrates features capturing syntactic dependency relations, semantic roles, verb subcategorization frames, and discourse context. We then combine these diverse cues within a supervised classification model, allowing us to learn the complex interplay between various linguistic signals. Through rigorous empirical evaluation, we demonstrate that our model significantly surpasses the performance of previous methods. Moreover, our analyses reveal that information from each of the textual scopes – sentence level, document level, and corpus level – contributes uniquely and meaningfully to the verb entailment learning task, validating our hypothesis that a more comprehensive approach is crucial for achieving state-of-the-art results. We believe this work represents a significant step forward in enabling more accurate and robust verb inference, ultimately paving the way for more sophisticated NLP systems.

Visual question answering (VQA) represents a significant advancement in the field of artificial intelligence, requiring a system to not only "see" and understand an image but also to reason about it in response to a natural language question. The task elegantly combines computer vision and natural language processing, demanding a sophisticated level of cognitive ability. While VQA has garnered substantial research attention, particularly within the English language domain, a critical gap remains in the availability of datasets for other languages. Simply translating existing English annotations is often insufficient, as nuanced cultural and linguistic differences can significantly impact the interpretation of images and questions. This dearth of multilingual VQA resources severely limits the development of truly global VQA systems capable of serving diverse user populations. To address this limitation, we present a novel contribution: a Japanese VQA dataset constructed through extensive crowdsourced annotation leveraging images sourced from the publicly available Visual Genome dataset. This marks the first publicly available VQA dataset specifically designed for the Japanese language, providing a valuable resource for the research community. Beyond dataset creation, our work explores the potential of cross-lingual transfer learning to enhance VQA performance in resource-scarce languages. Specifically, we investigate how knowledge gained from English VQA can be effectively transferred to improve a Japanese VQA system. Our approach centers around a popular VQA architecture employing attention mechanisms, a technique widely recognized for its ability to highlight regions of an image relevant to the given question. We hypothesize that attention maps generated from English questions can offer valuable insights into image regions to focus on, which can then inform the Japanese VQA model, even when the language itself differs significantly. Our experimental results demonstrate that leveraging English attention maps significantly outperforms training a Japanese VQA system solely on a monolingual corpus, effectively validating the utility of attention maps as a mechanism for cross-lingual knowledge transfer in VQA. This work paves the way for more efficient and effective development of VQA systems for a wider range of languages, ultimately moving closer to truly universal image understanding capabilities. Additionally, this research has implications for low-resource NLP more broadly, showcasing a practical method for benefiting from pre-existing, high-resource datasets in related tasks. The success of our approach suggests that attention mechanisms, with their inherent ability to capture relevant contextual information, hold promise as a powerful tool for cross-lingual transfer in various NLP applications.

The development and evaluation of computational models of language acquisition are inherently tied to the quality and quantity of input data. While many studies have focused on refining model architectures and incorporating sophisticated linguistic features, the foundational role of input size often receives less attention. A crucial question remains: how does the amount of training data influence the performance of word segmentation models, particularly those embodying different linguistic assumptions? Addressing this question presents a significant challenge, as existing corpora commonly used for word segmentation research are often not designed to isolate the effect of input size. They frequently consist of fixed-size samples or aggregated data, making it difficult to systematically vary the amount of input presented to a model. To overcome this limitation, this paper investigates the impact of input size on the performance of Bayesian word segmentation models using a novel corpus derived from the Providence Corpus (Demuth et al., 2006). The Providence Corpus, a rich source of longitudinal child language data, provides the ideal foundation for our study. We construct a dataset comprising longitudinal data from six children, allowing us to explore not only the effect of overall input size, but also intra-language variability and potential changes in model performance over time, thereby opening avenues for asking more nuanced questions about computational models of word segmentation. Our findings reveal a surprising and important result: input size can have dramatic and often counterintuitive effects on segmentation performance. Models that perform exceptionally well on smaller datasets can exhibit a marked decrease in accuracy when exposed to significantly larger amounts of data. This observation challenges the common assumption that increased input invariably leads to improved model performance, and highlights the importance of carefully considering the relationship between input size and model generalization. The dataset and our analysis contribute new insights into the complexities of computational language acquisition and provide a valuable resource for researchers in the field. By presenting a detailed examination of the effect of input size, we aim to encourage a more critical and data-driven approach to the development and evaluation of word segmentation models. The burgeoning field of web search has long recognized that users often formulate queries that are suboptimal – containing typos, ambiguous terms, or simply failing to convey the intended meaning effectively. Query alteration, the process of automatically suggesting and applying modifications to user queries to improve search results, has become a crucial component of modern search engines. While extensive research has been dedicated to query alteration in languages like English, the challenges in other languages remain relatively underexplored. Japanese, with its complex orthography and reliance on nuanced semantic context, presents a particularly difficult environment for query alteration. Existing approaches often rely on character-level similarity metrics, such as edit distance, or rely on specific character types (e.g., kana vs. kanji), limiting their effectiveness and generality. This paper addresses these shortcomings by proposing a unified approach to Japanese query alteration that transcends the limitations of character-based similarity and focuses instead on semantic relatedness. Our work builds upon established methods for query alteration in English (e.g., Steinberger et al., 2012), which leverage the power of machine learning to identify and apply query transformations. However, we recognize that a direct translation of these techniques to Japanese is insufficient due to the significant differences in the linguistic structure and character repertoire. The key innovation of our approach lies in its ability to consider orthographically dissimilar query-candidate pairs, expanding the search space beyond those traditionally considered. Further, we introduce a novel method for quantifying the semantic similarity between queries and their candidate alterations, addressing the significant data sparseness issues that plague many lexical semantic similarity approaches. To achieve this, we employ kernel-based lexical semantic similarity, a technique that implicitly captures higher-order relationships between words, mitigating the impact of unseen word combinations. Crucially, a practical query alteration system require efficient mechanisms for generating candidate alterations. We propose a streamlined and effective method for creating both training and testing data consisting of query-candidate pairs, balancing the need for comprehensive coverage with computational feasibility. Our approach also incorporates mechanisms to handle variations in query format, such as the inclusion of particles or honorifics, which are characteristic of Japanese. We evaluate our method on a substantial Japanese query log dataset, demonstrating that it achieves an impressive accuracy of approximately 80% on the query alteration task. This represents a significant improvement over previous methods that solely relied on semantic similarity, highlighting the efficacy of our unified approach and its ability to effectively leverage both orthographic and semantic cues for Japanese query alteration.

Data-to-text generation, the task of automatically creating natural language descriptions from structured data records, has become an increasingly important area of research within Natural Language Generation (NLG). Modern neural approaches, particularly those leveraging attention mechanisms and copy mechanisms within encoder-decoder architectures, have demonstrated remarkable progress in generating fluent and human-like text from databases. These models, building on foundational work by (Rush et al., 2015; See et al., 2017), have achieved state-of-the-art results on several benchmark datasets. However, a persistent challenge remains: ensuring the  factual precision  of the generated text. While fluency and grammatical correctness have improved significantly, these models frequently insert incorrect or irrelevant data elements into the generated descriptions, a phenomenon that undermines the utility of the generated text, particularly in domains where accuracy is paramount. This issue is prominently observed on more complex datasets, such as ROTOWIRE, which demands more intricate reasoning and data selection during the generation process. The core challenge lies in the inherent difficulty of the copy mechanism, which typically makes decisions about which data to copy at each decoding step. This early commitment can lead to errors if the model misinterprets the context or the relationship between the data and the intended meaning. Previous approaches have attempted to mitigate this by incorporating smoothing techniques or adjusting the copy weights, but these often fail to address the root cause of the problem: a lack of holistic consideration of the available data and the evolving context of the generated text. To address this crucial limitation, we propose a novel two-stage approach incorporating a  delayed copy mechanism  specifically designed to enhance data precision in data-to-text generation. Our approach separates the generation task into two distinct phases: template generation and data slot filling. First, an encoder-decoder model generates a template text containing placeholders or slots that represent the data to be inserted. This template guides the subsequent data selection process. Second, a dedicated delayed copy mechanism is employed to precisely fill these slots with the most appropriate data records from the input database. This mechanism distinguishes itself through a series of innovative features including double attention, position-aware attention, and a novel pairwise ranking loss function. By delaying the copy decision until the template is complete, our approach allows for a more comprehensive assessment of the input data and the evolving semantic context within the generated text. The two stages are trained independently, allowing for specialized optimization of each component.

Aspect-level sentiment classification (ALSC) is a fine-grained sentiment analysis task that aims to predict the sentiment polarity towards specific aspects of a product or service (Li et al., 2015). Unlike traditional sentiment classification, which focuses on the overall sentiment of a sentence or document, ALSC requires identifying the sentiment expressed towards each aspect mentioned. For example, in the sentence “The camera is great, but the battery life is terrible,” ALSC would classify the sentiment towards “camera” as positive and the sentiment towards “battery life” as negative. With the advance of deep learning, various approaches have been developed for ALSC. Many existing methods leverage attention mechanisms to capture the relevant information between the aspect and the context. These approaches often utilize a single, coarse-grained attention mechanism to weigh the importance of different parts of the context when predicting the sentiment towards a given aspect. However, this approach may result in information loss, particularly when the aspect consists of multiple words or requires a larger contextual window for accurate sentiment determination. Consider an aspect like “screen resolution,” which is more effectively understood with context than a single-word aspect. Previous works fail to account for aspects that span several words or require a wider contextual range for determining sentiment. To address this limitation, we propose a novel Multi-Grained Attention Network (MGAN) for ALSC. Our MGAN model incorporates both fine-grained and coarse-grained attention mechanisms to capture aspect-context interactions at different levels of granularity. The fine-grained attention mechanism focuses on word-level interactions, enabling the model to identify the most relevant words in the context for each aspect word. The coarse-grained attention mechanism, in contrast, considers the entire context as a whole, allowing the model to capture broader contextual cues. By combining these two attention mechanisms, MGAN can effectively capture both local and global aspect-context relationships. Furthermore, we introduce a novel aspect alignment loss to explicitly model the semantic relationships between aspects sharing the same context. Unlike previous approaches that treat each aspect independently, our aspect alignment loss encourages the model to learn consistent representations for aspects with similar contexts, thereby improving the overall ALSC performance. We evaluate the proposed MGAN model on three benchmark datasets: laptop and restaurant reviews from SemEval 2014 and a Twitter dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that MGAN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art ALSC methods on all three datasets. We also conduct ablation studies to evaluate the effectiveness of the aspect alignment loss, showing that it further improves performance by capturing valuable aspect-level interactions.

The ability to effectively communicate instructions—both generating clear, concise directions and accurately interpreting them—is a cornerstone of human interaction. Recent advancements in natural language processing have yielded impressive progress in machine translation, text generation, and question answering. However, a significant challenge remains in enabling machines to truly understand and utilize the  pragmatics  of language—the contextual factors and underlying intentions that shape communication. Existing approaches often treat instructions as literal sequences of words, failing to account for the unspoken assumptions, shared knowledge, and strategic goals that govern how humans convey and understand instructions, especially within complex, multi-step tasks. This limitation leads to generated instructions that are verbose, ambiguous, or even confusing, and to listener models that are brittle and easily misled by subtle variations in wording. In this paper, we address this gap by introducing unified pragmatic models for generating and following natural language instructions in sequential task settings. Our approach centers on the core idea that pragmatic reasoning – thinking about  why  a speaker chooses a particular instruction, and  how  a listener will interpret it – is essential for effective communication. Inspired by prior work in pragmatic inference (e.g., Goodman and Tenbrink, 2009; Krahmer and Pelletier, 2010), we build upon the established modular framework of speaker and listener models. Traditionally, pragmatic models employ "base" models representing basic linguistic competence. A pragmatic speaker leverages a base listener to simulate the interpretation of various candidate instruction formulations, selecting the one predicted to be most readily understood. Conversely, a pragmatic listener reasons counterfactually – considering how the current instruction would be affected by alternative descriptions. Crucially, our work extends this framework to handle the sequential nature of many real-world tasks, a feature largely overlooked in previous pragmatic modeling efforts. This allows our models to reason about the entire sequence of instructions rather than treating each instruction in isolation. We demonstrate that incorporating explicit pragmatic inference substantially improves both the generation and interpretation of instructions. Our experiments, conducted on diverse datasets involving complex, sequential tasks, show that our pragmatics-enabled listener models outperform state-of-the-art approaches in correctly interpreting human instructions – achieving significant gains in accuracy. Similarly, our pragmatic speaker models produce instructions that are not only more readily understood by humans but also lead to improved task completion rates and overall efficiency. The key contribution of this work is a pragmatic modeling framework that elegantly combines generation and interpretation, enabling a more holistic and sophisticated understanding of how language is used to convey complex instructions.

The burgeoning volume of online forum discussions represents a rich, untapped resource of knowledge and insight. Within these forums, questions posed by users are often followed by extensive discussions aimed at providing helpful answers and relevant context. Extracting these questions, their corresponding answers, and the surrounding context is a crucial task for knowledge discovery, question answering systems, and efficient forum navigation. However, this extraction process presents unique challenges due to the often informal, conversational, and non-hierarchical nature of forum posts. Existing approaches often struggle to effectively model the complex relationships within these discussions, leading to inaccurate extractions. This paper introduces a novel and unified approach to address this challenge, focusing on extracting both the question itself and the relevant context surrounding the answer from online forum threads. We propose customizing the Structural Support Vector Machine (SVM) method to tailor it specifically to the intricacies of forum discussions. Our approach moves beyond generic SVM applications by incorporating a comprehensive graphical representation of the thread structure, enabling a more nuanced understanding of the conversation flow. Furthermore, we develop specialized inference algorithms designed to handle the unique characteristics of forum data, bypassing the limitations of general-purpose inference techniques. Importantly, our model offers flexibility, allowing for adaptation to diverse task preferences through modifications to the loss function, thereby enabling fine-grained control over the extraction process. The value of this flexibility is particularly significant given the varying characteristics of different online forums and the potential for evolving extraction requirements. Empirical evaluation on a real-world dataset demonstrates the promising performance and adaptability of our proposed methods, highlighting their potential for practical application in a range of knowledge extraction scenarios. This work underscores the effectiveness of leveraging structured learning techniques, specifically within a customized SVM framework, to tackle the complexities of unstructured online forum data. Probabilistic Context-Free Grammars (PCFGs) have long been a cornerstone of statistical natural language processing, providing a powerful framework for modeling syntactic structure and enabling tasks like parsing and language modeling. Traditional PCFGs, however, operate under the assumption of full observability – that is, all variables are directly observed. In many real-world scenarios, this assumption doesn't hold. Latent-variable PCFGs, where some variables are hidden or unobserved, offer a more realistic model of language, accounting for phenomena like ungrammaticality, discourse structure, and variability in speaker behavior. However, learning these latent-variable PCFGs presents significant challenges. The standard Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm, frequently employed for learning in latent variable models, is not guaranteed to converge to a globally optimal solution in the context of PCFGs, particularly when dealing with the non-convex nature of the underlying likelihood function. Furthermore, ensuring the learnability and correctness of such a learning procedure remains a complex theoretical problem. This paper addresses these challenges by introducing a novel, provably correct learning algorithm specifically designed for latent-variable PCFGs. Our approach distinguishes itself through a two-stage strategy that incorporates both matrix decomposition and EM. The first stage leverages a matrix-decomposition algorithm applied to a co-occurrence matrix constructed from the available parse trees in the training data. This decomposition step aims to identify and extract latent structural patterns implicit within the observed data. By generating a constrained starting point, it mitigates some issues regarding local optima of EM. The second stage then employs standard EM applied to a carefully designed convex objective function derived jointly from the training samples and the output of the matrix decomposition. The convexity of this objective guarantees that the EM algorithm’s iterations monotonically improve the model parameters and will converge to a global optimum. This clever manipulation ensures both correctness and efficient learning. We demonstrate the practical effectiveness of our algorithm through empirical evaluation on both parsing and language modeling tasks. The results confirm that our approach is not only efficient but also achieves state-of-the-art performance, demonstrating a compelling balance between theoretical rigor and practical applicability. Importantly, the algorithm's provable correctness distinguishes it from previous methods and establishes a solid theoretical foundation for future research in latent-variable PCFG learning.     This introduction sets the stage and provides the necessary background to understand the paper's contribution. It highlights the problem, existing approaches, their limitations, and how this paper offers a unique and theoretically grounded solution.

The generation of natural language text from structured data is a long-standing goal in natural language processing, with applications ranging from report generation to data-to-text summarization. Traditional approaches often rely on rule-based systems or template-based methods, which while providing control over the generated text, are often brittle, require extensive manual engineering, and struggle to scale to complex domains. More recently, neural network approaches have shown promise in this area, offering greater flexibility and potential for automation. However, many existing neural text generation models face challenges when dealing with large vocabularies and complex structured inputs, particularly in domains like biography generation where the range of facts and entities can be vast. Generating coherent and informative biographical sentences requires not only fluent language but also the ability to effectively integrate specific facts from a structured knowledge base. In this paper, we address these challenges by introducing a novel neural model for concept-to-text generation that scales well to large, rich domains, specifically focusing on the biography domain. We introduce a new dataset of biographies extracted from Wikipedia, significantly larger than any publicly available resource for this task. This dataset comprises over 700,000 samples, featuring a rich vocabulary of approximately 400,000 words and diverse biographical facts. To tackle the inherent challenges of large vocabularies in neural language models, we extend existing conditional neural language models with a novel ‘copy mechanism’. This mechanism allows the model to selectively copy words directly from the input data, bypassing the need to generate them from the fixed vocabulary. Furthermore, recognizing that the meaning of a word can vary depending on the context and the specific data field it appears in, our model dynamically embeds words based on their field within the structured data. This provides the model with a richer representation of the input and allows it to generate more accurate and context-aware sentences. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our model through comprehensive experiments on the created biography dataset. Our results show that our neural model significantly outperforms a strong baseline—a Templated Kneser-Ney language model—achieving a near 15 BLEU point improvement. This substantial gain highlights the powerful capabilities of our approach for generating high-quality text from structured data in complex domains. The rest of this paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 reviews related work in data-to-text generation and neural language modeling. Section 3 details our model architecture, including the copy mechanism and field-specific embedding strategy.

Morphology, the study of word formation, is a fundamental aspect of natural language processing with broad implications for tasks like machine translation, information retrieval, and language modeling. Accurately modeling morphological patterns – the systematic relationships between a word’s lemma (base form) and its inflected forms – is crucial for achieving robust performance across these applications. Traditionally, morphological analysis has relied on rule-based systems or probabilistic models, both of which require substantial linguistic expertise and often struggle to generalize to unseen languages or irregular forms. Recent advances in machine learning have explored the potential of data-driven approaches to morphological analysis, offering a more flexible and adaptable solution. In particular, there's been a growing interest in leveraging supervised learning techniques to induce morphological paradigms – the complete set of inflected forms for a given word. A relatively recent and promising approach involves the identification and alignment of the longest common subsequence (LCS) within inflection tables. This non-probabilistic strategy aims to extract the core morphological pattern shared by a set of inflected forms, offering a simple yet surprisingly effective way to generalize across variations and irregularities. However, a key limitation of this approach in its initial formulation is its inability to reconstruct complete inflection tables for unseen words. Determining which inflections are relevant for a given lemma often requires a more sophisticated understanding of the language’s morphology than can be gleaned solely from LCS alignment. This paper builds upon the encouraging results of LCS-based paradigm learning by integrating it with a discriminative classifier. Our system combines the strengths of both approaches: the LCS alignment provides a computationally efficient means of identifying shared morphological patterns, while the classifier leverages labeled examples of inflection patterns (complete inflection tables) to learn the relationship between lemmas and their paradigms. This allows us to not only identify the core morphological pattern but also to predict the missing inflections, thereby enabling the reconstruction of complete inflection tables for unseen words. We present a framework that learns directly from labeled examples of inflection tables, effectively treating morphological paradigm induction as a supervised learning problem. We then evaluate our approach on a diverse set of 11 languages, demonstrating that it consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on the task of morphological paradigm reconstruction. Our results indicate that this combined approach offers a viable and efficient pathway to rapidly create high-accuracy morphological resources, potentially democratizing access to morphological analysis tools for less-resourced languages.

The remarkable success of recurrent neural networks (RNNs), particularly Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997), has revolutionized sequence modeling across numerous natural language processing tasks. LSTMs excel at capturing long-range dependencies within sequences, mitigating the vanishing gradient problem that plagues traditional RNN architectures. Consequently, they have become a mainstay in applications like machine translation, language modeling, and text generation. While LSTMs have proven remarkably effective, the vast majority of research has focused on the fundamental linear chain structure – treating sequential data as a one-dimensional chain of connected elements. However, natural language possesses a hierarchical and structured nature that directly contradicts this simplified model. Sentences are not merely linear sequences of words; they are organized into phrases, clauses, and ultimately, complex syntactic structures governed by grammatical rules. This hierarchical organization profoundly influences meaning and semantic interpretation. Ignoring this structure within the neural network architecture risks overlooking crucial contextual information and limiting the model's representational capacity. Existing sequence-modeling approaches largely disregard the inherent syntactic structure of sentences, resulting in representations that can fail to fully capture the nuanced semantic relationships between words and phrases. This limitation motivates the exploration of architectures that explicitly incorporate syntactic information. Recent advancements in neural network architectures have explored the incorporation of syntactic information, often through feature engineering or external parsing steps. However, these approaches often require separate parsing modules and introduce additional complexities. We propose a more integrated approach by directly modeling the syntactic structure within the neural network architecture itself. Specifically, we introduce the Tree-LSTM, a novel generalization of the LSTM framework to accommodate tree-structured network topologies. Instead of a linear chain, Tree-LSTMs process sentences according to their parse trees, allowing the network to capture hierarchical relationships between words and phrases in a more natural and efficient manner. This architecture allows for a more nuanced representation of sentence meaning by propagating information along the syntactic tree, incorporating both local and long-range dependencies. In this work, we demonstrate empirically that Tree-LSTMs surpass existing state-of-the-art models and strong LSTM baselines on two challenging and widely recognized benchmarks: predicting the semantic relatedness of two sentences (SemEval 2014, Task 1) and sentiment classification (Stanford Sentiment Treebank). Our results provide compelling evidence that incorporating syntactic structure into the LSTM framework significantly enhances semantic representation learning and improves performance on a variety of NLP tasks. References: Hochreiter, S., & Schmidhuber, J. (1997).

The notion of word difficulty has long been a central concern in fields ranging from applied linguistics and educational psychology to natural language processing. Computational estimations of this difficulty – often represented as a scalar value – are increasingly utilized in applications such as adaptive learning systems, automated assessment, and text simplification. However, the prevalent corpus-based approaches for estimating word difficulty often fall short, treating word knowledge as a monolithic entity rather than a dynamic, developmental process. These methods typically rely on measures such as word frequency, frequency of adjacent words, or the complexity of a word’s syntactic structure, ultimately yielding a static difficulty score that fails to capture the nuanced way individuals acquire and refine their understanding of words over time. This paper challenges the conventional paradigm of scalar word difficulty and introduces a new framework:  word meaning maturity . Word meaning maturity represents the degree of a learner’s understanding of a word at different stages of language acquisition. Unlike traditional difficulty metrics that provide a single, fixed value, maturity tracks the evolution of word knowledge, reflecting the gradual accumulation of semantic connections and contextual associations. We posit that a word’s "maturity" isn’t an inherent property but rather a function of the learner’s linguistic development; a word considered mature for an advanced learner might still appear challenging to a novice. This perspective shifts the focus from assessing the inherent complexity of a word to evaluating the learner’s ability to effectively utilize and comprehend it within a given context. To operationalize this concept, we propose a novel computational algorithm for estimating word maturity. Our approach draws upon the principles of Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA) and language acquisition models, treating the lexicon as a dynamic space where words evolve as learners encounter them in diverse contexts. The algorithm models language acquisition by iteratively expanding a learner's semantic representation of each word, based on the frequency and distribution of surrounding words in a large corpus of text. By tracking these changes in semantic representation over time, we can estimate the maturity level of each word. This contrasts with existing methods, which often rely on static measures or aggregate word usage patterns without considering the temporal aspect of language learning. We argue that this approach is better suited for modeling the gradual nature of vocabulary acquisition. We present empirical results demonstrating that this new metric correlates strongly with established external indicators of word knowledge while also revealing deeper semantic effects that traditional difficulty measures fail to capture.

The proliferation of social media platforms has created unprecedented opportunities to observe and analyze human behavior and opinion expression at scale. While this data offers valuable insights across numerous domains, it also presents challenges related to understanding and mitigating potentially harmful communication patterns. Among these patterns, dogmatism – characterized by rigidity in beliefs, unwillingness to consider alternative viewpoints, and an often-overconfident insistence on one’s own perspective – poses a significant concern, particularly in online spaces where it can contribute to polarization, echo chambers, and hostile discourse. While psychological research has extensively explored the concept of dogmatism, its manifestation and potential identification within the context of social media remains relatively underexplored. This paper addresses this gap by investigating linguistic and behavioral signals of dogmatism in social media and developing statistical models capable of identifying dogmatic commentary. Our work is motivated by the growing recognition that social media platforms can amplify and reinforce dogmatic tendencies. Understanding the characteristics of dogmatic online communication is essential for developing tools and strategies to foster more constructive dialogue, filter potentially harmful content, and ultimately create healthier online communities. Previous research has largely focused on identifying sentiment or toxicity in social media text, but rarely investigates the more nuanced characteristic of dogmatism. While overlapping, dogmatism differs from toxicity in that it is less overtly hostile but often more resistant to reasoned argument and compromise. To tackle this challenge, we adopt a data-driven approach, leveraging insights from established psychological theories of dogmatism. We operationalize key aspects such as overconfidence, intolerance of ambiguity, and a tendency toward absolute statements, translating these theoretical constructs into potentially observable linguistic features. To facilitate this, we built a corpus of Reddit posts, a platform known for its diverse range of user communities and conversational topics. This corpus was carefully collected and annotated using paid crowdsourcing, ensuring a high degree of inter-annotator agreement on the presence or absence of dogmatism in each post. Beyond replicating known correlates of dogmatism, our analysis revealed intriguing new signals. Notably, we found that dogmatic posts frequently  refrain  from explicitly signaling cognitive processes – that is, they tend to avoid phrases indicating reasoning, consideration of alternatives, or uncertainty. This suggests that dogmatic users may intentionally conceal the reasoning behind their assertions, projecting an aura of unquestionable certainty. Following the creation and evaluation of our predictive model, we then applied it to a massive dataset of unlabeled Reddit posts, assessing the prevalence of dogmatic communication across different domains and exploring the behavioral patterns of users who engage with dogmatic content.

The notion of coherence—the quality of being logical and consistent—has long been central to understanding human communication. In discourse analysis, coherence refers to the perceived connectedness and meaningfulness of a sequence of sentences or utterances (Reddy, 1990; van Dijk, 1980). While human readers effortlessly determine the coherence of text, developing computational models that accurately reflect this human judgment remains a significant challenge in natural language processing. Traditional approaches to discourse coherence modeling have often focused on lexical overlap (Lin, 1998; Barzilay & Lapata, 2008), entity grid analysis (Elhadad, 2000), or rhetorical structure theory (RST) (Mann & Thompson, 1988), relying on lexical similarity or pre-defined rhetorical relations. However, these models frequently struggle to capture the underlying intentional structure driving discourse, leading to limitations in their ability to identify true coherence. Existing lexical-based approaches can be overly sensitive to superficial word choices and ignore the deeper semantic connections that contribute to coherence. Similarly, RST-based models require extensive manual annotation or complex parsing, rendering them impractical for large-scale analysis. In this paper, we present a novel coherence model that deviates from these traditional approaches by asserting that syntactic patterns within text offer a valuable proxy for the communicative intentions guiding sentence production. Our core hypothesis is that coherent discourse is not merely a collection of related sentences but rather a carefully structured sequence where each sentence contributes intentionally to the overall communicative goal. Consequently, the sequence of sentences will exhibit discernible structural patterns that can be learned and exploited to determine coherence. We argue that focusing on these patterns, rather than solely on lexical relationships, allows us to capture the deeper, intentional structure underlying coherent discourse. Our model leverages readily available syntactic information—specifically, the sequence of grammatical relations between words—to identify these patterns. We formulate a methodology for extracting and analyzing syntactic features from text, enabling us to quantify the degree of structural coherence within a given discourse. We evaluate our model on several datasets, demonstrating its ability to accurately distinguish between coherent and incoherent news articles, achieving accuracies of up to 90%. Furthermore, we extend our analysis to academic conference articles, correlating our syntactic patterns with manual annotations of intentional structure and showcasing the model's ability to predict the coherence of key sections like abstracts, introductions, and related work. These findings suggest that our approach provides a promising new direction for computational coherence modeling, offering a robust and efficient alternative to existing methods.

The burgeoning volume of text data generated in interactive venues—social media platforms, online forums, chat applications—presents unique challenges for natural language processing. A particularly complex scenario arises when users engage in interleaved or simultaneous conversations, resulting in overlapping sequences of messages. Effectively processing this data requires disentanglement – the automatic grouping of these overlapping sequences into distinct, coherent conversations. While considerable work has been dedicated to this problem, existing methods often focus on leveraging readily available lexical and non-lexical cues such as keywords, user identifiers, and timestamps. However, a crucial element frequently overlooked is the profound interplay between a message’s meaning and its surrounding context—both the explicit temporal and social environments, and the more subtle, implicit contextual cues that shape its interpretation. Ignoring these contextual nuances can lead to inaccurate disentanglement and hinder downstream analysis. In this paper, we address this limitation by introducing a novel approach to disentanglement that explicitly incorporates context-based message expansion. Our core idea is to probabilistically augment each message with information derived from its surrounding conversational context. This expansion aims to create a richer, more accurate representation of each message, better reflecting its intended meaning within the larger conversational flow. We move beyond simply utilizing features like sending time or user identity, and instead delve into modeling the hidden dependencies and relationships embedded within the conversation history. This includes considering the preceding messages from the same speaker, the responses to those messages, and the broader conversational trajectory. Our method employs a probabilistic framework to infer the likelihood of specific contextual features being relevant to a given message, allowing us to selectively expand the message representation with the most pertinent information. This avoids the potential for noise and overfitting that can arise from indiscriminately including all contextual features. We detail a novel mechanism for capturing both explicit (e.g., immediately preceding messages) and implicit (e.g., latent stylistic patterns) contextual properties, and demonstrate how these can be effectively integrated into the message representation. Through extensive experimental evaluations on benchmark datasets of interleaved conversations, we demonstrate that our context-based message expansion approach consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art disentanglement techniques, highlighting the significant benefits of incorporating contextual understanding into this challenging NLP task. The results underscore the importance of moving beyond purely lexical and superficial features to achieve more accurate and robust disentanglement of interleaved text conversations. Defining the potential for deeper conversational analysis of previously intractable data.

Cross-lingual transfer learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for leveraging resources from one language to improve performance in another, particularly in scenarios where parallel data is scarce or unavailable. A key component of many cross-lingual approaches is the use of bilingual word embeddings – vector representations of words that capture their semantic similarity across different languages. Existing methods for learning bilingual word embeddings typically rely on either parallel corpora (Biemann et al., 2014;Mikolov et al., 2013) or complex alignment techniques (Artetxe et al., 2018). However, parallel data is often expensive to obtain, and alignment methods can be computationally expensive and sensitive to noise. Recent work has also begun exploring approaches leveraging comparable corpora or monolingual data in combination with translation lexicons (Conneau et al., 2020). While these approaches have made significant strides, there remains a need for simple, efficient, and adaptable methods for producing high-quality bilingual word embeddings, particularly when addressing specific downstream tasks. This paper introduces a novel and remarkably simple approach to learning task-specific bilingual word embeddings. Our method sidesteps the reliance on large parallel corpora or complex alignment procedures by employing a wrapper approach around readily available, off-the-shelf word embedding algorithms. The core idea is to leverage a small dictionary of task-specific word equivalence classes – essentially, pairs of words that are known to be semantically related within the context of a particular task – to create “mixed context-target” pairs. These pairs combine the contextual information from both languages, effectively guiding the embedding algorithm to learn cross-lingual representations. For example, if we are interested in sentiment analysis, our equivalence class might include words like "happy" and "joyeux" (French). We then construct mixed pairs like “The movie was happy” and “Le film était joyeux”, and use these to train a standard word embedding model. Our approach offers several key advantages. Firstly, it is algorithm-agnostic; we can seamlessly integrate any existing word embedding algorithm without modification. Secondly, it does not require parallel data – only a small, easily obtainable dictionary of task-specific word equivalences. And thirdly, it is highly adaptable; the model can be tailored to specific tasks simply by redefining the equivalence classes relevant to that task. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method through experiments on two distinct cross-lingual transfer learning tasks: unsupervised cross-language part-of-speech (POS) tagging and semi-supervised cross-language super sense (SuS) tagging.

The rise of large-scale natural language processing (NLP) models has necessitated the development of efficient inference techniques. While maximum a posteriori (MAP) inference – finding a single, optimal configuration of variables – has received considerable attention and benefited from relaxation methods like belief propagation (BP) and its variants (Wainwright & Jordan, 2008), marginal inference – computing the probability distribution over variables – remains a computationally challenging problem, particularly in complex models. Marginal inference is crucial for a diverse set of NLP tasks beyond just finding the most likely structure. These include conditional likelihood training (Goldberg & Nivre, 2005), posterior decoding for noisy data (Sha et al., 2011), and crucially, reliable confidence estimation (Cherry & Bleich, 2014) – the ability to determine when a model's predictions are trustworthy. Traditional marginal inference methods, such as those based on exact inference algorithms, often become intractable for models of realistic size. Approximation methods, like Monte Carlo methods, can be computationally expensive and lack theoretical guarantees. Recent advancements in relaxation techniques have demonstrated significant speedups for MAP inference on various NLP problems, including dependency parsing (Koo et al., 2017). These approaches approximate the intractable inference problem by propagating messages between variables within a factor graph, effectively “relaxing” the constraints imposed by the model. While this has proven effective for finding the single best configuration, extending this relaxation paradigm to marginal inference, and retaining its benefits of speed and efficiency, has remained an open problem. In this paper, we bridge this gap by introducing Relaxed Marginal Inference (RMI), a novel framework extending relaxation techniques to enable efficient marginal inference within complex graphical models. Our core idea is to perform marginal inference over a strategically chosen subgraph of the full factor graph, leveraging the principles of relaxation to approximate the marginal probabilities. We demonstrate the efficacy of RMI within the context of second-order dependency parsing, a notoriously computationally expensive task due to the interactions between features. We achieve a remarkable tenfold increase in parsing speed compared to traditional marginal inference methods, while maintaining comparable accuracy. Furthermore, we establish a theoretical bound on the error introduced by performing inference over this reduced subgraph, providing a quantitative measure of the approximation's quality. Finally, we emphasize that the RMI framework is inherently adaptable. While we focus on belief propagation (BP) as the inference algorithm within the relaxation loop, the core principles of our approach are general and readily applicable with any marginal inference method, opening avenues for future work exploring alternative algorithms and further improvements in efficiency and accuracy.

The burgeoning fields of topic modeling and word embedding have independently revolutionized how we extract latent semantic information from textual data. Topic models, such as Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) (Blei et al., 2003), excel at uncovering overarching themes within collections of documents, revealing how words tend to co-occur at a coarser granularity—typically across entire documents or sentences. Conversely, word embedding techniques, like Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) and GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014), focus on capturing nuanced relationships between words by modeling their co-occurrence within localized contexts, often defined by small sliding windows. While both approaches are undeniably valuable, they operate at fundamentally different scales, potentially limiting their ability to fully capture the multifaceted nature of language semantics. Traditional topic models, in their pursuit of broad thematic understanding, can sometimes lose sight of the fine-grained relationships between individual words. Conversely, word embedding models, while adept at capturing local context, often struggle to represent the broader conceptual themes that emerge from larger bodies of text. This inherent disconnect has motivated a search for integrated approaches that can harness the strengths of both paradigms. In this paper, we propose Latent Topic Embedding (LTE), a novel model designed to bridge this gap by seamlessly unifying topic generation and word embedding learning within a single, coherent framework. LTE aims to derive latent semantics by strategically capturing word co-occurrence information across multiple levels of granularity, effectively synthesizing the advantages of both topic modeling and word embedding. Our model offers a unified approach that allows words to be influenced by both document-level topic distributions and local context windows. To facilitate efficient parameter estimation, we further introduce an efficient Monte Carlo Expectation-Maximization (MC-EM) algorithm tailored to the specific structure of LTE. This algorithm enables the model to effectively learn both topic structures and word embeddings in a computationally tractable manner. The key contributions of this work can be summarized as follows: 1) A novel unified model, LTE, for simultaneously learning latent topics and word embeddings. 2) An efficient MC-EM algorithm for parameter estimation in LTE. 3) Empirical validation demonstrating that LTE outperforms state-of-the-art topic modeling and word embedding techniques on a range of real-world applications, suggesting that our integrated approach provides a more comprehensive and nuanced understanding of latent semantics. We believe that LTE represents a significant step towards a more holistic understanding of language and its underlying structure.

Chinese Word Segmentation (CWS) remains a fundamental task in natural language processing for the Chinese language. Unlike many other languages, Chinese lacks clear word boundaries, making accurate segmentation crucial for downstream applications such as machine translation, information retrieval, and sentiment analysis. Currently, state-of-the-art CWS methods predominantly rely on supervised learning approaches, achieving impressive accuracy on benchmark datasets. However, a significant challenge arises when these models are applied to out-of-domain texts—texts from a different genre, topic, or style than the training data. Performance degrades substantially in such scenarios due to a mismatch between the training and testing distributions. The reliance on large-scale, manually annotated corpora for supervised learning amplifies this problem, as creating such corpora is a time-consuming and expensive process. Furthermore, adapting existing models to new domains often requires laborious feature engineering or complex algorithmic modifications. The need for robust and adaptable CWS systems, particularly those capable of generalizing to diverse domains with minimal supervision, is increasingly apparent. This paper addresses the challenge of out-of-domain CWS by proposing a novel and effective approach: automatic corpus expansion leveraging readily available web information. Our central idea is that the vast amount of text data available on the web contains valuable, albeit often unsegmented, information relevant to improving CWS performance. We argue that many sentences appearing on the web, while potentially differing in style and context from a carefully curated training corpus, exhibit structural properties that make them relatively easy to segment. These sentences can then be exploited to augment the training data, effectively broadening the model's exposure to diverse linguistic patterns. Instead of directly incorporating all web data – which can be noisy and unreliable – we focus on strategically selecting reliable, segmented sentences to incorporate into the training set. By framing the problem as one of intelligent corpus expansion, we sidestep the need for extensive feature engineering or complex algorithm design, offering a simpler and more scalable solution. Our approach operates in two key stages: first, identifying easily segmentable sentences from web data; and second, incorporating these sentences into the training corpus to retrain a more robust CWS model. We demonstrate through extensive experimental evaluation that our method consistently and significantly improves CWS performance on out-of-domain datasets, providing a valuable alternative to traditional methods centered on complex algorithmic enhancements. Furthermore, our work offers a fresh perspective on CWS research – emphasizing the potential of automatically expanding training corpora as a powerful strategy for improving performance and adaptability.

The automatic syntactic parsing of spontaneous speech presents a unique challenge compared to the processing of written text. This is due, in large part, to the frequent occurrence of disfluencies – hesitations, repetitions, corrections (reparanda), and false starts – that deviate from standard grammatical structures. Traditional syntactic parsers, trained on written corpora, perform poorly when directly applied to transcribed spontaneous speech, often misinterpreting these disfluencies as grammatical errors. Consequently, significant research effort has been devoted to developing robust parsing models capable of handling the complexities of disfluent speech. Within the broader landscape of disfluency modeling, the focus on repairs – self-initiated corrections of previous speech – presents a particularly interesting avenue for investigation. Repairs offer a window into the real-time linguistic processes of speech production, reflecting moments of error detection and correction. However, accurately modeling the syntax of repairs remains a nontrivial task. Existing approaches often treat reparanda as inherently ungrammatical, leading to parser performance degradation or necessitating complex pre-processing steps to remove or modify them. This paper challenges the conventional wisdom that reparanda are generated or recognized as erroneous  during  their utterance. We propose that erroneous aspects of speech repairs are often identified and corrected  post hoc , after the initial utterance segment has been produced. This intuition suggests that the underlying syntactic structure of fluent and disfluent speech, particularly segments containing similar structural patterns, should share a considerable degree of grammatical similarity. Therefore, we argue that syntactic parsing models should aim to minimize the divergence in grammar rule application between fluent and disfluent speech segments. To explore this hypothesis, we introduce three novel syntactic models specifically designed for parsing speech containing repairs. These models represent distinct approaches to incorporating repair information into the parsing process, each designed to illuminate a specific aspect of their impact on syntactic structure. Importantly, these models are developed with a focus on isolating the mechanisms of impact; by systematically varying specific components, we aim to rigorously test the influence of different variables on parsing accuracy in the presence of repairs, and to provide a clearer understanding of how these linguistic phenomena interact within a syntactic parsing framework. The subsequent sections detail the three models, their underlying assumptions, and the experimental methodology used to evaluate their performance. We anticipate that these models will contribute to a more nuanced understanding of syntactic processing in disfluent speech and pave the way for improved and more robust parsing systems. The demand for adaptable and robust language models (LMs) has become increasingly critical in modern natural language processing. Traditional statistical language models, while effective for tasks within their training domain, often exhibit a significant performance drop when applied to out-of-domain (OOD) scenarios. This degradation stems from their inability to generalize beyond the observed vocabulary and linguistic patterns, leaving them vulnerable to novel word combinations, topics, and stylistic variations encountered in new tasks. Recent advancements in neural language models offer improved generalization capabilities, but they too can struggle with extreme OOD shifts and require substantial training data. This motivates the need for language modeling approaches that are inherently more resilient to domain variations. Latent Word Language Models (LWLM) represent a promising direction, offering a framework for capturing semantic similarities between words and generating sequences based on underlying latent concepts. However, standard LWLM models often lack the flexibility to adequately represent complex linguistic phenomena or adapt to unforeseen OOD characteristics. In this paper, we address this limitation by introducing a novel hierarchical latent word language model (h-LWLM). Our approach extends the foundational principles of LWLM by incorporating a multi-layered latent variable space, establishing a hierarchical structure that allows for a more nuanced and flexible representation of linguistic knowledge. We argue that this hierarchical structure empowers the model to capture dependencies and patterns not explicitly present in the training data, thereby enhancing its robustness to OOD tasks. The key innovation of h-LWLM lies in its ability to implicitly learn higher-order linguistic features and relationships, enabling it to generate more coherent and contextually appropriate sequences even when confronted with unfamiliar data. Furthermore, we detail a practical training method based on layer-wise inference, coupled with an approximation technique to facilitate efficient implementation. To validate the effectiveness of our proposed model, we conduct extensive experiments in the context of speech recognition, a challenging application particularly susceptible to OOD variations. Our results demonstrate that h-LWLM consistently outperforms standard LWLMs and competitive baselines in OOD settings, showcasing its potential as a robust language modeling solution for a wider range of NLP applications. We believe this work represents a significant step toward creating language models that can adapt and generalize effectively across diverse domains, ultimately facilitating more reliable and versatile natural language processing systems. ### Hoping this is satisfactory. Surface realisation – the task of generating a surface string from a representation of meaning – is a core component of many natural language generation (NLG) systems. While significant progress has been made in recent years, particularly with the rise of neural approaches, data-driven methods grounded in linguistic theory remain valuable for achieving high-quality, controllable generation. This paper focuses on a challenging aspect of surface realisation in German: modelling voice (active vs. passive) in conjunction with word order variation. German, with its relatively free word order, presents a particularly interesting case study for voice and word order interactions, as the choice of voice often influences permissible word order arrangements. Traditionally, surface realisation models have treated voice and word order as separate phenomena, or have incorporated voice as a relatively late-stage decision. However, this overlooks the potential for rich interactions between these elements, and the possibility that earlier underspecification of voice can inform and improve word order choices. The core challenge lies in striking a balance between underspecification – allowing the system flexibility to express the same meaning in multiple ways – and precision – ensuring that the generated surface string faithfully reflects the intended meaning. Previous work has explored underspecification as a means to improve the fluency and naturalness of generated text, but less attention has been paid to its impact on modularity and predictability of grammatical features like voice. Our work addresses this gap by investigating the relationship between the degree of underspecification in the input and the accuracy with which a surface realisation model can predict the voice of the original source string. We introduce and evaluate a data-driven surface realisation model for German, built upon a large-scale reversible grammar framework. This allows us to systematically control the level of underspecification in the input representations, and to examine the impact on generation quality and predictability. A key innovation of our system is its ability to generate candidate sets that include both active and passive voice variants, allowing us to directly study their interplay with word order alternations. Critically, our approach frames surface realisation as a regeneration task: the model is trained to reconstruct strings from underlying semantic representations, which encourages it to learn linguistically plausible surface forms. This enables a more principled investigation of the impact of underspecification. Through extensive experimentation on a realistic German corpus, we demonstrate that appropriate levels of input underspecification can significantly improve the accuracy of voice prediction, achieving a substantial gain over a baseline system – 91.5% accuracy compared to 82.5% - highlighting the potential of underspecification in guiding voice and word order choices within surface realisation models.

Chinese word segmentation (CWS) is a fundamental task in natural language processing for Chinese, as unlike many Western languages, Chinese text lacks explicit word delimiters. Accurate CWS is crucial for downstream tasks such as machine translation, information retrieval, and sentiment analysis. Simultaneously, the rapid evolution of language necessitates effective new word detection (NWD) capabilities, allowing systems to identify and incorporate previously unseen terms into their vocabularies. Jointly performing CWS and NWD offers potential benefits, leveraging shared contextual information to improve the accuracy of both tasks. Existing approaches often treat CWS and NWD as separate problems, or utilize simpler feature representations that fail to fully capture the nuances of the Chinese language. Recent work has explored joint modeling using conditional random fields (CRFs) to capture dependencies between segmentation and word boundaries (Chen et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2016). However, effectively training these joint models, particularly with high-dimensional feature spaces, remains a computational challenge. Training a word segmentation system on large-scale corpora is already a resource-intensive undertaking. The inclusion of high-dimensional features, especially enriched edge (label-transition) features that capture intricate relationships between segmentation decisions, exacerbates this problem, leading to significantly prolonged training times. Traditional training methods, such as stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with fixed learning rates, struggle to efficiently handle the vast parameter space and the varying frequencies of different features in large datasets. Furthermore, the performance of SGD is highly sensitive to the chosen learning rate, requiring careful tuning. To address these challenges, we present a novel and efficient training method for joint Chinese word segmentation and new word detection. Our approach is based on adaptive online gradient descent, where learning rates are dynamically adjusted based on the observed frequencies of individual features. This allows the model to quickly adapt to the data and converge to a good solution even with high-dimensional feature spaces. Our method achieves an order of magnitude reduction in training time compared to existing approaches, while maintaining or even surpassing their accuracy on benchmark datasets. Crucially, our proposed training method is a general-purpose optimization technique and is not limited to the specific task of CWS and NWD discussed in this paper, making it a valuable contribution to the broader machine learning community. We believe its ability to handle large-scale, high-dimensional data with online adaptation opens up new possibilities for rapid model development and deployment in various NLP applications.

Text classification is a fundamental task in natural language processing, enabling a wide range of applications from spam detection and sentiment analysis to topic categorization and news article classification. While supervised learning approaches have traditionally dominated this field, the requirement for large, labeled datasets is often a significant bottleneck. Obtaining such datasets can be costly, time-consuming, and even infeasible in some domains. Semi-supervised learning (SSL) offers a compelling alternative, leveraging both a small amount of labeled data and a larger pool of unlabeled data to improve classification performance. This makes SSL particularly attractive when labeled data is scarce or expensive to acquire. Traditional SSL techniques often rely on methods like self-training, co-training, or transductive support vector machines. However, recent advances in deep learning have spurred renewed interest in SSL, particularly with the development of sophisticated neural network architectures capable of effectively modeling complex data distributions. The power of deep learning, coupled with the efficiency gains offered by SSL, has resulted in numerous innovative approaches, many seeking to creatively combine the strengths of supervised and unsupervised learning paradigms. However, many existing deep SSL methods grapple with issues of noise amplification from pseudo-labeling or difficulties in harmonizing the objectives of supervised and unsupervised training. In this paper, we tackle the challenge of semi-supervised text classification by proposing a novel deep hybrid model and a unique fine-tuning algorithm that we term “Bottom-Up-Top-Down” (BUTD) learning. Our model combines the representational power of a generative neural network with the discriminative capabilities of a classifier, leveraging the strengths of both approaches. The core innovation lies in our fine-tuning algorithm, which operates iteratively, performing a bottom-up generative learning pass followed by a top-down refinement of model parameters. This cyclical process allows the model to progressively refine its understanding of the data, iteratively reducing the discrepancy between the generative and discriminative components. Specifically, during each increment of the online learning process, the fine-tuning algorithm acts as a top-down mechanism, pseudo-jointly modifying the model parameters in response to the bottom-up generative learning pass. The generative component helps to uncover underlying data structure and regularities, while the discriminative component steers the learning process towards improved classification accuracy. We demonstrate that this BUTD learning algorithm effectively mitigates noise and promotes a harmonious integration of supervised and unsupervised learning. The resulting model consistently outperforms a variety of competitive models and baselines across a range of experimental settings and varying splits between supervised and unsupervised training data, highlighting its efficacy and robustness for semi-supervised text classification.

The burgeoning volume of digital text necessitates efficient methods for extracting meaningful insights, and topic modeling has emerged as a cornerstone technique for this purpose (Blei et al., 2003). Recent advancements have focused on online topic modeling, which leverages stochastic variational inference to dynamically update topic distributions as data streams in (Kulesza & Wong, 2008; Nguyen et al., 2010). This approach enables real-time analysis of vast datasets, making it particularly well-suited for applications such as social media monitoring and news analytics. A crucial component of online learning is the optimization algorithm used to update model parameters, and Adaptive Gradient Algorithm (ADAGRAD) (Duchi et al., 2011) has become a popular choice due to its ability to adapt learning rates for each parameter individually. The core idea behind ADAGRAD is to normalize the learning rate for each parameter by the accumulation of its past squared gradients, allowing for more rapid progress in directions with infrequent updates and slowing down progress in directions with frequent updates. However, despite the intuitive appeal of ADAGRAD and the demonstrated success of online topic modeling, a surprising and often overlooked issue arises when combining these two techniques: their performance is often suboptimal, and in many cases, they fail to converge effectively. This observation contradicts the expected benefits of ADAGRAD and motivates a thorough investigation of the underlying cause. While several explanations have been proposed, this work aims to offer a clear and concise theoretical justification for this phenomenon. Our central argument is that the characteristic nature of gradients in online topic modeling, specifically their frequently large magnitudes, leads to an overly rapid shrinkage of learning rates when used in conjunction with ADAGRAD. This rapid shrinkage effectively stifles the model's ability to fully converge before the training process concludes, preventing it from reaching its optimal parameter configuration. We provide a detailed analysis demonstrating how the accumulation of squared gradients in ADAGRAD, combined with the inherent properties of topic model gradients, results in this detrimental effect.
