Graphical models offer a powerful framework for representing and reasoning about complex dependencies in data. These models are ubiquitous across diverse fields, from computer vision and natural language processing to bioinformatics and machine learning. A central challenge in working with graphical models is performing approximate inference – determining the posterior distribution over the model's variables given observed evidence. Exact inference is often intractable in large or complex models, necessitating the development of approximation techniques. Expectation Propagation (EP) (Makikinen and Frey, 2009) has emerged as a compelling alternative to traditional methods like Belief Propagation (BP) (Pearl, 1988). EP distinguishes itself by maintaining tractability by projecting messages exchanged between nodes into a restricted family of functions, ensuring computational efficiency. However, standard EP can sometimes lead to complex messages, which may negate the desired speed gains. Furthermore, in many real-world applications, simpler models tend to generalize better, even if they marginally sacrifice accuracy on the training data. To address these concerns, we introduce Penalized Expectation Propagation (PEP), a novel algorithm that extends EP with a structured sparsity penalty. This penalty explicitly encourages the learning of simpler messages, thus striking a balance between computational speed and inference accuracy. The core idea is to regularize the message learning process, guiding the algorithm toward solutions with sparser, more interpretable message functions. This is particularly beneficial in scenarios where the message space is high-dimensional or complex. In this work, we focus on applying PEP to graphical models operating over strings. String-valued random variables appear in numerous NLP tasks, ranging from phonological modeling and speech recognition to DNA sequencing and text analysis. Inference in these models often involves approximating complex, finite-state distributions over sequences of symbols. We demonstrate how to instantiate PEP in this context by adaptively approximating these distributions using variable-order n-gram models. This allows us to maintain tractability while capturing important dependencies between symbols in the string. The variable-order approach further enhances the flexibility of the model, enabling it to adapt to the complexity of the data. We empirically evaluate our approach on phonological inference problems, demonstrating substantial speedups compared to existing algorithms while maintaining competitive accuracy levels. Our results highlight the potential of PEP as a practical and effective method for approximate inference in graphical models over strings, offering a pathway towards more efficient and interpretable solutions. The key contribution is therefore the introduction of a structured sparsity penalty within the EP framework, tailored specifically for string-valued random variables, yielding both speed and practical utility.

Relation extraction (RE) aims to identify semantic relationships between entities mentioned in text. Traditional supervised RE methods rely on manually labeled data, which is expensive and time-consuming to obtain. Distant Supervision (DS) (Mintz et al., 2009) provides a compelling alternative by automatically generating training data using existing knowledge bases (KBs). For example, if a KB states that “Barack Obama” is the “President of” “United States”, then every sentence containing both entities is labeled as an instance of the “President of” relation. While DS significantly alleviates data annotation efforts, it inherently introduces noise – many sentences containing the entity pair may not truly express the target relation. For instance, "Barack Obama visited the United States" does not express the "President of" relationship. The presence of such noisy instances can severely degrade the performance of RE models, particularly those employing deep learning techniques. Recent advances in deep learning have shown promising results in RE, with various neural network architectures being successfully applied to the task (Zheng et al., 2015; Zeng et al., 2016; Yao et al., 2017). However, these models often struggle to cope with the inherent noise in DS-generated training data. Traditional methods for addressing noise in DS often involve filtering or weighting noisy instances, which typically require external knowledge or hand-crafted rules. A more principled approach involves explicitly modeling the noise distribution and incorporating it into the learning process. In this paper, we tackle the challenge of noisy training data in DS-based RE by focusing on characterizing the latent noise patterns using a dynamic transition matrix. We hypothesize that the relationships between different relation labels in the noisy data can be effectively captured by a transition matrix, which describes the probability of transitioning from one relation to another. By learning this transition matrix, we can gain insights into the noise distribution and potentially mitigate its impact on the RE model. Crucially, our approach achieves this without relying on any direct supervision about the noise itself. Instead, we leverage a novel curriculum learning strategy to train the transition matrix, gradually exposing the model to more challenging examples. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: (1) We demonstrate that a dynamic transition matrix can effectively capture the noise patterns in distantly supervised relation extraction data and characterize the probability of transitions among different relation labels. (2) We propose a novel curriculum learning based method to train the transition matrix without explicit noise supervision.

Text readability is a critical aspect of communication, impacting comprehension, engagement, and overall user experience. While extensively studied for languages like English, computational approaches to readability assessment in low-resource languages remain relatively unexplored. This paper addresses this gap by focusing on Bangla, a language with a rich literary tradition and a significant digital presence. The core premise underlying readability research is that the ease with which a text can be understood is not solely a property of the text itself, but is also heavily influenced by the characteristics of the intended reader. Factors such as educational background, familiarity with the topic, and linguistic proficiency play a crucial role in shaping the perception of textual difficulty. Furthermore, inherent properties of the text—sentence length, word frequency, lexical complexity, and grammatical structure—also contribute significantly to readability. Previous studies have primarily focused on the text-centric view of readability, often employing a fixed set of features to estimate difficulty irrespective of the reader’s profile. However, such approaches neglect the crucial interplay between reader and text. This limitation motivates our investigation, where we aim to model readability considering both the target reader’s background and the text’s inherent features. Specifically, we ask: How does the perceived difficulty of a Bangla text vary depending on the reader's background, and which text features are most predictive of readability for different reader groups? To answer these questions, we present a novel computational study on Bangla text readability. Our contribution begins with the creation of a unique dataset of 135 Bangla documents annotated by 50 readers representing two distinct background groups. This allows us to directly assess the impact of reader background on perceived reading difficulty. Building on this dataset, we identified a comprehensive set of 20 textual features potentially influencing readability. These features are categorized into “classic” features (e.g., average sentence length, syllable count per word) and “non-classic” features (e.g., frequency of specific grammatical markers, usage of complex compounds), reflecting a broader perspective beyond traditional readability formulas. A preliminary correlation analysis reveals intriguing insights into how these features influence perceived text hardness, demonstrating varying effects depending on the reader’s background. We then employed Support Vector Machines (SVM) and Support Vector Regression (SVR) techniques to explicitly model the reading difficulties. Crucially, we developed separate models tailored for each reader background group, allowing for the capture of nuanced variations in readability perception. Moreover, we systematically explored different feature combinations to evaluate their relative contributions in predicting readability.

The interconnected nature of information across documents presents a significant challenge for natural language understanding. Resolving coreferences—determining which mentions in different documents refer to the same entity—and linking named entities to a structured knowledge base (KB) are two crucial tasks for enabling effective cross-document reasoning. Cross-document coreference resolution (CCR) aims to identify equivalence classes of mentions across a corpus, effectively grouping mentions that refer to the same real-world entity. Simultaneously, named entity linking (NEL) seeks to disambiguate mentions by mapping them to their corresponding entities within a KB, or designating them as "null" if they do not represent existing entities. Traditionally, CCR and NEL have been treated as separate, independent problems, reflecting historical development and ease of modular implementation. However, this separation overlooks the significant potential for mutual benefit that arises when these tasks are addressed jointly. Treating CCR and NEL in isolation disregards the valuable context each task provides for the other, hindering overall performance. The inherent connections between coreference and entity linking suggest a synergistic relationship. Knowing that two mentions corefer can significantly constrain the possible KB entities to which they could link, providing valuable information for the NEL task. Conversely, accurately linking mentions to specific KB entities can provide distant supervision and contextual information that helps resolve coreferences, particularly when mentions are ambiguous or lack immediate contextual clues. The performance of both tasks can be improved through this collaborative approach. Despite this recognized potential, joint models for CCR and NEL remain relatively underdeveloped. Existing approaches often rely on complex, supervised architectures or intricate feature engineering, limiting their practicality and generalizability. To bridge this gap, we propose C3EL (Cross-Document Co-reference and Entity Linking), an unsupervised framework designed to jointly tackle CCR and NEL. Our key innovation lies in the iterative and interleaved nature of our model, leveraging the output of one task to inform and improve the other in a reciprocal manner. C3EL incorporates two distinct phases. First, the CCR stage attempts to identify coreference chains, providing crucial contextual information about the entities involved. Second, the NEL stage disambiguates mentions by linking to the KB, offering distant supervision and enriching the feature space for CCR. The interleaving strategy focuses computational resources on the most promising unresolved mentions within each iteration, significantly boosting efficiency. We demonstrate that incorporating global context derived from the CCR phase enhances the feature space and performance of the NEL phase, while the distant KB features provided by NEL refine the accuracy of the CCR process.

The burgeoning success of deep learning has revolutionized numerous natural language processing (NLP) tasks. Among these, multi-task learning (MTL) has emerged as a powerful paradigm, leveraging shared representations to improve performance across related tasks. By training a single model on multiple objectives simultaneously, MTL aims to exploit commonalities and transfer knowledge, ultimately leading to enhanced generalization and efficiency. However, a critical limitation of many existing MTL approaches lies in their indiscriminate sharing of features. While linking layers to facilitate knowledge transfer seems intuitive, it often overlooks the potential for interference between tasks. The assumption that all tasks benefit from all features is frequently violated. In reality, sharing information from irrelevant or even detrimental features can contaminate the representation space, leading to confusion and degraded performance. This 'feature pollution' problem arises because tasks often have distinct underlying structures and require specialized feature representations. Current methods often fail to address this challenge, treating all feature flows as equally valuable, irrespective of their relevance to specific tasks. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel multi-task convolutional neural network (MTCNN) incorporating a "Leaky Unit," a mechanism that dynamically regulates feature sharing between tasks. Unlike traditional MTL networks that indiscriminately pass information, our Leaky Unit introduces a memory and forgetting mechanism. This allows the network to selectively retain and propagate relevant features while suppressing irrelevant or harmful ones, effectively filtering feature flows between tasks. The core idea is to mimic biological neural systems, which exhibit plasticity - the ability to strengthen useful connections and prune unnecessary ones. Our Leaky Unit learns to "remember" beneficial features and selectively "forget" those that prove detrimental, leading to a more refined and task-specific representation space. We hypothesize that this selective sharing will mitigate the interference problem and improve the overall performance of the MTCNN. We validate this hypothesis through extensive experimentation on five diverse datasets for text classification. The results demonstrate that our Leaky Unit based MTCNN consistently outperforms baseline MTL models, highlighting the benefits of learning  what  to share, rather than simply sharing everything. Synchronous context-free grammars (SCFGs) offer a powerful formalism for modeling correspondence between sentences in parallel corpora, enabling state-of-the-art machine translation systems. However, a longstanding challenge in utilizing SCFGs efficiently lies in the computational complexity of decoding. A fundamental tenet in the field has long been that SCFG decoding necessitates a transformation into Chomsky Normal Form (CNF) to achieve a manageable cubic time complexity – O(n³), where n represents the length of the input sentences. This transformation is most commonly achieved through the synchronous binarization technique introduced by Zhang et al. (2006), which recursively decomposes non-binary rules into a series of binary rules, effectively representing the grammar in a CNF-compatible format. Despite its widespread adoption, synchronous binarization has a significant practical drawback: the substantial increase in the number of rules, dramatically inflating the constant factors associated with the cubic time complexity. As noted by DeNero et al. (2009), even with cubic time complexity, the practical running time can be severely affected by this rule inflation. They addressed this concern by proposing Lexical Normal Form (LNF), a superset of CNF that also allows for cubic time decoding, but under specific, previously implicit, assumptions regarding the grammar structure. This paper builds upon and extends the work of DeNero et al., explicitly articulating and formally defining the implicit assumptions underlying LNF decoding. Through this rigorous analysis, we demonstrate that LNF's applicability can be broadened to encompass a larger class of grammars, which we term “scope-3” grammars. These scope-3 grammars possess a structural property that permits cubic-time decoding without the need for binarization. Crucially, we show that grammars extracted using established techniques, such as the GHKM algorithm, can be easily adapted to this framework. By simply pruning the relatively few non-scope-3 rules from these extracted grammars – a computationally inexpensive operation – we can retain the desirable properties of SCFGs while circumventing the performance overhead associated with synchronous binarization. Empirical results on translation tasks demonstrate that this streamlined approach, decoding SCFGs directly without binarization, yields significantly improved translation performance compared to systems employing synchronous binarization, thus challenging the conventional wisdom and opening new avenues for efficient SCFG-based machine translation. We anticipate that our findings will encourage further exploration of grammar normalization techniques that prioritize both computational efficiency and translation quality. --- I hope this is helpful! The ability to automatically solve mathematical word problems has long been a challenging task in natural language processing and artificial intelligence. While humans effortlessly parse and compute solutions from textual descriptions, enabling machines to do the same has proven remarkably difficult. Early approaches to this problem relied heavily on rule-based systems and statistical learning techniques, often requiring extensive feature engineering to capture the relevant linguistic and mathematical relationships within the problem statement. These methods, while achieving some success, frequently struggled with the inherent variability in language and the complexity of mathematical expressions. The core difficulty lies in bridging the gap between natural language and formal mathematical representation – understanding the meaning of the words and translating that meaning into a solvable equation. Recent advancements in deep learning have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in various NLP tasks, including machine translation, question answering, and text generation. These successes have spurred renewed interest in applying deep learning techniques to math word problem solving, with the hope of achieving more robust and generalizable solutions that require less human intervention. Previous deep learning-based approaches have often focused on either extracting numerical values and operators from the text or on generating executable code. However, these methods still typically involve some form of hand-crafted features or intermediate representations, limiting their ability to fully leverage the power of deep neural networks. In this paper, we propose a novel deep neural solver that directly translates math word problems into equation templates using a recurrent neural network (RNN) model. Unlike previous statistical learning approaches, our method minimizes the need for complex feature engineering, allowing the RNN to learn the mapping from natural language to mathematical structure directly from the data. We hypothesize that the sequential processing capabilities of RNNs are well-suited for capturing the syntactic and semantic relationships within math word problems, facilitating the accurate generation of equation templates. Furthermore, we introduce a hybrid model that combines the RNN model with a similarity-based retrieval model, leveraging the strengths of both approaches to further enhance performance. By retrieving similar problems from a large dataset and incorporating their equation templates, our hybrid model can effectively handle ambiguous or novel problem formulations, demonstrating improved robustness and generalization ability. We evaluate our proposed models on a large dataset of math word problems, demonstrating that both the RNN model and the hybrid model significantly outperform state-of-the-art statistical learning methods. Our results suggest that deep neural networks, particularly RNNs, hold significant promise for automating the solution of math word problems, paving the way for more intelligent and adaptable educational tools and automated problem-solving systems.

Estimating the prevalence of different classes within a collection of unlabeled data is a fundamental problem with broad applications, ranging from assessing public opinion to monitoring disease outbreaks. Prevalence estimation aims to determine the relative frequency of different classes – for instance, the proportion of documents expressing positive sentiment in a large corpus, or the percentage of patients exhibiting a specific condition within a population. Traditional approaches to prevalence estimation often rely on aggregating predictions from multiple discriminative classifiers, followed by adjustments to account for classifier biases (Estes et al., 2011; Angelino et al., 2013). However, these methods typically produce point estimates of prevalence without explicitly quantifying the uncertainty associated with these estimates. Such uncertainty quantification is crucial for reliable inference and decision-making, particularly in domains where the consequences of inaccurate prevalence assessments can be significant. Failing to properly reflect the uncertainty in prevalence estimates undermines the scientific validity of conclusions drawn from the data. In this work, we address this gap by presenting a novel generative probabilistic modeling approach to prevalence estimation that explicitly accounts for uncertainty. Rather than solely focusing on aggregating classifier outputs, our method models the underlying data distribution and allows for the construction and evaluation of confidence intervals for prevalence estimates. Our key contribution is demonstrating how readily available, off-the-shelf discriminative classifiers can be reinterpreted within a generative framework. Specifically, we show how to infer an implicit individual-level likelihood function from a trained discriminative classifier, effectively transforming it into a generative model. This enables fast and simple group-level Bayesian inference, allowing us to directly estimate prevalence and its associated uncertainty. Leveraging this generative interpretation allows for principled and efficient calculation of confidence intervals, providing a more complete picture of the prevalence landscape. We rigorously evaluate our approach and demonstrate that it achieves superior confidence interval coverage compared to existing methods and exhibits significantly greater robustness to shifts in the class prior between training and testing phases—a common challenge in real-world prevalence estimation scenarios. Our work moves beyond point prevalence estimates to provide scientifically grounded inferences, enabling more informed decision-making based on a clear understanding of the associated uncertainty. The intersection of language, power, and gender has long been a fertile ground for sociolinguistic research. Studies have consistently demonstrated that language use is not neutral, but rather reflects and reinforces societal power structures, with gender often serving as a crucial lens through which these dynamics are observed. While much of this research has focused on spoken interactions, the prevalence of written communication in professional settings, particularly email, presents a unique opportunity to investigate these phenomena in a large-scale, readily accessible dataset. This paper explores the complex interplay of power, gender, and language use within the well-known Enron email corpus. Previous analyses of the Enron data have touched upon aspects of power dynamics (Gilbert, 2006; Park and Gilbert, 2008), but largely overlooked the potential for gender to moderate these relationships. We aim to address this gap by systematically examining how gender and the surrounding communication environment – what we term “gender environment” – influence linguistic manifestations of power. Our work builds upon established sociolinguistic theories positing that women often navigate power imbalances through subtle, face-saving communicative strategies, and that women may employ language more explicitly to foster and sustain social connections compared to men (Cameron, 1985; Tannen, 1990). To facilitate this investigation, we introduce a significant extension to the publicly available Enron email corpus. This extension incorporates reliable gender identifications for the senders of approximately 87% of the messages, a vital resource for detailed gender-aware analysis. We then test two specific, testable hypotheses derived from the sociolinguistic literature, focusing on the linguistic strategies women and men employ when communicating within organizational structures. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of "gender environment" – operationalized as the gender composition of an email thread – to the computational analysis of written conversation. We argue that the social dynamics within an email exchange are not solely determined by the individual sender's gender, but are also shaped by the presence and gender of other participants. This nuanced perspective allows us to examine how power manifestations differ across various gender environment configurations. Finally, building on our understanding of gendered language use and power dynamics, we explore the potential for leveraging gender information to improve the accuracy of automated power prediction systems in email interactions. We demonstrate that incorporating gender features significantly enhances the ability of machine learning models to accurately discern the direction of authority between email participants. Our findings contribute to a growing body of work that utilizes computational methods to investigate social phenomena embedded within naturally occurring language data, providing valuable insights into the subtle ways gender and power are negotiated in digital communication.

The human language processing (HLP) community has long sought to build computational models that mirror the cognitive processes underlying sentence comprehension (Lewis, 2010). Traditional parsing models, such as chart parsers (Tomlinson et al., 1993), while achieving high syntactic accuracy, often lack the constraints of human working memory, considering the entire sentence at once. Hierarchical Hidden Markov Models (HHMMs) offer a compelling alternative by incorporating incremental processing and bounded working memory—characteristics closely aligned with observed human reading behavior (Joshi et al., 1991;Thornton & Bergen, 2010). HHMMs operate by incrementally building a hierarchical parse tree, maintaining a limited number of partially formed hypotheses in parallel. This aligns with the well-established notion that humans do not process sentences in a strictly left-to-right, top-down fashion, but rather construct interpretations incrementally, revising hypotheses as new information becomes available (Trevor, 2001). Moreover, recent work has demonstrated that HHMM parsers can achieve parsing accuracies comparable to more traditional, computationally intensive chart-based techniques, while remaining cognitively plausible (Krishnan et al., 2017). A key aspect lacking in much prior HHMM research is a thorough investigation of their ability to generate complexity metrics—quantitative measures that reflect the incremental cognitive effort involved in processing a sentence. Such metrics are invaluable for understanding how syntactic structure influences reading times, eye movements, and other physiological measures of cognitive load (Rayner, 1998). Existing computational models of HLP have been successful in predicting these measures using various complexity metrics, including surprisal – the degree to which a word violates expectations given the preceding context (Forstius et al., 2016). However, it remains an open question whether HHMMs, with their unique incremental and memory-constrained architecture, can similarly generate reliable complexity signals. This paper addresses this gap by exploring the utility of HHMMs for generating complexity metrics. We focus on a right-corner HHMM parser—a variant that builds the parse tree from rightmost constituents—and validate its ability to reflect human reading difficulty. Beyond standard surprisal calculations within the HHMM framework, we introduce a novel metric, the  embedding difference , designed to test the hypothesis that intermediate states within the HHMM represent syntactic working memory. Specifically, this metric quantifies the change in vector representations of these states as the parser incrementally constructs the tree. We then evaluate the predictive power of these metrics against empirical reading time data. Our results demonstrate that HHMM surprisal outperforms established complexity metrics, and that the embedding difference makes a significant and independent contribution, further supporting the notion that HHMMs capture aspects of human syntactic working memory.

In the digital age, personal data has become a valuable commodity, driving business models across various sectors. Website privacy policies serve as the primary legal documents informing users about how their data is collected, utilized, and shared. Ideally, these policies should clearly outline data practices, empowering users to make informed decisions about their online activities. However, a persistent and concerning reality is that privacy policies are frequently riddled with ambiguous language, rendering them difficult to comprehend for both ordinary users and regulatory bodies. This opaqueness undermines user trust, hinders informed consent, and complicates the enforcement of data protection regulations like GDPR and CCPA. This lack of transparency presents a significant challenge, creating barriers to effective privacy management and increasing the vulnerability of individuals to potential data misuse. Recognizing this critical issue, we address the pressing need for automated tools capable of identifying and quantifying vagueness within privacy policies. While previous research has explored aspects of privacy policy analysis, a systematic focus on vagueness detection has been largely absent. This paper fills this gap by tackling the problem of automatic vagueness detection in privacy policies – a novel and crucial step toward enhancing policy usability and accountability. To facilitate this research, we undertake the creation of the first publicly available corpus of human-annotated vague words and sentences specifically sourced from privacy policy documents. This corpus serves as the foundation for our empirical investigations into both word-level and sentence-level vagueness. We investigate a spectrum of modeling approaches, ranging from context-agnostic methods to sophisticated context-aware techniques, designed to predict the presence of vague words within a given context. Furthermore, we delve into the intricacies of sentence vagueness, proposing and evaluating auxiliary-classifier generative adversarial networks (AC-GANs) – a powerful framework for learning nuanced representations that capture the qualitative aspects of vague language. Our experimental results, conducted across a diverse dataset of privacy policies, demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approaches, highlighting their potential for real-world application. Finally, beyond technical contributions, we offer practical suggestions for resolving vagueness and ultimately improving the usability and accessibility of privacy policies, contributing to a more transparent and user-centric digital environment. . Machine learning methods have achieved impressive results in a wide range of natural language processing tasks. Among these, error correction, particularly in the context of non-native language learners, presents a unique set of challenges and opportunities. While traditional error correction systems often focus on identifying and correcting isolated errors, a more sophisticated approach considers the broader context of the sentence or text. Context-sensitive error correction, which leverages surrounding words and phrases, has demonstrably improved correction accuracy (Ng et al., 2005;Sheikh et al., 2011). The use of discriminative classifiers, trained on large datasets of corrected text, has further advanced the field, allowing for accurate mapping of erroneous forms to their correct counterparts. However, a fundamental assumption underlying many of these approaches is the generation of an exhaustive set of potential corrections for each error. This typically involves considering all possible prepositional choices, or other potentially erroneous words within the language. This exhaustive candidate generation strategy can be computationally expensive and, more importantly, often leads to a large number of implausible corrections being evaluated, degrading the performance of the subsequent classification stage. In the realm of second language acquisition, errors tend to cluster around specific linguistic phenomena, reflecting common transfer patterns from the learner’s native language or overgeneralization of grammatical rules. For example, non-native English speakers frequently misapply prepositions—a notoriously challenging area of English grammar—due to differences in prepositional usage across languages. Rather than treating all prepositions as equally likely candidates for correction, it seems intuitive and advantageous to focus on those that are most commonly confused. This motivates the exploration of  confusion sets , a restricted set of candidate corrections defined by the observed patterns of error in non-native text. This paper investigates a novel approach to context-sensitive error correction, centered on the idea of generating targeted confusion sets for candidate corrections rather than employing exhaustive sets. We specifically focus on preposition error correction within the context of non-native English writing. Our central thesis is that limiting the set of candidate corrections to a more realistic set of potential confusions—those prepositions frequently observed to replace each other in errors—leads to improved error correction performance. We begin by creating an annotated corpus of non-native English text, explicitly identifying common prepositional errors. From this corpus, we derive a probability matrix representing the likelihood of different prepositional confusions. Subsequently, we propose several strategies for generating confusion sets, employing this knowledge to constrain the candidate set during the classification process.

The burgeoning field of forensic linguistics has identified subtle linguistic markers indicative of an author’s native language, even when writing in a second language (L2). Inferring an author’s L1 from L2 writing, often termed native language identification (NLI), has traditionally been approached as a classification problem. Prior work has largely relied on feature engineering techniques, commonly utilizing character n-grams, a limited selection of part-of-speech (PoS) tags, and unigram function words as input to machine learning classifiers (e.g., Bingel et al., 2005; Dehak et al., 2009; Choudhury et al., 2010). While effective to some degree, this approach struggles to capture the long-range dependencies and complex collocations that are seemingly indicative of L1 influence, particularly in higher-order features. Syntax-based approaches, theoretically capable of modelling such longer-range dependencies, have often been hindered by the computational complexity of parsing and the dependency on accurate, language-specific parsers. Adaptor grammars, a relatively unexplored area within computational linguistics, offer a potentially promising avenue for addressing this challenge. Originally developed to model morphological and syntactic variation, adaptor grammars provide a framework for representing arbitrarily long n-grams conditioned on a context of PoS tags and words—effectively capturing collocations of variable length guided by grammatical structure. This capacity aligns well with the linguistic intuition that L1 interference manifests not only in isolated lexical choices or character patterns but also in systematic deviations from the target language's grammatical norms. By incorporating such collocations into a machine learning model, we hypothesize that NLI performance can be improved beyond that of traditional n-gram-based approaches. This paper investigates the application of adaptor grammars to the NLI task. We move beyond simple character n-grams to explore the utility of learned collocations, combining them with traditional features and exploring both maximum entropy (maxent) and induced syntactic language model (ISLM) classification approaches. Our contributions include a novel, minimalist baseline NLI system to provide a clear point of comparison, a method for extracting adaptor grammars from parallel corpora, and an analysis of the relative performance of various feature sets and classification techniques. We evaluate our approach on a standard NLI dataset and demonstrate that learned collocations, when integrated into a maxent model, yield significant performance gains over the baseline, indicating the potential of adaptor grammars for capturing subtle L1 influences in L2 writing. However, we also find that the ISLM approach presents a more nuanced picture, suggesting that the complexity of induced syntactic structures may introduce challenges in leveraging adaptor grammar features effectively for NLI.

The ultimate goal of natural language processing is to enable machines to understand and process human language in a way that mimics human comprehension. A crucial step towards this goal is constructing a robust sentence-level semantic representation. Two fundamental tasks contributing to this understanding are Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) and Semantic Role Labeling (SRL). WSD aims to identify the correct sense of a word in a given context, acknowledging that many words have multiple meanings. SRL, on the other hand, focuses on identifying the semantic roles played by different constituents in a sentence with respect to a predicate (e.g., agent, patient, instrument). While both tasks are individually well-studied, traditional approaches have largely treated them in isolation. This separation neglects potentially valuable logical constraints and dependencies that exist between WSD and SRL. For instance, the sense of a verb can significantly influence the expected semantic roles of its arguments, and conversely, the semantic roles assigned to constituents can provide valuable clues for WSD. Previous research has explored the benefits of incorporating information from one task into the other, often employing pipeline systems where WSD is performed first, and its output is then used to improve SRL, or vice versa. Such systems, while demonstrating some potential for improvement, are limited by their inherently sequential nature. Information flow is unidirectional, and errors made in one stage propagate to subsequent stages, potentially compounding the overall performance. Moreover, these pipeline systems typically lack the ability to capture complex logical interactions and mutual dependencies between WSD and SRL in a principled way. To overcome these limitations, this paper proposes a novel approach that jointly models WSD and SRL within a Markov Logic Network (MLN). Markov Logic Networks provide a powerful framework for representing and reasoning with complex relational knowledge, combining the expressiveness of first-order logic with the efficiency of Markov random fields. We formulate an MLN that encompasses both WSD and SRL, defining logical constraints that reflect the dependencies between word senses and semantic roles. The model learns these constraints from data, allowing it to capture intricate relationships that might be missed by pipeline systems or simpler statistical models. Specifically, we define first-order logic formulas that express how the sense of a verb influences the likely semantic roles of its arguments, and how the assigned semantic roles can inform the correct sense selection. By jointly inferring both word senses and semantic roles, our model leverages the complementary information from both tasks to achieve more accurate results.

Information retrieval (IR) has long faced the challenge of bridging the gap between a user’s information need, expressed as a query, and the content of available documents. Traditional IR models, heavily reliant on lexical matching, often struggle to capture the underlying semantic meaning and nuances within both queries and documents. This limitation frequently results in suboptimal retrieval performance, failing to surface relevant documents that employ different terminology than the query, or, conversely, retrieving irrelevant documents based on superficial lexical overlap. Recognizing this deficiency has spurred significant research into incorporating semantic knowledge into IR systems. The idea is simple: if we can understand the relationships between words – synonyms, hyponyms, meronyms, and so on – we can better match queries to documents even when they don't share the exact same terms. This pursuit has seen a resurgence in recent years, fueled by the increasing availability and sophistication of collaborative knowledge bases. Resources like Wikipedia, Wiktionary, and WordNet, built upon collective human knowledge, offer rich lexical semantic information that can be leveraged to enhance IR systems. While these knowledge bases have been utilized in computational linguistics for some time, their application to improve IR is still an area of active exploration. A central question remains: how best to incorporate these knowledge resources into IR models? Simply including synonyms often isn’t enough; a nuanced understanding of the relationships between query and document terms is crucial for accurate relevance assessment. This paper addresses this core question by undertaking a detailed analysis of the lexical semantic relations that naturally occur between query and document terms. We move beyond simple lexical matching to investigate how these relations—represented through various semantic relatedness measures—can be used as indicators of document relevance. Our work aims to dissect the information contained within these relationships, comparing and contrasting the strengths and weaknesses of three prominent knowledge bases – Wikipedia, Wiktionary, and WordNet – in representing these semantic connections for the purpose of improved information retrieval. Ultimately, we seek to identify the most beneficial ways to harness the power of these collaboratively-built resources to build more effective and semantically-aware IR systems. We believe a thorough understanding of how query and document terms are related semantically is a vital step towards realizing the full potential of knowledge-based IR. <!--stackedit_data: eyJoaXN0b3J5IjpbLTc1MDQxOTYxNV19 --> <!--stackedit_data: eyJoaXN0b3J5IjpbLTE5OTQ3MTQ0MjJdL1sgMTM5MzQ2MTI0MV19 --> <!--stackedit_data: eyJoaXN0b3J5IjpbLTE5OTQ3MTQ0MjJdL1sgMTM5MzQ2MTI0MV19 --> <!--stackedit_data: eyJoaXN0b3J5IjpbLTc1MDQxOTYxNV19 -->

Coreference resolution, the task of identifying all mentions referring to the same entity in a text, is a crucial component of many natural language understanding systems. While significant progress has been made in recent years, coreference resolution remains a challenging problem, particularly when dealing with complex linguistic phenomena such as anaphora and cataphora. A recurrent observation in contemporary coreference resolver design is that the inclusion of non-anaphoric mentions, i.e., mentions that do not refer to another mention in the text, can degrade system performance (Clark and Ziering, 2006;McEnery et al., 2006; Schäfer and Schäfer, 2013). Consequently, substantial effort has been dedicated to developing techniques for identifying and filtering out such non-anaphoric mentions  before  applying coreference resolution algorithms. This pre-processing step, termed  anaphoricity determination , aims to reduce the search space for the coreference resolver, ultimately leading to improved accuracy. Existing approaches to anaphoricity determination typically rely on hand-crafted features, statistical classifiers, or rule-based systems (Verspoor et al., 2007; Schäfer and Schäfer, 2013). These methods, while effective to varying degrees, often suffer from brittleness and a lack of generalizability across different domains and text types. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach to anaphoricity determination based on graph cuts, a powerful optimization technique widely used in computer vision and image processing (Boykov and Kolmogorov, 2004). Our approach frames anaphoricity determination as a graph partitioning problem, where nodes represent mentions in the text and edges represent relationships between mentions. By formulating the problem in this way, we can leverage graph cut algorithms to identify the optimal partitioning of the graph into anaphoric and non-anaphoric sets. This approach offers several advantages over existing methods. First, it is inherently global, considering the relationships between all mentions in the text simultaneously, rather than relying on local heuristics. Second, it is more flexible, allowing for the incorporation of various types of features representing mention characteristics and contextual information. Finally, it is amenable to efficient implementation, leveraging established graph cut algorithms and libraries. To validate the effectiveness of our graph-cut-based anaphoricity determination approach, we conduct extensive experiments on the ACE (Automatic Content Extraction) coreference resolution evaluation datasets (Lerman et al., 2000). We compare its performance against several competing anaphoricity determination methods, integrating each approach into a state-of-the-art learning-based coreference resolution system. Our results demonstrate that our graph-cut-based approach consistently outperforms the baseline methods in terms of improving overall coreference resolution accuracy, suggesting its potential for enhancing the performance of coreference resolution systems.

The rapid proliferation of online social systems has brought unprecedented opportunities for communication and connection, yet it has also amplified challenges associated with antisocial behavior. Harassment, personal attacks, and general negativity are pervasive issues that detract from the intended benefits of these platforms and can severely impact user wellbeing. Traditional approaches to addressing these problems often involve detection and mitigation  after  undesirable behavior has already occurred, a reactive strategy that frequently proves insufficient to prevent escalation and minimize harm. This paper addresses a critical gap in existing research by shifting the focus to  proactive  intervention. We introduce the novel task of early conversational failure prediction: predicting, from the very initial interactions of a conversation, whether it is likely to devolve into antisocial behavior. This proactive approach aims to enable timely interventions – such as automated warnings, moderation assistance, or even preemptive conversation redirection – at a stage when the interaction may still be salvageable, before lasting damage is done. Existing work in online social behavior often concentrates on detecting specific instances of toxic language or offensive content (Davidson et al., 2017;Glavas & McTear, 2018). While crucial, this reactive stance fails to capture the subtle, often gradual, shifts in conversational dynamics that precede overt aggression. Conversations rarely erupt out of nowhere; rather, they often follow a trajectory characterized by escalating tension, declining politeness, and increasingly confrontational exchanges. Recognizing these early warning signs requires an understanding of pragmatic devices – linguistic tools and strategies employed to manage social interactions and guide their course. This includes elements such as politeness markers, rhetorical prompts, topic transitions, and subtle shifts in tone. By focusing on these conversational nuances, rather than solely on the presence of overtly offensive language, we aim to develop models capable of anticipating problematic trajectories before they fully materialize. To facilitate this investigation, we have developed a framework for characterizing and analyzing the pragmatic devices used to initiate and structure online conversations. This framework allows us to systematically examine the relationship between initial conversational choices and subsequent interaction patterns, identifying features that are predictive of eventual failure. We then apply this framework in a controlled experimental setting to demonstrate the feasibility of detecting early warning signs of antisocial behavior. Our preliminary findings highlight the potential for developing prediction models that can contribute to safer and more constructive online social environments. This work represents a significant step towards building proactive systems that can mitigate online antisocial behaviors and foster healthier online interactions.

Minimum Error Rate Training (MERT) has become a cornerstone technique in modern machine translation (MT) system optimization. The fundamental principle of MERT involves iteratively tuning MT system parameters to maximize performance on a development or “tuning” set, as judged by an automatic evaluation metric like BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002). While highly effective when the final evaluation also relies on BLEU, the reality of MT evaluation is often more nuanced. Human evaluation, involving judgments of fluency, adequacy, and overall translation quality, remains a crucial component in assessing MT system performance, particularly in high-stakes applications. Consequently, the reliance on automatic metrics like BLEU as the sole driver of MERT can lead to systems optimized for deceptive scores, rather than true translation quality as perceived by human experts. Directly incorporating human judgments into the MERT process presents a significant challenge. Human evaluation is time-consuming, expensive, and inherently variable. The prospect of repeatedly soliciting human judgments during the iterative MERT optimization loop appears computationally and logistically impractical. However, the inherent value of human assessment cannot be discounted. This paper explores the feasibility of human-in-the-loop MERT, specifically addressing the bottleneck of continuous human input during the tuning process. We propose a novel approach that leverages human judgments to build a reusable resource, thereby minimizing the need for active human involvement during the MERT optimization itself. Our work centers around a newly developed metric, RYPT (a working title), designed to integrate human feedback into the MERT framework in an efficient manner. Unlike traditional approaches that require ongoing human evaluation, RYPT operates on a pre-existing database of human judgments, collected in an initial investment phase. This database serves as the foundation for the metric, allowing it to approximate human preferences without demanding real-time human input during the training process. This database building phase is the "human-in-the-loop" component, designed to be a one-time resource. Furthermore, we investigate a crucial aspect of MERT: the diversity of translation candidates generated during optimization. Traditional MERT algorithms often converge towards a limited set of high-scoring outputs, potentially sacrificing translation variety. We analyze the redundancy inherent in these candidate sets and demonstrate how this redundancy can be strategically exploited to improve the robustness and generalizability of the optimized system. We hypothesize that by considering a wider range of candidates, RYPT can provide a more accurate reflection of human judgment compared to traditional BLEU-based MERT.

The field of statistical machine translation (SMT) has witnessed remarkable progress over the last decade, largely due to advances in neural network architectures and training methodologies. However, even with the rise of neural machine translation (NMT), traditional SMT systems, particularly those leveraging log-linear models, continue to offer competitive performance and remain valuable for their interpretability and efficiency on resource-constrained tasks. A critical challenge within SMT, and one that has historically limited its potential, is the effective application of discriminative training techniques at scale. Traditional discriminative training approaches have often been restricted to fine-tuning a small number of feature weights or training relatively simple features. This limitation stems from the computational demands of optimizing a large number of parameters within a log-linear framework, particularly when dealing with the complex interactions between features. The core idea behind discriminative training in SMT is to move beyond maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) – where models are trained to predict the correct translation – and instead directly optimize a task-specific scoring function. This allows the model to learn a more nuanced relationship between input and output, accounting for factors like translation quality, fluency, and adequacy. However, scaling this approach to handle the vast parameter spaces characteristic of modern SMT systems has proven difficult. Previous attempts at larger-scale discriminative training have been limited by computational constraints and the difficulty of preventing overfitting. Such limitations have hindered our ability to fully exploit the potential of discriminative methods to improve translation quality. In this paper, we address these challenges by proposing a novel approach to discriminative training of SMT models that significantly scales up the number of trainable parameters. Specifically, we demonstrate a framework capable of training features with an unprecedented 150 million parameters – a full order of magnitude larger than previous efforts. Furthermore, we explore the integration of discriminative training to mitigate the performance degradation that often accompanies model pruning, a common technique for reducing the computational cost and memory footprint of SMT systems. Pruning, while effective in reducing model size, can often lead to a loss of probability mass and a subsequent decline in translation quality. Our approach aims to redistribute this lost probability mass using discriminative training, thereby preserving translation accuracy while maintaining a smaller, more efficient model. We validate our approach on the NIST MT06 dataset, demonstrating significant improvements over a strong baseline system and highlighting the effectiveness of our proposed techniques.

The use of vulgar language – often referred to as “swearing” or “cursing” – is a pervasive and complex feature of human communication. While often viewed negatively, vulgar expressions serve a remarkably diverse range of functions, extending far beyond simple displays of aggression. From reinforcing group solidarity and signaling informality to injecting humor or emphasizing emotional intensity, these words are deployed in nuanced ways that reflect social dynamics and contextual cues. Despite their prevalence and functional richness, the pragmatic aspects of vulgarity remain surprisingly underexplored, particularly through quantitative analysis and natural language processing (NLP) techniques. Existing research tends to focus on the offensive nature of these words, rather than the multitude of intentions behind their usage. This gap in understanding poses a significant challenge for various downstream NLP applications, including sentiment analysis, toxicity detection, and even nuanced dialogue understanding. A model that merely recognizes the presence of a vulgar word, without considering  why  it's being used, is unlikely to provide accurate or meaningful insights. Furthermore, the strategic deployment of vulgarity is often intertwined with demographic factors like age, gender, and socioeconomic background, adding another layer of complexity that necessitates further investigation. To address these limitations, this paper presents a novel exploration of the pragmatic intentions behind vulgar expressions and their relationship to social factors. We propose that a deeper understanding of these intentions can significantly enhance performance across a range of NLP tasks. Our contributions begin with the creation of a new dataset: a carefully curated collection of 7,800 tweets, sourced from users with publicly available demographic information, where every instance of a vulgar word has been annotated with one of six distinct categories representing potential uses—such as aggression, humor, informality, emphasis, identity signaling, or venting. This dataset provides the foundation for our subsequent analyses. Using this resource, we conduct the first detailed analysis of the pragmatic aspects of vulgarity, examining how contextual features correlate with different categories of usage, and how these usages vary across different demographic groups. Furthermore, we develop and evaluate a machine learning model capable of predicting the category of a vulgar word based solely on its surrounding context, achieving a macro F1 score of 67.4 across our six categories– a noteworthy achievement given the subtle and multifaceted nature of the task. Finally, we demonstrate the real-world utility of our approach by showing that incorporating this understanding of vulgar word usage significantly improves performance on a challenging benchmark dataset for hate speech detection, surpassing state-of-the-art results.

Phrase-based statistical machine translation (PBMT) has been the dominant paradigm for decades, achieving impressive results across a wide range of language pairs. However, conventional maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) approaches employed in PBMT face several limitations. A primary challenge arises from the scarcity of parallel training data, especially for low-resource language pairs. This paucity of data forces models to rely on a limited vocabulary of translation units (phrases), neglecting potentially valid, but infrequent, phrase translations. Consequently, many PBMT systems struggle to generalize beyond the observed training data, leading to suboptimal translation quality. Furthermore, the discrete nature of phrase representations in PBMT inherently restricts the ability to capture nuanced similarities between phrases, hindering the system's capacity to handle unseen or rare vocabulary. To mitigate these shortcomings, we investigate a class of continuous space translation models that represent translation units in a continuous vector space, enabling a more flexible and robust approach to translation estimation. This allows us to move beyond simple discrete phrase matching and instead leverage semantic similarity within the continuous space. In this paper, we propose a novel architecture for continuous space translation modeling, built upon a multi-layer neural network with a SOUL (Structured Output Learning) architecture (Chen et al., 2013). The SOUL framework allows us to directly optimize structured prediction tasks, enabling the joint learning of translation unit representations and their associated translation probabilities. By jointly optimizing this representation and the estimation process, we capture rich contextual information and improve the generalization capability of the translation model. Our approach overcomes the limitations of traditional discrete phrase representations by embedding translation units in a continuous space, facilitating the discovery of semantic relationships and better handling of unseen phrases. We evaluate our proposed model on both small-scale and large-scale English-to-French translation tasks. Our experimental results demonstrate that our continuous space translation model, when integrated as a rescoring component atop an existing n-gram translation system, yields significant improvements in translation performance, showcasing the effectiveness of our approach in overcoming the limitations of conventional MLE-based PBMT models. To the best of our knowledge, this is one of the first works to demonstrate the effectiveness of continuous space representations within a phrase-based translation framework, paving the way for future research in this promising direction.
