Distantly supervised relation extraction (DS-RE) has emerged as a viable approach to automatically learning relation patterns from text, circumventing the need for costly manual annotation. The core idea behind DS-RE is to leverage existing knowledge bases (KBs) – which contain assertions of the form (entity1, relation, entity2) – to automatically label sentences as positive or negative instances for a given relation. Sentences containing entity pairs mentioned in the KB are considered positive instances, while others are treated as negative. However, this approach is inherently noisy, as sentences labeled as positive often do not actually express the target relation. Addressing this noise remains a central challenge in DS-RE. Attention mechanisms have proven highly effective in mitigating this noise by enabling models to focus on the most relevant parts of a sentence when predicting the relation between the entity pair. Traditional attention models in DS-RE often utilize a 1-dimensional (1-D) vector attention mechanism, which aggregates information linearly. While successful in many cases, these approaches often struggle to effectively capture the complex contextual dependencies that indicate the presence or absence of a relation. The nuances of language necessitate considering different aspects of an instance – its words and its role within the broader sentence – to accurately identify valid positive instances. Further, the multi-instance learning (MIL) nature of DS-RE – where a single sentence can contain multiple instances (word groups) – presents additional challenges for attention mechanisms. To address these limitations, we propose a novel multi-level structured self-attention mechanism tailored for DS-RE within a MIL framework. Our approach leverages bidirectional recurrent neural networks (BiRNNs) to encode sentences, followed by two innovative levels of attention. First, we introduce a structured word-level self-attention mechanism that learns a 2-dimensional (2-D) matrix representation, where each row vector captures a weight distribution over different aspects of an instance in relation to the two target entities. This allows the model to selectively focus on specific words that are most indicative of the relation, rather than treating all words equally. Crucially, this structured representation enables the capture of complex word dependencies and contextual nuances. Second, to specifically address the MIL nature of DS-RE, we introduce a structured sentence-level attention mechanism. This mechanism also learns a 2-D matrix, with each row vector representing a weight distribution over different valid instances within the sentence. This allows the model to identify and prioritize the most reliable instances that support the relation.

The challenge of creating high-quality bilingual word embeddings remains a crucial task in cross-lingual information retrieval, machine translation, and multilingual NLP. Traditional approaches often rely on parallel corpora, which are costly and scarce for many language pairs. Furthermore, methods utilizing comparable corpora can suffer from alignment errors, introducing noise into the resulting embeddings. Recent work has explored leveraging shared semantic space, often through exploiting the inherent relationships between textual and visual data. The intuition is that concepts can be grounded in the visual world, providing a bridge between languages even in the absence of direct parallel text. For instance, the word “cat” in English and “gatto” in Italian both refer to the same visual entity – a feline animal. This shared visual grounding offers a powerful avenue for learning cross-lingual embeddings. Building upon this intuition, we introduce a novel deep learning framework that leverages images to enhance bilingual text embeddings. Our approach exploits bilingual image tags and descriptions, grounding each language's lexical representation in the shared visual realm. This allows the model to learn embeddings that are highly correlated across languages, even without requiring parallel corpora. The core of our model is built upon Partial Canonical Correlation Analysis (PCCA), a statistical technique designed to maximize the correlation between two sets of variables, conditioned on a third. The original PCCA formula works with linear projections aiming to discover linear correlations, but in reality, textual and visual data lie in a complex non-linear space. To address this limitation, we propose a Deep PCCA (DPCCA) model, a non-linear extension of PCCA that utilizes deep neural networks to learn these projections. This enables the model to better capture the underlying relationships between text and images in their respective high-dimensional spaces. Crucially, we also develop a novel stochastic iterative algorithm specifically tailored for optimizing this complex DPCCA architecture, allowing for efficient training on large datasets. Our experimental evaluation, conducted on multilingual word similarity and cross-lingual image description retrieval tasks, demonstrates that our PCCA and DPCCA models significantly outperform a wide range of existing methods. Notably, and demonstrating the power of this shared visual grounding, our models achieve these superior results even though they do not have access to any visual signal during test-time inference. The learned embeddings are inherently cross-lingual, highlighting the effectiveness of leveraging images as a bridge between languages. This work opens new avenues for cross-lingual learning, particularly in scenarios where parallel data is scarce or unavailable.

Discourse analysis is a crucial aspect of natural language understanding, encompassing the study of how sentences are organized and related to form coherent texts. Computational models of discourse have traditionally relied on identifying discourse markers (connectives) and analyzing their rhetorical relations to understand the overall structure and meaning of a text. Existing discourse treebanks, such as the Penn Discourse Treebank (PDTB) (Miltsatidis et al., 2009), have greatly facilitated this research, but their design and annotation schemes are largely based on English linguistic structures. Adapting these approaches to other languages, particularly those with significantly different syntactic and rhetorical conventions, presents considerable challenges. Chinese, with its flexible word order and reliance on implicit relationships, poses a particularly complex case for discourse analysis. Traditional Chinese discourse analysis often struggles to explicitly represent the hierarchical relationships between discourse segments, relying heavily on contextual interpretation rather than formalized structures. The Rhetorical Structure Theory (RST) (Mann and Thompson, 1988) provides a theoretical framework for representing discourse structure, organizing text into hierarchical units connected by rhetorical relations. However, effectively implementing RST in Chinese requires a suitable annotation scheme that accommodates the language's specific characteristics. This paper addresses these challenges by proposing a novel Connective-driven Dependency Tree (CDT) scheme for representing discourse structure in Chinese. Unlike previous approaches that treat connectives as mere signposts of discourse transitions, our CDT scheme leverages them as structural elements directly defining the hierarchical organization of the discourse. We draw inspiration from both the PDTB and RST, but adapt them specifically to the Chinese language, integrating the principles of dependency grammar to ensure coherence with the underlying syntactic structure. The core idea is to represent elementary discourse units (EDUs) as leaf nodes in a tree, with connectives serving as non-leaf nodes that explicitly define the relationships between the EDUs and establish the overall discourse hierarchy. Crucially, we employ dependency theory to determine the “nuclei” of these EDUs—the central concepts or propositions—globally within the discourse, rather than relying on local heuristics. This allows for more accurate representation of the semantic focus of each discourse segment. Guided by our CDT scheme, we have manually annotated a Chinese Discourse Treebank (CDTB) consisting of 500 documents. This corpus provides a valuable resource for training and evaluating computational models of Chinese discourse. Preliminary evaluations demonstrate the appropriateness of the CDT scheme for capturing Chinese discourse structure and confirm the utility of the CDTB corpus for advancing research in Chinese natural language processing.

The burgeoning field of word embedding representations has yielded various models – from traditional count vector models to sophisticated neural network architectures like Word2Vec, GloVe, and FastText – each offering a unique perspective on capturing semantic and syntactic information within vector spaces. While these models have demonstrated remarkable success in downstream NLP tasks, the question of “good” word representations remains a subject of ongoing investigation. Existing intrinsic evaluation methods, while helpful, often fall short of providing a complete picture of what these representations truly encode. The vast majority of current intrinsic evaluations focus on assessing the overall similarity between word vectors, treating them as points in a high-dimensional space and measuring distances or cosine similarities between them. However, this point-based perspective overlooks a crucial aspect of natural language: the need for structured subspaces that allow models to capture complex linguistic phenomena. Consider the seemingly simple task of identifying antonyms or resolving syntactic dependencies. These tasks necessitate the existence of well-defined subspaces within the embedding space—regions representing semantic opposition or grammatical roles—that are not adequately captured by a simple aggregate similarity score. This paper argues that current intrinsic evaluation methodologies are fundamentally limited by their point-based approach. Treating word vectors as isolated points obscures the crucial role of subspaces in encoding linguistic structure. To address this limitation, we propose a novel framework for intrinsic evaluation centered around the concept of  subspace evaluation . Our methodology identifies four fundamental criteria, derived from common challenges encountered by NLP systems, that are indicative of robust word representations. These criteria concern the ability of embeddings to capture antonymy, syntactic analogy, relational analogy (e.g., "king - man + woman = queen"), and semantic similarity beyond simple lexical overlap. We then develop targeted tests designed to directly assess whether these representations contain the necessary subspaces to satisfy each criterion. Rather than evaluating the entire embedding space as a whole, our tests focus on identifying and characterizing the relevant subspaces. By shifting the focus from overall vector similarity to subspace properties, our approach provides a more nuanced and informative assessment of word embedding quality. We demonstrate the utility of our methodology through a comparative analysis of a count vector model and several contemporary neural network models. Our results highlight important distinctions in how these models represent linguistic information, showcasing the strengths and weaknesses of each approach with respect to the four identified criteria. Ultimately, this work aims to move beyond superficial similarity metrics and provide a deeper understanding of the structural properties underlying effective word embedding representations, paving the way for more informed model selection and development.

The web represents a vast and largely unstructured repository of information, encompassing a diverse range of document types, formats, and generation processes. Extracting structured knowledge from this landscape is a critical challenge in natural language processing. Specifically, identifying mentions of real-world entities – such as people, organizations, locations, and various specialized entities – is a fundamental task underlying many downstream applications, from information retrieval and question answering to knowledge graph construction. While traditional entity recognition often relies on supervised machine learning models trained on manually annotated data, the sheer volume and inherent noisiness of web data make such an approach prohibitively expensive and often impractical. Certain entity types, however, exhibit predictable patterns that can be effectively captured using regular expressions (REs). Dates, times, email addresses, URLs, product codes, and course numbers are just a few examples of entities that frequently conform to definable patterns. Despite their utility, applying REs directly to web data suffers from limitations. The diversity of web documents and the myriad ways in which they are generated invariably introduce noise and variations that render any single RE imperfect. Achieving both high precision and high recall with a purely RE-based approach is often an unattainable goal. Traditional approaches to noisy data often advocate for extensive manual annotation or complex rule engineering. However, such methods often struggle to scale when encountering novel or highly variable entity types. This paper proposes a novel framework that leverages the complementary strengths of REs, deep learning, and human expertise to address the challenges of entity mention mining from noisy web data. Our central hypothesis is that REs, even imperfect ones, can serve as valuable sources of weak supervision, guiding and augmenting the training of deep learning models. Rather than attempting to create perfect REs, we embrace a more pragmatic approach: harvesting existing REs or generating new ones, and then using them to generate a large, albeit noisy, dataset of candidate entity mentions. This dataset then serves as training data for a neural network model. The crucial innovation lies in integrating human feedback: a small set of documents are manually annotated by experts, and the model is then fine-tuned on this revised dataset, allowing it to correct errors and refine its understanding of the entity type. This iterative process allows us to efficiently bootstrap high-performance entity recognition systems even in the presence of significant noise and limited labeled data. Our experimental results demonstrate that this integrated framework achieves impressive accuracy across diverse entity types, while demanding significantly less human annotation effort than conventional supervised learning approaches.

Phrase-based statistical machine translation (PB-SMT) has become a dominant paradigm in machine translation due to its balance of effectiveness and computational tractability (Koehn et al., 2003). At its core, PB-SMT relies on translating a source sentence into a target language by identifying and reordering phrases from the source language, guided by a statistical model learned from parallel corpora. The standard decoding process in PB-SMT follows a left-to-right approach, where the decoder incrementally builds the target sentence from left to right, considering possible phrase translations and reorderings at each step. While this methodology has proven remarkably successful, the inherent directionality of the decoding process has received comparatively less attention. The assumption that a left-to-right strategy is optimal stems from the intuitive notion that the source sentence, being the input, should be processed sequentially from beginning to end. However, it is not apparent that this assumption necessarily holds universally across all language pairs. The influence of linguistic typology and the peculiarities of source and target language structures raise the possibility that a different decoding direction might be advantageous. Specifically, it is conceivable that processing the source sentence from right to left could better capture certain grammatical or semantic dependencies, particularly in languages with significantly different word orders. Furthermore, the biases inherent in a left-to-right decoding strategy might disproportionately impact translation quality for certain language pairs, hindering the discovery of optimal translation hypotheses. This work seeks to systematically investigate the impact of decoding direction on PB-SMT performance, exploring both left-to-right and right-to-left decoding strategies, and ultimately proposing a bidirectional approach that integrates both. Our motivation is to understand the extent to which language-specific characteristics influence the effectiveness of the decoding direction and to develop a more robust and generally applicable translation framework. To this end, we conducted a comprehensive experimental evaluation across a diverse set of 272 language pairs, encompassing a wide range of typological features. The scale of this evaluation allowed us to identify patterns and trends in decoding direction performance across various language families and grammatical constructions. Surprisingly, our results revealed that, for a majority of language pairs, decoding from right to left consistently outperformed the standard left-to-right approach. This observation challenges the prevailing assumption about the optimality of left-to-right decoding and underscores the importance of considering the interplay between language structure and translation strategy.

Event extraction has emerged as a crucial task in natural language processing, enabling machines to understand the happenings described in text and their associated participants. Traditional event extraction systems often rely heavily on the presence of event keywords to trigger the extraction process, limiting their ability to identify events and their roles in situations where such keywords are absent or ambiguous. This dependence on keywords can lead to missed events, particularly those described in a more subtle or narrative fashion. Our work addresses this limitation by focusing on the identification of event role fillers within "secondary contexts" – those surrounding mentions of events that lack explicit event keywords. This capability is essential for a more robust and comprehensive event extraction system. Current event extraction approaches frequently employ a single-stage extraction process, aiming to simultaneously identify events and their associated roles. However, such an approach can be computationally expensive and often suffers from a lack of precision, particularly in complex documents. We hypothesize that a more effective strategy involves a layered approach, progressively focusing on relevant information within the document. To this end, we introduce a multilayered event extraction architecture designed to "zoom in" on event-related details in a gradual and targeted manner. Our proposed architecture consists of several interconnected modules, each responsible for a specific aspect of the extraction process. Initially, a document genre classifier analyzes the entire document to identify segments likely to contain event narratives. This step helps filter out irrelevant text and concentrates the extraction effort on promising sections. Subsequently, two types of sentence classifiers are employed: one to identify sentences containing potential event mentions, and another to further refine these mentions by distinguishing between event-related and non-event-related sentences. Finally, noun phrase classifiers are utilized to extract role fillers associated with the identified events, focusing specifically on those occurring within the secondary contexts surrounding the event mentions. These classifiers are organized in a pipeline fashion, allowing each module to build upon the output of the previous stage, progressively narrowing down the search for relevant information. By sequentially applying these filters, our system aims to more accurately pinpoint event-related information, even in the absence of explicit event keywords. We evaluate our system on the MUC-4 event extraction dataset and demonstrate that this multilayered approach consistently outperforms previous state-of-the-art systems, showcasing the potential of progressive refinement for improved event extraction. Our results suggest that peeling back the layers of textual information and focusing on secondary contexts is a promising direction for future research in event extraction.

The acquisition of language in early childhood represents a remarkable feat of learning, requiring infants to simultaneously construct a lexicon—a set of known words—and a phonetic system that maps lexical items to their diverse surface pronunciations. Consider the seemingly simple word “the,” which can manifest as [ði] or [ðə] depending on context and speaker variability. Traditional approaches to modeling language acquisition have largely treated these two components – lexical and phonetic – as separate endeavors. While significant progress has been made in understanding how children acquire vocabulary (e.g., through statistical learning of word frequencies; Newport, 1988) and how they develop a phonetic inventory (e.g., through perceptual learning; Werker & Tees, 1984), a unified framework that captures the interplay between these processes remains a challenge. Contemporary behavioral research, however, provides compelling evidence that lexical and phonetic development are intertwined—infants appear to acquire knowledge of both concurrently, leveraging information from one domain to inform learning in the other (e.g., Jusczyk et al., 1993; Fernald & Kuhl, 1987). This interconnectedness suggests that a more holistic model of language acquisition is required, one that jointly learns lexical and phonetic representations. The limitations of current models stem from modularity and limited inter-module interaction. Many lexicon acquisition models assume a predefined phonetic inventory and fixed pronunciations for lexical items (e.g., statistical co-occurrence models), neglecting the inherent variability of spoken language. Conversely, phonetic models often operate in isolation, without the benefit of lexical knowledge to guide their learning. Consequently, these models offer an incomplete picture of the complex learning processes observed in infants. To address these limitations, we propose a novel Bayesian model that unifies lexical and phonetic acquisition. Our model aims to capture the simultaneous development of a language model over lexical items and a probabilistic model of pronunciation variability, all without explicit access to a gold-standard lexicon. The core innovation lies in a clustering approach that groups together phonetic variants associated with the same lexical item, enabling the model to learn a distribution over pronunciations for each word. This clustering is guided by a log-linear model of pronunciation variability, which leverages articulatory features to explain observed phonetic differences. By integrating lexical and phonetic information within a single framework, our model offers a more ecologically valid and computationally tractable approach to simulating early language acquisition. This work diverges from existing approaches by eschewing handcrafted features or pre-determined phonetic categories, instead learning both representations from raw acoustic data.

The task of unsupervised word segmentation presents a significant challenge in natural language processing, particularly for morphologically rich languages like Chinese. Unlike languages such as English or Spanish, Chinese lacks explicit word delimiters, making it necessary to infer word boundaries from the raw stream of phonemes. Traditional Chinese word segmentation methods often rely on supervised learning approaches, requiring large, annotated corpora which are costly and time-consuming to create. This reliance on labeled data limits their adaptability to new domains or dialects. Recent advances in unsupervised learning have begun to address this limitation, exploring techniques that leverage statistical regularities and prior linguistic knowledge to infer word boundaries without explicit supervision. In this paper, we investigate a promising framework for unsupervised segmentation – Adaptor Grammars – and examine its applicability to the challenging task of Mandarin Chinese word segmentation. Adaptor Grammars (AGs) represent a powerful paradigm for non-parametric linguistic modeling and inference, allowing for the efficient expression and evaluation of a wide range of probabilistic models over sequential data (Jurafsky & Martin, 2008). Originally developed for unsupervised word segmentation from phonemic representations of child-directed speech in English (Xu & Cohen, 2012), AGs have demonstrated state-of-the-art performance by effectively capturing statistical patterns in the input data. The core idea behind AGs is to define a grammar that generates sequences of segments – in this case, Chinese phonemes – with varying probabilities. These probabilities are learned from the data itself, allowing the grammar to adapt and discover natural word boundaries. Building upon this prior success, we sought to determine whether Adaptor Grammars could be effectively applied to the significantly different linguistic characteristics of Mandarin Chinese. Unlike English, Mandarin possesses a complex syllable structure, marked tonal distinctions, and a rich system of compounding and other morphological processes. Therefore, simply porting existing AG-based models from English to Mandarin requires careful consideration and adaptation. In this work, we systematically explore a variety of Adaptor Grammar models tailored for Mandarin segmentation, manipulating different features and dependency structures to evaluate their impact on segmentation accuracy. We hypothesized that models explicitly encoding inter-word "collocational" dependencies—the statistical tendencies of certain segments or syllables to co-occur within words—would prove particularly effective. Furthermore, we explored the potential benefits of incorporating linguistic knowledge about Mandarin’s syllable structure and tonal system into the models, anticipating that these features might provide valuable cues for boundary detection. Surprisingly, our results revealed that while incorporating syllable structure and tone information indeed improved segmentation accuracy, the most significant gains stemmed from effectively modeling inter-word dependencies, suggesting that these dependencies capture essential information that might be redundant when compared to tonal or syllabic

The ability to understand the temporal relationships described in natural language text is a fundamental component of many natural language understanding tasks, including information extraction, question answering, and event sequence modeling (Verhagen, 2011). A critical sub-problem is classifying the temporal relations between events and their associated time expressions. For example, in the sentence “The meeting occurred after lunch,” the temporal relation is “AFTER.” Existing approaches to temporal relation classification have often relied on extensive feature engineering, leveraging lexical features, syntactic patterns, and even hand-crafted rules (Elming et al., 2011; Moore, 2000). While effective, these methods require significant domain expertise and can be brittle when applied to new datasets or domains. Furthermore, the availability of large, high-quality labeled datasets for training has historically been a bottleneck in advancing the field. This paper presents a simplified yet highly effective approach to temporal relation classification that minimizes feature engineering and demonstrates a novel method for acquiring high-quality annotations through selective crowdsourcing. Our core contribution lies in a tree-based similarity measure calculated using dependency parses. Rather than relying on complex feature engineering, our method leverages the structural information encoded in dependency parse trees to quantify the similarity between a given event-time expression pair and a set of gold standard examples representing different temporal relations. A convolution kernel operating on these parse trees provides a rich representation of the relationship, allowing the classifier to learn directly from the structure of the sentences. Remarkably, this comparatively simple approach surpasses the performance of current state-of-the-art systems, highlighting the potential of structure-aware methods in temporal relation classification. Recognizing that training data remains a significant impediment to further progress, we investigated the feasibility of crowdsourcing annotations for temporal relations. Previous work has shown that crowdsourcing can be a viable alternative to expert annotation for various NLP tasks, but quality control remains a key challenge. To address this, we devised a selective crowdsourcing strategy that leverages the inherent structure of the temporal relation classification problem. By assessing the difficulty of individual instances, we strategically target instances likely to benefit most from annotation, allowing us to achieve a substantial accuracy improvement (73.2%, an 8.6% gain) over the previous state-of-the-art while simultaneously reducing annotation effort by up to 37%. This demonstrates the efficiency and effectiveness of our approach for acquiring high-quality annotations in a cost-effective manner. Ultimately, we believe our work contributes both a novel, structurally-informed classification method and a practical strategy for overcoming the data scarcity problem in temporal relation classification.

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has achieved remarkable progress in recent years, fueled by the availability of massive parallel corpora and advances in deep learning architectures (Bahdanau et al., 2014;Wu et al., 2016). However, the performance of NMT systems degrades significantly when applied to low-resource language pairs, where parallel training data is scarce. Acquiring extensive, high-quality parallel corpora for less-spoken languages remains a significant bottleneck in extending NMT capabilities globally. Traditional approaches to addressing this challenge include back-translation (Sennrich et al., 2016), transfer learning from high-resource languages (Zoph et al., 2016), and leveraging monolingual data through methods like iterative back-translation (Sennrich and Zhang, 2019). While these techniques offer some improvements, they often struggle to fully compensate for the lack of direct parallel supervision, particularly when facing drastically different language families or structures. Recent research in meta-learning offers a promising avenue to overcome these limitations. Meta-learning, also known as “learning to learn,” aims to train models that can rapidly adapt to new tasks with limited data, by leveraging experience gained from solving a diverse set of related tasks. The core idea is to learn initial model parameters that are well-suited for fast fine-tuning on new tasks. This paradigm aligns naturally with the low-resource NMT scenario, where the goal is to quickly adapt a model to a new language pair with minimal parallel data. In this paper, we explore the application of meta-learning to low-resource NMT, specifically focusing on extending the Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) algorithm (Finn et al., 2017). MAML seeks to learn a good initialization for model parameters such that a small number of gradient steps on a new task leads to significant performance gains. We frame low-resource translation as a meta-learning problem, where we train a model on a set of multilingual, high-resource language pairs, enabling it to learn to quickly adapt to unseen low-resource languages. To tackle the challenge of input-output mismatch that arises when training a multilingual NMT model, we incorporate the universal lexical representation (Gu et al., 2018b), which projects words from different languages into a shared semantic space. This shared space helps to bridge the gap between languages with different vocabularies and morphologies, making it easier to transfer knowledge across languages. We rigorously evaluate our meta-learning strategy using a diverse set of eighteen European languages as source tasks and five distinct languages (Romanian, Latvian, Finnish, Turkish, and Korean) as target tasks.

The burgeoning field of opinion mining seeks to automatically extract subjective information from text, identifying not only the sentiment expressed but also the targets of that sentiment (Liu, 2012). While significant progress has been made in opinion mining for individual languages, the ability to seamlessly transfer knowledge and models across languages remains a challenging and largely unexplored area. Cross-lingual opinion mining aims to address this gap, enabling the application of opinion mining techniques to languages where labeled data is scarce or unavailable. A key obstacle in this endeavor is the lack of parallel corpora with fine-grained opinion annotations, which are crucial for training effective supervised systems. Existing approaches often rely on complex techniques such as delexicalization (Linguistic Data, 2018) or bootstrapping, which can be computationally expensive or suffer from performance degradation. In this paper, we introduce a novel cross-lingual framework for fine-grained opinion mining that overcomes these limitations through bitext projection. Our approach requires only a functional opinion mining system in a source language (e.g., English) and a readily available word-aligned parallel corpus between the source and target languages. The core idea is to project opinion frames – structured representations of opinion targets, sentiments, and associated words – from the source language to the target language. This allows us to automatically annotate a parallel corpus in the target language with opinion frames, effectively generating pseudo-labeled data that can be used to train a new opinion mining system without requiring expensive manual annotations. A critical component of our framework is a new dependency-based model for opinion mining. Unlike many existing models that rely on computationally intensive techniques such as integer programming or reranking, our model leverages syntactic dependency information to identify opinion targets and sentiment orientations. We demonstrate that this dependency-based model achieves state-of-the-art performance on English opinion mining tasks, rivaling or surpassing methods that employ more complex and resource-intensive techniques. Furthermore, in the cross-lingual setting (specifically, English to Portuguese), our approach demonstrates a significant advantage over both a supervised system trained on limited labeled data in Portuguese and a delexicalized model utilizing universal dependency tags and bilingual word embeddings. This highlights the efficiency and effectiveness of our bitext projection approach combined with the strength of our dependency-based opinion mining model. We believe that our work represents a significant step towards building robust and adaptable cross-lingual opinion mining systems, opening up new avenues for understanding and analyzing public opinion across diverse languages and cultures.

The burgeoning volume of unstructured text data available online presents a significant challenge and opportunity for information extraction. A crucial step in this process is entity linking (EL), also known as named entity disambiguation (NED). Entity linking aims to identify mentions of entities within text and connect them to their corresponding entries in a structured knowledge base (KB), such as Freebase or Wikidata. This process is vital for a multitude of applications, including question answering, information retrieval, and knowledge graph construction. Effectively linking entities allows us to bridge the gap between the vast expanse of unstructured text and the well-organized knowledge stored within KBs, thereby enabling richer information access and improved user experiences on the web. For example, a user searching for “Apple” can be directed to information about either the fruit or the technology company, depending on the context of the search query. Traditional approaches to entity linking often frame the task as a classification problem: given a mention, the goal is to classify it into one of the possible KB entities. While successful, these classification-based methods have inherent limitations. They typically treat each candidate entity independently, failing to exploit the rich relational information intrinsically embedded within the knowledge base. Entities are rarely isolated; they exist within a complex web of relationships, and considering these relationships can significantly improve linking accuracy. For instance, if a mention appears in a sentence describing a “CEO,” linking it to the CEO of a known company is more likely to be correct than linking it to a CEO of a lesser-known entity. In this paper, we challenge the classification paradigm and propose a novel learning to rank (LTR) framework for entity linking. We argue that entity linking is fundamentally a ranking problem: given a mention, the task is to rank candidate entities from the KB in order of their likelihood of being the correct link. Our approach leverages the relational structure of the KB to effectively inform the ranking process, considering not just the mention itself, but also the connections between candidate entities and other entities within the KB. This allows our model to capture contextual cues and semantic similarities that are often overlooked by classification-based methods. We specifically incorporate mechanisms to factor in the contextual relevance of each candidate entity, weighting them according to their relationships within the knowledge graph. Experimental results on the TAC 2009 dataset demonstrate the significant advantages of our LTR framework.

The burgeoning field of task-oriented dialogue systems has achieved remarkable progress in areas like booking flights or ordering food. However, negotiation dialogues present a particularly complex challenge, requiring agents to not only understand and respond to user utterances, but also to strategically manage resources and reach mutually beneficial agreements. Recent advances in neural dialogue modeling have shown promise in this domain, treating negotiation as an end-to-end task where a single model learns to map dialogue history to responses (Li et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2017). While effective to some degree, these end-to-end approaches often struggle to provide control over the agent's negotiation strategy. The inherent complexity of learning both strategy and language generation simultaneously can lead to degenerate solutions, where the agent prioritizes maximizing rewards over achieving a truly satisfactory outcome, or falls into repetitive, unproductive dialogue patterns. This lack of strategic control hinders both interpretability and the ability to incorporate domain-specific knowledge. Furthermore, the reliance on reinforcement learning (RL) for training in such complex environments often exacerbates these issues, requiring extensive exploration and leading to unstable learning dynamics. To address these limitations, we propose a novel, modular approach to negotiation dialogue that explicitly  decouples  strategy and generation. Our core insight is that negotiation can be effectively modeled as a sequence of high-level decisions—the strategy—followed by a separate process of generating natural language to communicate that strategy. We represent this strategy using  coarse dialogue acts , which are abstract representations of the agent’s intended action (e.g., propose(price=50), accept(offer=45), counteroffer(price=40)). This allows for a clearer separation of concerns: strategy is determined independently, and generation focuses solely on crafting a compelling linguistic realization of that strategic intent. This decoupling offers numerous advantages. First, it allows for flexible control over the negotiation strategy. We can employ supervised learning to mimic expert negotiators, utilize reinforcement learning to optimize for specific reward functions, or leverage domain-specific knowledge to guide the agent towards pre-defined goals. Critically, this separation prevents the degeneracy problems often seen in end-to-end RL-based approaches. Second, we utilize a retrieval-based generation mechanism, effectively curating a set of candidate utterances and selecting the one best suited to the current context. This approach inherently maintains context-awareness and facilitates the generation of diverse, human-like responses without requiring extensive end-to-end training. To evaluate our approach, we benchmark it on the recently introduced DEALORNODEAL game (Clark et al., 2019), known for its challenging negotiation dynamics.

Human-robot interaction (HRI) is rapidly expanding beyond simple task execution towards collaborative efforts requiring natural and effective communication. Dialogue systems are crucial for enabling this collaboration, allowing humans and robots to exchange information and coordinate actions. However, evaluating the usability and effectiveness of these dialogue systems remains a significant challenge. Traditional methods often focus solely on objective metrics, like task completion time or success rate, which may not fully capture the nuances of user experience and satisfaction. Subjective measures, such as user questionnaires, provide valuable insights into perceived usability but can be influenced by factors independent of the system’s performance. This paper aims to bridge this gap by comprehensively evaluating a human-robot dialogue system using both objective and subjective measures, and to analyze the interplay between them. Specifically, we developed a human-robot dialogue system designed to facilitate collaboration in a tangible, engaging task: building wooden construction toys. This task provides a natural context for human-robot interaction, requiring users to understand and follow instructions, provide feedback, and coordinate actions with the robot. We then conducted a study involving naïve subjects interacting with the system under varied conditions. Following these interactions, participants completed a user-satisfaction questionnaire, providing a rich dataset of subjective opinions regarding the system’s usability and overall experience. This study yielded a wide spectrum of both objective metrics – such as dialogue length, task completion time, and the number of robot assistance requests – and subjective feedback – including ratings of ease of use, perceived naturalness, and overall satisfaction. To move beyond simply reporting these metrics and to understand their relative importance in shaping user opinions, we employed a method inspired by the PARADISE evaluation framework (Walker et al., 1997). PARADISE provides a principled approach for deriving a performance function that maps system characteristics to user satisfaction. By applying this methodology to our data, we were able to identify the key factors driving user satisfaction. Our findings revealed that the number of repetition requests – instances where users had to ask the robot to repeat an instruction – had a demonstrably negative impact on satisfaction. Conversely, shorter dialogue lengths and users’ ability to accurately recall the system’s instructions were positively correlated with higher satisfaction ratings. This suggests that clarity, conciseness, and ease of understanding are paramount in designing effective human-robot dialogue systems. Furthermore, the analysis provides valuable insights into the linguistic behaviors and instructional strategies that contribute to a more positive and productive collaborative experience.

The notion of creativity has captivated researchers across diverse fields, from the arts and sciences to cognitive psychology and artificial intelligence. While creativity is often associated with groundbreaking innovations and novel ideas, its underlying mechanisms remain a subject of ongoing investigation. In the realm of natural language processing, understanding and quantifying creativity, particularly in lexical composition – the way words are combined to form phrases and expressions – poses a unique and challenging problem. Everyday language is replete with combinations of words, yet only a select few spark a sense of originality, interest, or even artistic merit. Why do phrases like "disadvantageous peace" or "metal to the petal" resonate with our minds as creative expressions, whereas commonplace pairings such as "quiet teenager" or "geometrical base" fail to elicit the same response? This paper seeks to address this fundamental question by presenting a statistical exploration of lexical compositions and their relationship to perceived creativity. Our motivation stems from the observation that while computational models have achieved remarkable progress in various NLP tasks, a systematic understanding of creativity in language remains elusive. Existing approaches often focus on novelty or surprise, but these measures fail to capture the nuances of human judgment regarding creativity. A phrase can be statistically rare without being perceived as creative, and vice versa. We hypothesize that creativity in lexical composition is not solely determined by the individual words involved or their frequencies but rather by a complex interplay of factors encompassing semantic relationships, contextual associations, and unexpected juxtapositions. To investigate this hypothesis, we adopt a quantitative approach, drawing upon principles of information theory and lexical semantics. We begin by examining various correlates of perceived creativity, exploring how measures such as word frequency, semantic distance, and connotation can predict human ratings of lexical compositions. In particular, we leverage information theoretic measures like mutual information and surprisal to quantify the unexpectedness of word pairings, and analyze the connotative strengths and orientations of individual words to assess their potential to evoke emotional or imaginative responses. The initial exploratory phase will involve examining the relationship between such features and human judgments of creativity, establishing a baseline for the more sophisticated analysis that follows. Building upon this foundation, we present a series of experiments based on supervised learning techniques. We construct a dataset of lexical compositions annotated with human judgments of creativity and train machine learning models to predict these ratings based on a diverse set of features derived from lexical, semantic, and statistical properties of the phrases.

Phrase-based statistical machine translation (PBSMT) has long been a cornerstone of machine translation research and practice. Its modularity and relative ease of implementation have made it a robust and widely deployed approach. Central to the success of PBSMT systems is the ability to accurately model reordering phenomena, which arise from the significant syntactic and word order differences between languages. Traditional PBSMT systems rely heavily on reordering models to capture these dependencies, and lexicalized reordering models have emerged as a particularly effective class of such models. However, despite their success, lexicalized reordering models face inherent limitations that hinder their ability to fully capture the complexities of reordering. These drawbacks primarily stem from their context insensitivity, susceptibility to ambiguity, and vulnerability to data sparsity. Context insensitivity arises because lexicalized models typically consider only the immediate phrase pair in isolation, disregarding the broader linguistic context that influences reordering decisions. This can lead to inaccurate reordering probabilities when the optimal ordering depends on preceding or following phrases. Furthermore, lexicalized reordering models often struggle with ambiguity, where a single phrase pair can have multiple plausible orderings depending on the context. Finally, the sparsity of training data, particularly for less frequent phrase pairs, poses a significant challenge, leading to unreliable reordering estimates. To address these shortcomings, we propose a novel neural reordering model that leverages the power of deep learning to overcome the limitations of traditional approaches. Our model moves beyond the isolated analysis of phrase pairs by explicitly conditioning reordering probabilities on the words within both the current and preceding phrase pairs. This significantly enhances context sensitivity and reduces reordering ambiguity. To mitigate the data sparsity problem, we adopt a shared classifier architecture, representing all phrase pairs as continuous space vectors, thereby allowing the model to generalize from limited data. The core idea is that by mapping phrase pairs to a continuous vector representation, we can effectively “smooth” the reordering probabilities and avoid overfitting to sparse training data. The resulting model offers a powerful and flexible alternative to lexicalized reordering models, and preliminary experimental results on the NIST Chinese-English translation task demonstrate significant improvements over state-of-the-art lexicalized reordering models, validating the efficacy of our approach. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. First, we provide a brief overview of related work in reordering modeling within both statistical and neural machine translation frameworks. Next, we detail the architecture and training procedure of our proposed neural reordering model.

Commonsense knowledge is a foundational element of human understanding, enabling us to reason about the world, make predictions, and navigate everyday situations. While explicit knowledge about facts like “Paris is the capital of France” is readily captured in structured knowledge bases (KBs) like Freebase, commonsense knowledge—the vast collection of implicit, everyday understandings—remains significantly less formalized. This poses a challenge for various natural language processing tasks, including question answering, natural language inference, and dialogue systems, which often require drawing upon commonsense reasoning. ConceptNet (Speer and Havasi, 2012) represents a valuable attempt to capture this commonsense knowledge, offering a curated resource of relationships between concepts expressed as phrases. However, ConceptNet, like most KBs, is inherently incomplete, leaving a significant gap in the expressed commonsense knowledge. Addressing this incompleteness is a central problem in the field of knowledge base completion (KBC). Traditionally, KBC has focused on enriching KBs like Freebase, which feature a relatively fixed and bounded set of entities. The core task involves predicting missing relationships between these entities. However, ConceptNet presents a unique challenge for KBC due to its representation of concepts as phrases rather than discrete entities, and the resulting unbounded nature of its concept set. This modularity allows for a greater level of expressiveness, but makes traditional KBC approaches, which rely on entity embeddings and fixed vocabulary, less applicable. In this paper, we tackle the problem of commonsense knowledge base completion by framing it within the traditional KBC paradigm, adapting existing techniques to handle ConceptNet’s phrase-based representation. Our core contribution lies in developing neural network models capable of scoring the validity of tuples comprising arbitrary phrases. Unlike prior work that restricts scoring to known entities, our models are designed to operate on the unbounded set of phrases found in ConceptNet. We evaluate the performance of these models by their ability to discriminate between true, held-out tuples from ConceptNet and randomly generated, false tuples. We demonstrate the efficacy of a bilinear model employing a simple additive architecture for representing phrases, achieving strong performance on this discrimination task. Further, we conduct a manual evaluation to assess the quality of novel tuples generated by our trained model, finding that these tuples achieve a quality level comparable to medium-confidence tuples already present in ConceptNet. This suggests our approach can effectively contribute to the enrichment and expansion of commonsense knowledge resources. By enabling the systematic completion of ConceptNet, we hope to facilitate progress in a wide range of downstream NLP applications reliant on commonsense reasoning.

Information Extraction (IE) has long been a central task in natural language processing, aiming to automatically identify and structure semantic relationships from unstructured text. Traditional IE systems, however, are largely constrained by the need for large, manually annotated datasets specific to each relation type they aim to extract. This dependence on supervised learning severely limits their applicability to the vast and ever-evolving landscape of information found on the web, where new relations constantly emerge. Open Information Extraction (OpenIE) seeks to alleviate this bottleneck by automatically discovering semantic relations without a predefined schema. Systems like TextRunner (Angermueller et al., 2011) represent a significant step forward, capable of extracting an unbounded number of relations directly from text. Nevertheless, a persistent challenge remains: how to improve the precision and recall of these open systems to make them practically useful. Current OpenIE systems often suffer from extracting noisy or irrelevant relations, hindering their downstream application. While these systems perform admirably, their performance highlights the need for optimized approaches in relation extraction. This paper addresses this challenge by introducing WOE (Wikipedia-enhanced Open Extraction), a novel OpenIE system that achieves a significant improvement in both precision and recall compared to existing state-of-the-art models, most notably TextRunner. The core innovation of WOE lies in its self-supervised learning approach. Recognizing the vast wealth of structured knowledge contained within Wikipedia, we leverage its infoboxes – structured tables that describe entities and their attributes – as a source of training data. Specifically, we establish heuristic matches between Wikipedia infobox attribute value pairs and the corresponding sentences in Wikipedia articles. By utilizing this readily available, automatically generated data, WOE effectively trains its relation extractor without requiring costly manual annotation. Furthermore, WOE mirrors the design choices of TextRunner, eschewing lexicalized features and maintaining the ability to handle an unbounded set of semantic relations, ensuring broad applicability. Finally, WOE offers considerable flexibility in its implementation. Operating in two distinct modes, WOE can achieve comparable speed to TextRunner when relying on part-of-speech (POS) tag features alone. However, when incorporating dependency-parse features, WOE demonstrates even greater improvements in precision and recall, showcasing its adaptability to varying computational constraints and performance demands. This paper presents WOE, effectively demonstrating that wikipedia can be leveraged as a valuable source of data for Open Information Extraction. In the subsequent sections, we detail the architecture and training methodology of WOE, present a thorough evaluation of its performance alongside TextRunner, and analyze the effectiveness of its dependence on Wikipedia data.

The burgeoning availability of online academic resources has transformed how researchers share and disseminate their work. A crucial component of this online presence is the academic homepage, serving as a digital curriculum vitae showcasing a researcher's expertise, research interests, and collaborative endeavors. Accurate and comprehensive extraction of publication information from these homepages is therefore invaluable for automatically building researcher profiles, constructing collaboration networks, and assessing research impact. However, extracting publication strings from academic homepages presents a significant challenge. The unstructured nature of web pages, coupled with the diverse layout and presentation styles across different universities and departments, results in substantial variability in how publication information is displayed. Publication strings may appear in various positions on a homepage and adopt a multitude of formats, making it difficult to develop a robust extraction system. Existing methods often struggle to generalize across this positional and structural heterogeneity. To address this challenge, we propose PubSE (Publication String Extraction), a novel hierarchical model designed specifically for extracting publication strings from academic homepages. Our model leverages a Bi-LSTM-CRF architecture, a proven approach for sequence labeling tasks, and extends it with a hierarchical structure to capture the diverse positional and structural characteristics of publication information across different homepages. Specifically, PubSE first identifies potential regions on the homepage where publication information is likely to be located. Then, it applies a sequence labeling model to these regions to identify the publication strings. This hierarchical approach allows the model to adapt to the varying layouts and structures commonly found across academic homepages. Furthermore, we introduce an alternating training method, a novel approach that optimizes the different components of our hierarchical model effectively. To validate the efficacy of PubSE, we conducted extensive experiments on a real-world dataset of academic homepages. Our results demonstrate that PubSE significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches, achieving up to an 11.8% improvement in F1-score. This substantial performance gain underscores the effectiveness of our hierarchical model and alternating training strategy in accurately extracting publication information from the inherently diverse landscape of academic homepages. The ability to automatically extract this information provides a valuable resource for various research-related applications, ultimately contributing to a deeper understanding of the scholarly landscape. --- I hope this fulfills your prompt. The rise of social media has created an unprecedented digital archive of language use, reflecting the incredible diversity of human communication. While this explosion of data presents exciting opportunities for natural language processing (NLP), a significant challenge remains: the under-representation and inadequate handling of dialectal variation within existing NLP tools. Dialects, reflecting regional, social, and ethnic identities, are a vital component of linguistic diversity, yet current NLP models often struggle to accurately process and understand language associated with these communities. A particularly compelling case study lies in the examination of African-American English (AAE), a vibrant and historically rich dialect with unique linguistic features. Though AAE is increasingly prevalent in online spaces, it remains largely absent from the datasets and methodologies that underpin many NLP applications. This disparity can lead to biased outcomes and limit the effectiveness of NLP tools for the very communities they are intended to serve. This paper addresses this critical gap by conducting a focused case study of AAE on Twitter. Our work is motivated by the need to develop more inclusive and equitable NLP technologies that can accurately handle the linguistic diversity present in social media data. We hypothesize that by leveraging demographic information associated with geo-located tweets, we can distantly supervise a model to identify instances of AAE-like language and subsequently analyze its linguistic characteristics. Previous work has largely overlooked the connection between demographic information and dialectal variation in social media, focusing instead on purely linguistic features. Further, existing language identification and dependency parsing tools are often trained on corpora that are overwhelmingly dominated by standard dialects, leading to poor performance when applied to less represented dialectal varieties. We aim to empirically demonstrate this limitation, specifically examining the performance of existing tools on AAE-like text compared to text associated with speakers of standard American English. By identifying and mitigating these performance disparities, we hope to contribute to the development of more robust and equitable NLP technologies. To this end, we propose a distantly supervised model that leverages demographic data (specifically, self-reported race/ethnicity) associated with geo-located tweets to identify AAE-like language. We then conduct a series of analyses to verify that this identified language exhibits characteristics consistent with known AAE linguistic phenomena, such as habitual  be  and copula deletion. Finally, we construct an ensemble classifier for language identification that demonstrably improves performance on AAE-like text and release a novel corpus of tweets containing AAE-like language, providing a valuable resource for future research.

Dependency parsing, the task of analyzing the grammatical structure of sentences by identifying syntactic relationships between words, has become a cornerstone of modern natural language processing (NLP) (Nivre, 2008). Achieving high accuracy in dependency parsing is crucial for a wide range of downstream applications, including machine translation, information extraction, and question answering. The performance of dependency parsers is heavily influenced by the inference algorithm employed to decode the best parse tree given a model's scores. Traditionally, high-order features have proven invaluable for capturing nuanced syntactic dependencies (McDonald & Pereira, 2005; Mc- Cann et al., 2005), yet incorporating these features introduces a significant computational hurdle: the decoding problem becomes NP-hard (Basu et al., 2016). Consequently, a considerable amount of research effort has focused on developing sophisticated optimization techniques to tackle this combinatorial problem, including techniques like dual decomposition (Huang & Chiang, 2009) and Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling (Pereira et al., 2002). These methods, while effective, often come with substantial computational overhead and complexity. In this paper, we challenge this prevailing view by proposing a surprisingly simple and effective alternative: a randomized greedy inference algorithm. Our central thesis is that, despite its apparent simplicity, a well-designed greedy algorithm can achieve near-optimal parsing accuracy, rivaling or even surpassing more complex optimization methods. We argue that the inherent structure of dependency parsing, particularly in the context of high-order features, allows the randomized greedy approach to effectively escape local optima and converge to high-quality solutions. To support this claim, we present a three-pronged analysis and empirical evaluation. First, we provide a theoretical analysis quantifying the number of local optima that the randomized greedy algorithm must traverse during the parsing process for first-order dependency parsing. Second, we demonstrate that our greedy algorithm outperforms dual decomposition, a state-of-the-art optimization method, when applied to second-order dependency parsing. Finally, and most compellingly, we present extensive empirical results across 14 languages from the CoNLL shared tasks, demonstrating that our randomized greedy approach, incorporating up to third-order features and global constraints, consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, including dual decomposition and MCMC sampling. These findings suggest that a shift in mindset may be warranted in dependency parsing: that seemingly “greedy” approaches, when strategically randomized, can provide a powerful and surprisingly effective solution to a complex combinatorial problem. The burgeoning field of representation learning has become a cornerstone of modern Natural Language Processing (NLP), driving advancement across a diverse range of tasks. However, current approaches often grapple with limitations in capturing the multifaceted nature of text – particularly the intricate interplay between local semantic nuances and the overarching global structure. Many existing representation models either fail to adequately encode structural information or rely on rigid, pre-defined structures, hindering both performance and generalization capabilities in downstream applications. This deficiency is especially prominent in text classification tasks, where the meaning of a text is not solely determined by individual word meanings but also by the relationships between those words and how they contribute to the overall textual organization. In this paper, we address this challenge directly by introducing a novel framework designed to simultaneously learn both local semantic and global structure representations for text classification, without relying on computationally expensive and often imperfect parsers. Our core contribution is the Sandwich Neural Network (SNN), a model architecture capable of automatically extracting these essential textual components. The SNN is predicated on the insight that semantic and structural information contribute to text representation in varying degrees, depending not only on the corpus as a whole but also on the specific characteristics of individual instances. Consequently, simply concatenating these representations is insufficient to achieve optimal performance; a more nuanced fusion strategy is required. To tackle this fusion problem, we propose two innovative strategies: the Adaptive Learning Sandwich Neural Network (AL-SNN) and the Self-Attention Sandwich Neural Network (SA-SNN). AL-SNN dynamically learns the weights assigned to the semantic and structural components at the corpus level, effectively adapting to the prevalent relationships within the training data. Furthermore, SA-SNN extends AL-SNN by incorporating a self-attention mechanism that allows it to further tailor the weighting scheme at the individual instance level, capturing fine-grained dependencies and nuances that might be missed by a corpus-level approach. Our experimental evaluation, conducted across a range of text classification benchmarks including sentiment analysis (MR, SST-5), question type classification (TREC), and subjectivity classification (SUBJ), demonstrates the effectiveness of our proposed approach. We achieve competitive results, attaining accuracies of 82.1% on MR, 50.4% on SST-5, 96% on TREC, and 93.9% on SUBJ, highlighting the benefits of adaptive learning and instance-specific weighting for fusing local semantic and global structural information in text representation. These results suggest that our SNN-based architectures offer a promising avenue for advancing the state-of-the-art in text classification and related NLP tasks. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

The ability to understand and reason about quantities—how much of something there is—is a fundamental aspect of human cognition. This capacity extends beyond simply counting objects; it encompasses a broader range of skills including comparing sets (e.g., "which group has more?"), understanding vague quantifiers (e.g., "a few," "many"), and estimating proportions (e.g., "what fraction of the objects are red?"). While often studied in isolation, accumulating evidence suggests that these seemingly distinct quantification mechanisms are deeply intertwined within the human mind, underpinned by a shared, nonsymbolic cognitive ability. This shared foundation allows us to rapidly and intuitively estimate and compare the magnitudes of sets directly from visual scenes—a skill that is remarkably robust even in the absence of formal numerical training. Inspired by this understanding, we investigate the possibility of jointly learning these different quantification tasks in a computational model, specifically exploring whether information learned from simpler tasks can benefit performance on more complex ones. Current computational approaches to quantity estimation often treat these tasks as separate problems, hindering the potential to leverage inter-task dependencies. Our work addresses this limitation by proposing a multi-task learning framework designed to integrate set comparison, vague quantification, and proportional estimation within a single model. We hypothesize that learning these tasks concurrently will capture the underlying cognitive processes involved in nonsymbolic magnitude processing, leading to improved performance and generalization capabilities. In this paper, we present a computational model that demonstrates this potential. We find that incorporating information from lower-complexity tasks—namely, set comparison and vague quantification—significantly enhances the accuracy of proportional estimation compared to when the proportional task is learned in isolation. Furthermore, our model exhibits encouraging generalization capabilities, accurately estimating proportions for novel combinations of target and non-target objects not encountered during training. Importantly, consistent with behavioral findings showing the interference of absolute numerical information in proportional estimation tasks, we observe that performance degrades when the model is tasked with simultaneously providing the absolute count of target objects, further supporting the notion of a shared, magnitude-based processing system. This research contributes to a deeper understanding of how quantity is represented and processed in the brain, and provides a powerful new approach for developing computational models that can robustly estimate and reason about quantities from visual scenes. # PAGE 1# Welcome to the Berkeley Artificial Intelligence Research (BAIR) Lab!
