The availability of high-quality paraphrase resources is crucial for numerous natural language processing tasks, including machine translation, text summarization, question answering, and dialogue generation. Paraphrases, expressing the same meaning using different wording, enhance the robustness and flexibility of NLP systems. While existing paraphrase lexicons offer valuable resources, their coverage is often limited, hindering the performance of applications that rely on them. Acquiring paraphrases is a challenging problem, particularly when aiming for both high coverage and accurate semantic equivalence. Traditional methods often rely on manually curated lists or thesauri, which are expensive to create and maintain, and tend to miss subtle variations in expression. Alternatively, distributional semantic approaches can identify paraphrases based on word co-occurrence, but often struggle with capturing nuanced semantic relationships. This paper addresses the challenge of paraphrase acquisition by proposing a novel method that significantly expands existing paraphrase lexicons while maintaining a reasonable level of accuracy. Our key insight is that paraphrases frequently exhibit generality through lexical variants – words belonging to the same semantic class or morphological family – even when the surface forms differ. For example, the paraphrase pair “amendment” – “amending” demonstrates this principle. Recognizing this, our approach moves beyond simply identifying paraphrases with identical word forms and instead leverages patterns induced from seed paraphrases, utilizing the inherent flexibility provided by lexical variants. We apply these induced patterns to monolingual corpora to discover new paraphrase pairs, many of which consist of entirely different words from the original seed set. This process enables a substantial boost in paraphrase coverage. We present a fully empirical method, requiring no reliance on external semantic resources beyond the initial seed paraphrases and the monolingual corpus. Experiments demonstrate that our method can expand seed sets by impressive factors, ranging from 42 to 206, achieving significantly improved coverage compared to previous techniques that only consider exact word matches. Critically, we also assess the quality of the newly acquired paraphrases through a rigorous human evaluation. The results confirm that the acquired paraphrases maintain reasonable quality, especially when starting with high-quality seed sets, highlighting the effectiveness of our approach in balancing coverage and accuracy. The remaining sections of this paper detail our method, discuss experimental setup and results, and conclude with a summary and future directions. # ### #### ##### ###### ####### ######## ######### ########## ############ ############. ## ## ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##. ##.

The problem of aligning sentences in parallel corpora is a fundamental challenge in computational linguistics, underpinning efforts in machine translation, cross-lingual information retrieval, and bilingual lexicon construction. Synchronous grammars, which explicitly model the correspondence between syntactic structures in two languages, offer a compelling framework for capturing this translational equivalence. Unlike word-alignment models that focus on individual word pairings, synchronous grammars represent alignments as derivations within a shared grammar, allowing for non-monotonic alignments and capturing structural correspondences beyond simple one-to-one mappings. However, inducing synchronous grammars from parallel corpora has traditionally been hampered by significant computational hurdles. Previous approaches often relied on restrictive heuristics or incorporated constraints derived from existing word-alignment models, limiting their ability to fully capture the nuances of translational equivalence. Moreover, many inference algorithms faced intractability issues when dealing with the complexity of derivation forests inherent in synchronous grammar models. Addressing these challenges, we present a novel approach to phrasal synchronous grammar induction that overcomes these limitations. Our model directly induces a synchronous grammar from parallel sentence-aligned corpora, eschewing the need for external heuristics or word-alignment constraints. We leverage a hierarchical Bayesian prior to encourage the generation of compact grammars, favoring smaller translation units and promoting interpretability. Crucially, our inference procedure utilizes a novel Gibbs sampler over synchronous derivations, effectively circumventing the intractability problems that have plagued previous models. This Gibbs sampler operates iteratively, sampling grammatical rules and derivation steps in a highly efficient manner. This efficiency allows our model to be applied to significantly larger translation corpora than previously feasible, unlocking the potential to learn more comprehensive and accurate representations of translational equivalence. The core motivation behind this work stems from a desire to move beyond reliance on external alignment cues and learn synchronous grammars directly from the data, maximizing the expressiveness and robustness of the resulting models. By sidestepping the complexities of derivation forests and leveraging the efficiency of Gibbs sampling, we offer a substantial advance in the field of synchronous grammar induction, paving the way for more accurate and scalable machine translation and cross-lingual analysis tools. Our model provides a principled framework for capturing the structural correspondences between languages, ultimately contributing to a deeper understanding of how meaning is conveyed across linguistic boundaries. We believe that this approach offers notable advantages over existing methodologies, particularly concerning its scalability and reduction of reliance on heuristic dependencies. The focus on phrasal units further enables the capture of idiomatic expressions and complex constructions that are frequently missed by word-level alignment techniques.

The integration of syntactic information into language models (LMs) has consistently demonstrated improvements across various natural language processing tasks, including speech recognition, machine translation, and text generation. Traditional approaches often rely on explicitly incorporating syntactic features, such as parse trees or dependency relations, which can be computationally expensive, particularly for large corpora and complex syntactic structures. Part-of-speech (POS) tags, representing the fundamental grammatical categories of words, have been a standard, relatively lightweight syntactic feature incorporated into LMs for decades (Rosenfeld, 1999). However, the descriptive power of POS tags alone can be limiting, particularly when modeling long-range dependencies and subtle syntactic nuances. While more sophisticated syntactic representations, such as those derived from full syntactical parse trees (e.g., Chomsky’s formal grammar), offer richer structural information, the computational cost and reliance on accurate syntactic parsing significantly hinder their widespread adoption within large-scale LMs. SuperARV tags (Kurata and Nagao, 2004) represent an intriguing intermediate point, offering a more detailed view of syntactic function than POS tags, yet remaining computationally manageable. However, these tend to be language-specific and require considerable linguistic expertise to define and annotate. This paper explores a novel approach: a scalable joint language model that leverages fine-grain syntactic tags without imposing the substantial computational burden of full parsing or the deep linguistic knowledge required for custom tagsets. We argue that a sweet spot exists between the simplicity of POS tags and the complexity of full parsing, and we advocate for the use of relatively simple tags—those that do not demand extensive linguistic expertise but nevertheless offer a significantly richer representation of syntactic structure compared to standard POS tags. These tags can be readily derived from automatically generated, imperfect parse trees, ensuring ease of adoption across diverse languages. We address the challenges inherent in scaling a joint LM to large tagsets and corpora, proposing solutions that demonstrate robust performance. We introduce and evaluate two novel fine-grain tagsets, showcasing their effectiveness in a speech recognition task, comparing results against POS tags and SuperARV tags. Our findings demonstrate the substantial potential of this approach for improving language modeling accuracy while maintaining computational feasibility. Finally, we outline promising future directions for research, including exploring the application of this model to other NLP tasks and investigating methods for automatically learning optimal tagsets from unannotated data. We believe this work represents a significant step towards bridging the gap between computationally efficient language models and rich syntactic representations, paving the way for more powerful and adaptable NLP systems.

Sentiment analysis of product reviews has become a crucial area of research due to its widespread applications in e-commerce, market research, and customer relationship management. The ability to automatically extract and understand customer opinions about products can provide valuable insights for businesses to improve their offerings and marketing strategies. However, existing approaches to sentiment analysis on product reviews often fall short in effectively capturing the nuances of customer feedback, particularly when dealing with complex product attributes and their associated sentiments. Traditional sentiment analysis techniques often treat reviews as a bag of words, failing to leverage the hierarchical relationships between product attributes and their sentiments. Consequently, they struggle to accurately interpret reviews that mention multiple attributes with conflicting or complex sentiment expressions. For instance, consider a review of a camera that praises its image quality but criticizes its battery life. Naive sentiment analysis models might average these sentiments, leading to a misleading overall impression. Furthermore, many approaches struggle to handle sentences or reviews that express sentiments toward several attributes simultaneously, resulting in incomplete or inaccurate sentiment extraction. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel Hierarchical Learning – Sentiment Ontology Tree (HL-SOT) approach for sentiment analysis on product reviews. Our approach capitalizes on the structured knowledge inherent in product attributes and their associated sentiments by utilizing a Sentiment Ontology Tree (SOT). This tree represents a hierarchical organization of product attributes, allowing us to model the relationships between different attributes and their corresponding sentiments. For example, in the context of a camera, the SOT might include attributes like "Image Quality," "Battery Life," "Design," and "Price," with each attribute potentially having sub-attributes or related concepts. The Hierarchical Learning (HL) process then leverages this structured knowledge to iteratively refine the sentiment labels assigned to product attributes within reviews. This allows the model to understand the context and dependencies between different attributes, leading to more accurate and nuanced sentiment extraction. Unlike methods that treat attributes as independent entities, HL-SOT considers the hierarchical structure to determine sentiments with fine-grained accuracy. Our approach differs from existing methods in its ability to effectively handle reviews mentioning multiple attributes and complex sentiment expressions. By modeling the hierarchical relationships within the SOT and employing a hierarchical learning process, we can better disambiguate sentiments toward different attributes and capture the overall sentiment toward the product. Preliminary empirical analysis on a human-labeled dataset demonstrates the promising and reasonable performance of our HL-SOT approach, outperforming existing baseline methods in capturing nuances in sentiment expressions.

Grammatical Error Correction (GEC) is a challenging natural language processing task with broad applications, from educational tools to professional writing assistance. The goal is to automatically identify and correct grammatical errors in a given text, producing a fluent and error-free output. Significant progress has been made in recent years, largely driven by advances in machine learning. Two dominant paradigms have emerged as state-of-the-art approaches: machine learning classification and machine translation. Both approaches have yielded impressive results, but they operate under fundamentally different principles and exhibit distinct strengths and weaknesses. The classification approach frames GEC as a sequence labeling problem, where each word or phrase is assigned a label indicating whether it is correct or requires correction, and if so, what correction is needed. This allows for a modular design, enabling the integration of various linguistic features and error-specific knowledge. Conversely, the machine translation (MT) approach casts GEC as translating from an “errorful” language to a “correct” language, leveraging powerful neural architectures pre-trained on massive parallel corpora. This paradigm shift has demonstrated the potential of neural networks to learn complex patterns and subtle grammatical rules. Despite their individual successes, neither approach is without limitations. This paper undertakes a comprehensive comparative study of these two leading paradigms, going beyond simple benchmark comparisons to analyze their internal workings and error profiles. Through careful error analysis of systems built upon both frameworks, we identify core strengths and weaknesses of each. We observe that the machine translation approach excels at handling complex grammatical errors and benefits from learning from vast amounts of parallel data, obviating the need for extensive linguistic engineering. However, it can struggle with generalization beyond the training data and may exhibit brittleness when encountering novel error types. Conversely, the classification approach offers superior generalization capabilities and the flexibility to incorporate diverse knowledge sources and train in low-resource settings, even without human-annotated correction data. However, it may be less effective at capturing the nuanced dependencies and long-range context often required for correcting complex errors. Recognizing the complementary nature of these approaches, we propose a novel algorithmic framework that aims to synthesize their respective advantages. Our approach intelligently combines elements of both classification and machine translation, leveraging the strengths of each while mitigating their weaknesses. We implement and evaluate several systems based on existing resources, demonstrating a significant relative improvement – over 20% – and a substantial absolute gain of 7.4 F-score points compared to previous state-of-the-art GEC systems.

The burgeoning volume of online information presents a significant challenge for users seeking relevant and timely results. Consequently, personalized search, which aims to tailor search results to individual user preferences, has become a central focus of research in information retrieval. A cornerstone of personalized search is the user profile – a representation of a user’s interests that can be used to filter and rank search results. However, traditional approaches to building user profiles often rely exclusively on a user’s search history within a given system. This reliance presents a critical limitation: when users have limited interaction history with the platform, the resulting profile is often sparse and incomplete, hindering the effectiveness of personalization. This research addresses this challenge by exploring a novel approach to user profiling that explicitly leverages social data and external knowledge, even when a user's direct interaction history is minimal. The core idea is to construct richer, more informative user profiles by integrating not only a user’s explicit actions within the search system (e.g., clicks, queries) but also their social annotations on web content, alongside an external knowledge base gleaned from broader usage patterns across the user base. This approach recognizes that social annotations – likes, shares, ratings – provide valuable signals about a user’s interests that go beyond simple keyword matching and captures nuanced preferences. Furthermore, building an external knowledge base from aggregated usage data allows us to infer user interests even when individual user activity is limited. We propose a novel framework that simultaneously incorporates these three key sources of information – social annotations, user-generated documents (e.g., saved articles), and an external knowledge base – into a probabilistic latent topic model. This model, presented here, allows us to discover underlying interests (topics) that are reflected in these diverse data streams. Building on this enhanced user profiling approach, we develop a personalized social query expansion strategy. Specifically, we introduce a topical query expansion model that leverages the inferred user profiles to identify relevant terms and documents that might not be directly related to the user’s initial query but are aligned with their broader interests. The effectiveness of our proposed approach has been rigorously evaluated using a large public social annotation dataset. Our experimental results demonstrate that our models significantly outperform existing personalized query expansion techniques that rely solely on user profiles constructed from historical usage data, highlighting the benefits of integrating social data and external knowledge for enhanced personalization in web search.

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has revolutionized the field of Machine Translation, achieving state-of-the-art results across various language pairs. The prevailing paradigm for NMT is the encoder-decoder framework, typically employing recurrent neural networks (RNNs) such as LSTMs or GRUs to encode the source sentence into a context vector and then decode it into the target language. While this approach has demonstrated remarkable progress, it still faces inherent limitations that hinder its potential for even greater accuracy and fluency. A key challenge lies in the encoder’s ability to effectively capture and retain long-range dependencies within the source sentence. RNNs, by their very nature, struggle with vanishing gradients and the difficulty of propagating information across numerous time steps, leading to a tendency to “forget” distant information. This is particularly problematic when translating sentences with complex grammatical structures or intricate semantic relationships. Furthermore, traditional encoder-decoder models often treat source words as independent units during the encoding process, overlooking the crucial relationships that exist between them. In reality, the meaning of a word is heavily influenced by its context, and accounting for these inter-word relationships can significantly improve the quality of the translated output. Consider, for example, the sentence "The cat sat on the mat." Understanding the relationship between "cat," "sat," and "mat" is essential for accurate translation, and neglecting this connection can lead to suboptimal results. Existing approaches have attempted to address these limitations through various mechanisms, such as attention mechanisms, which allow the decoder to focus on relevant parts of the source sentence. However, the attention mechanism primarily focuses on aligning source and target words, and does not explicitly model the relationships  between  source words themselves. In this paper, we address these shortcomings by introducing a novel approach that leverages Relation Networks to refine source representations within the encoder-decoder framework. Our core idea is to explicitly model the relationships between source words and incorporate this relational information into the encoding process. Relation Networks are designed to learn representations of pairwise relationships between entities, allowing the encoder to capture contextual information beyond simple word co-occurrence. By associating source words with each other based on their relationships, our method enhances the encoder’s memorization capability, enabling it to retain distant information more effectively. Specifically, we integrate Relation Networks into the encoder to compute representations of each word considering its relationships with other words. These relational representations, along with the original word embeddings, are then fed into the attention mechanism during decoding, allowing the decoder to leverage both the individual word representations and their contextual relationships.

The generation of lyrics that harmonize seamlessly with a given melody represents a fascinating and challenging intersection of music information retrieval and natural language processing. While automated music composition has seen significant advancements, the task of producing lyrics that not only make sense linguistically but also align rhythmically and emotionally with the underlying melody remains largely unexplored. Previous attempts at lyrics generation have often struggled to achieve this synergy, resulting in lyrics that feel disconnected from the music, lacking either coherence or musicality. A key obstacle in this domain has been the scarcity of datasets containing lyrics explicitly synchronized with their corresponding melodies. Such datasets are crucial for training models to learn the intricate relationship between linguistic structure and melodic phrasing. Existing datasets often lack precise alignment information, hindering the development of models capable of capturing this nuanced connection. In this paper, we address this challenge by introducing a novel, data-driven approach to lyrics generation conditioned on a melody. Our model leverages a recurrent neural network (RNN) architecture and is trained on a newly constructed dataset specifically designed to bridge the gap between lyrics and melody. This dataset, comprising 1,000 lyrics-melody pairs, incorporates precise syllable-note alignments along with word, sentence, and paragraph boundaries – information that is critical for generating lyrics that flow naturally and harmonize well with the musical structure. The creation of this dataset represents a significant contribution in itself, providing a valuable resource for future research in this area. Prior work in lyrics generation has largely focused on unsupervised approaches or models trained on broad corpora of lyrics, often without explicit consideration for the accompanying melody (e.g., (Lample et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2018)). While these models can generate syntactically correct and semantically coherent lyrics, they frequently fail to capture the rhythmic and melodic constraints that govern the flow of a song. Our approach differs fundamentally by explicitly conditioning the lyrics generation process on a featurized representation of the melody. This allows the model to learn patterns and dependencies between musical and linguistic elements, ultimately leading to the generation of lyrics that are not only fluent but also musically compatible. Before presenting the model, we conduct a thorough quantitative analysis of the relationship between word/sentence/paragraph boundaries in lyrics and melodic structures, uncovering notable correlations that inform our model design. We demonstrate that our proposed model effectively generates lyrics that maintain consistent boundaries aligned with the music's phrasing, offering a compelling step forward in the quest for truly harmonious music-lyrics generation.

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has revolutionized the field of Machine Translation, achieving state-of-the-art results across numerous language pairs. At the core of most NMT systems lies a decoding algorithm responsible for generating the target sequence given the encoded source representation. While various decoding strategies exist, beam search has emerged as the dominant approach, consistently outperforming simpler alternatives like greedy search in terms of translation quality. Beam search maintains a fixed number of promising candidate translations (the "beam") at each decoding step, exploring a larger hypothesis space than greedy decoding. The intuition is straightforward: explore multiple possibilities to escape suboptimal local optima and discover the globally best translation. However, despite its widespread adoption and demonstrated effectiveness, beam search suffers from a well-documented and perplexing limitation: increasing the beam size beyond a certain threshold (typically around 5) often degrades translation quality. This phenomenon, often referred to as the "beam search curse," has been observed across various NMT models and language pairs, prompting questions about the fundamental behavior of beam search and the limits of its efficacy. While anecdotal explanations exist, a comprehensive understanding of the underlying mechanisms driving this curse has been lacking. In this paper, we undertake a rigorous investigation into the beam search curse, aiming to explain  why  it occurs and, crucially, to develop methods for mitigating its negative impact. Our work builds upon prior observations of the beam search curse, but moves beyond mere reporting of the problem towards a deeper analytical understanding. We propose a series of novel methods for (re-)scoring and stopping beam search hypotheses, specifically designed to circumvent the quality degradation associated with larger beam sizes. Importantly, our approaches aim for hyperparameter-free operation, avoiding the need for extensive tuning which often accompanies other advanced decoding techniques. We systematically evaluate several re-scoring strategies, exploring the role of context, language model likelihood, and other factors in refining the beam’s content. Furthermore, we examine various stopping criteria, assessing their impact on translation quality and computational efficiency. Our experimental results, conducted on a challenging Chinese-to-English translation task, demonstrate that our proposed methods consistently outperform the standard length normalization heuristic—a widely used technique for mitigating length bias in beam search—by a significant margin of +2.0 BLEU. Remarkably, our methods achieve the overall best results among all the approaches tested, highlighting the potential of our approach to unlock the benefits of beam search without incurring its typical pitfalls.

The volume of news content generated globally each day is staggering. This influx originates from diverse sources, spanning countless languages, making it increasingly difficult for individuals and organizations to stay informed about current events. Traditional methods of media monitoring often involve manual filtering and aggregation, a process that is both time-consuming and inherently limited in scale. The ability to automatically cluster news articles, regardless of their language, into coherent narratives offers a powerful solution, enabling efficient tracking of unfolding events and facilitating a broader understanding of global perspectives. The challenge, however, is significant. Clustering algorithms typically operate on static datasets with a predefined set of topics or cluster labels. Applying such approaches to the dynamic realm of streaming news presents unique hurdles, particularly when dealing with multiple languages. As news stories evolve, new topics emerge, and existing ones fade, requiring a clustering system to adapt continuously and discover an ever-growing number of relevant cluster labels in real-time. Moreover, news events frequently unfold across linguistic boundaries. A single story might be reported in German, English, and Spanish, each with nuanced phrasing and terminology. Effective clustering must therefore not only identify monolingual groupings but also recognize and merge cross-lingual articles that describe the same event. Existing cross-lingual clustering approaches often rely on computationally expensive techniques like machine translation or complex alignment models, making them unsuitable for real-time processing of massive news streams. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel and efficient method for multilingual clustering of streaming news. Our approach overcomes the limitations of traditional clustering techniques by adopting an online, label-discovery paradigm. Unlike methods that require prior knowledge of cluster labels, our system dynamically identifies and maintains a growing set of stories as they arrive in the stream. We prioritize simplicity and computational efficiency, designing a system that can scale to handle the demands of high-volume news feeds. Through rigorous experimentation on publicly available news datasets in German, English, and Spanish, we demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art results, effectively aggregating articles from multilingual sources into meaningful and coherent story clusters while maintaining scalability and responsiveness. Our work represents a significant step towards enabling more efficient and comprehensive media monitoring in an increasingly interconnected world. We believe that this capability holds immense potential for researchers, journalists, and organizations seeking to navigate the complexities of the global news landscape. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

The notion that words possess different meanings across various domains is a cornerstone of linguistic understanding. Consider the word "apple"—it can refer to a fruit in a nutrition context, a technology company in a business setting, or perhaps even a specific geographical location. This domain dependence profoundly impacts the semantic richness of language, yet existing approaches to word representation learning often overlook this crucial aspect. Current methods, largely driven by the success of distributional semantics (Mikolov et al., 2013; Pennington et al., 2014), typically train word embeddings on a single, monolithic corpus, resulting in representations that average across all meanings and fail to capture the nuanced domain-specific semantics. This limitation hinders performance in downstream tasks that rely on understanding domain-specific language, such as sentiment analysis in specialized sectors like finance or medicine. The growing availability of text data from diverse domains presents a unique opportunity to address this shortcoming. Cross-domain word representation learning aims to develop word embeddings that effectively capture the distinct meanings associated with different domains. However, existing cross-domain approaches often require labeled data or rely on complex alignment techniques, which are impractical in many real-world scenarios. Furthermore, many existing methods struggle to simultaneously model both domain-specific semantics  and  maintain consistency across domains—a delicate balance crucial for achieving robust and transferable representations. In this paper, we propose a novel  unsupervised  method for learning domain-specific word representations, requiring no labeled data whatsoever. Our approach leverages the shared vocabulary between a source and a target domain to facilitate knowledge transfer and domain adaptation. The core idea is to identify a subset of "pivot" words—frequent words present in both domains—and use them as bridges to learn domain-specific representations. We formulate a unique optimization objective that enforces two key constraints. First, we ensure that the learned word representations accurately predict the context of these pivot words within each domain. Second, we encourage the pivot word representations to be semantically similar across the source and target domains, thereby preserving a degree of cross-domain consistency. We further introduce a novel domain adaptation strategy that transfers knowledge learned from the source domain to improve the performance on the target domain. The simplicity and elegance of our approach, combined with its unsupervised nature, make it highly practical and broadly applicable. Extensive experimental results on a benchmark sentiment classification dataset demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art domain-insensitive and cross-domain word representations, achieving new state-of-the-art results for sentiment classification across a wide range of domain pairs.

Machine translation (MT) has witnessed remarkable progress in recent years, largely propelled by the rise of neural network-based sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models (Sutskever et al., 2014;Bahdanau et al., 2015). These models, leveraging the power of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and attention mechanisms, have demonstrably outperformed traditional statistical machine translation (SMT) approaches (Koehn et al., 2003) in various translation scenarios. However, despite their success, seq2seq models can still struggle to accurately capture the semantic nuances and relationships between words and phrases across languages, particularly when dealing with low-resource language pairs or specialized domains. A primary limitation arises from the models’ reliance on purely distributional semantics learned directly from parallel corpora, which can be noisy and incomplete, failing to fully represent the underlying meaning of words and phrases. Furthermore, the "black box" nature of these models hinders interpretability and makes it challenging to effectively incorporate external knowledge sources to improve translation quality. To address these challenges, we propose a novel approach that integrates knowledge-based semantic information into the seq2seq framework. This paper introduces Knowledge-Based Semantic Embedding (KBSE), a method designed to bridge the semantic gap between source and target languages by leveraging structured knowledge from external knowledge bases (KBs). Our core hypothesis is that representing sentences in a semantic space enriched with KB information can facilitate more accurate and contextually appropriate translations. Instead of solely relying on word co-occurrence patterns observed in training data, we aim to ground the translation process in a shared semantic representation that reflects real-world knowledge. In KBSE, we first map the source sentence into a semantic space constructed using a KB, such as WordNet or ConceptNet. This mapping captures the relationships between words and concepts within the KB, providing a richer semantic representation than simple word embeddings. Subsequently, we employ a recurrent neural network (RNN) with an attention mechanism to generate the target sentence, conditioned on this knowledge-based semantic representation. Crucially, this architecture ensures that the underlying meaning of the source sentence is preserved throughout the translation process, while also guiding the generation of a fluent and accurate target sentence. We evaluate our proposed KBSE method on two distinct translation tasks: an electric business data domain and a movie data domain. Our experimental results demonstrate that KBSE outperforms both traditional SMT methods and existing encoder-decoder models, highlighting the benefits of incorporating knowledge-based semantic information in machine translation. This work represents a significant step towards developing more robust, interpretable, and knowledge-aware machine translation systems.

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has revolutionized the field of Machine Translation, achieving state-of-the-art results across numerous language pairs (Sutskever et al., 2014; Bahdanau et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2016). The end-to-end nature of NMT, coupled with its ability to learn complex dependencies, has largely eclipsed the dominance of earlier approaches like phrase-based statistical machine translation (SMT) (Koehn et al., 2003). However, despite this significant progress, NMT systems still operate at a relatively granular level – processing text word by word. This word-by-word approach neglects the inherent phrase-level structure that is crucial for robust natural language understanding and ultimately, effective translation (Sag et al., 2002; Villavicencio et al., 2005). Phrases, as building blocks of meaning, carry semantic information that can be lost or misinterpreted when translated solely at the word level. Consider, for example, idioms, multi-word expressions, or even simply common collocations, where the overall meaning is not simply the sum of its constituent words. Capturing and leveraging this phrase-level information holds the potential to significantly improve the fluency and accuracy of NMT systems. The challenge lies in effectively incorporating this phrase-level knowledge into the NMT architecture, which is fundamentally designed for sequential word processing. Naive attempts to simply concatenate phrases into the input or output sequences may lead to excessively long sequences and computational inefficiencies. Furthermore, the end-to-end training paradigm of NMT makes it difficult to directly incorporate external knowledge sources or models. Existing approaches to address this issue include incorporating subword units like Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) (Sennrich et al., 2016) or morphemes, which partially capture phrase-like structures, but often fall short of representing meaningful phrases in their entirety. In this paper, we propose a novel method to leverage the strengths of both NMT and SMT by dynamically integrating a phrase memory from an SMT system into the NMT encoder-decoder architecture. This approach allows us to harness the phrase-level translation expertise encoded in a well-trained SMT system (which inherently operates on phrases) while maintaining the flexibility and learning capacity of NMT. Our key innovation lies in the dynamic rewriting of the phrase memory during the decoding process. Guided by the contextual information provided by the NMT model, the SMT model iteratively generates relevant target phrases, ensuring that the phrase memory contains the most suitable phrases for the current decoding context. The NMT decoder then uses this dynamically updated phrase memory to estimate probabilities and, when appropriate, select a phrase to translate, effectively enabling phrase-level translation within the NMT framework.

The problem of unsupervised grammar induction asks how to learn a grammar from raw text without any labeled data—no part-of-speech tags, no parse trees, nothing beyond the sequence of words themselves. This is a fundamentally challenging task, requiring a system to simultaneously discover the underlying syntactic structures of a language while avoiding overfitting to the idiosyncrasies of a limited training corpus. While fully unsupervised parsing has seen considerable progress in recent years, it remains an active area of research with substantial room for improvement. A key obstacle lies in the difficulty of effectively searching the vast space of possible grammars. Many existing algorithms struggle to generalize beyond the training data, resulting in parsers that perform poorly on unseen text. Recent work, such as that by Seginer (2007), has demonstrated promising results, but further enhancements are desired to improve robustness and accuracy. In this paper, we address this challenge by introducing a novel training algorithm, which we term Zoomed Learning. The core idea behind Zoomed Learning is to intelligently select subsets of training and test data to guide the grammar induction process. Our algorithm explicitly seeks to identify “zoomed-in” portions of the data—smaller subsets—where training on one subset and evaluating on a paired subset yields better results than training on the entire corpus. This approach is inspired by the concept of curriculum learning, where learning is facilitated by presenting materials in a meaningful order, starting with simpler concepts and gradually increasing complexity. However, unlike traditional curriculum learning, Zoomed Learning does not rely on pre-defined notions of simplicity or difficulty; instead, the training data itself guides the selection of effective subsets. The motivation for this approach stems from the observation that different portions of a large corpus likely contain varying degrees of syntactic complexity and noise. By focusing on subsets where the parser exhibits improved performance, we aim to distill the most informative signals from the training data and minimize the impact of irrelevant or misleading material. We evaluate the effectiveness of Zoomed Learning by applying it to the leading algorithm for fully unsupervised parsing, as introduced by Seginer (2007), across three diverse English domains: the Wall Street Journal (WSJ), the Brown Corpus (BROWN), and the GENIA corpus (GENIA). Our experimental results demonstrate that Zoomed Learning consistently improves parser F-score, with gains of up to 4.47% across the three datasets, highlighting its potential for enhancing the performance of unsupervised grammar induction systems.

The availability of high-quality, broad-coverage treebanks—annotated corpora that explicitly represent syntactic structure—is a cornerstone of modern syntactic parsing. However, constructing such treebanks is an expensive and time-consuming endeavor, particularly for resource-poor languages where linguistic expertise and annotation resources are scarce. This scarcity presents a significant bottleneck for the development of robust syntactic parsers, limiting access to advanced natural language processing capabilities for a substantial portion of the world’s languages. Recent advances in machine translation and cross-lingual transfer have illuminated a promising path towards addressing this challenge: grammar induction. This paradigm leverages the wealth of parallel text (bitext) available between resource-rich and resource-poor languages, combined with accurate parsers in the resource-rich language, to bootstrap syntactic structure in the target language. Previous approaches to grammar induction have often relied on projecting full, pre-existing parses from the source language onto the target language, which can be brittle and introduce errors if the syntactic structures of the two languages differ substantially. This work explores a more flexible and statistically grounded framework for dependency grammar induction, explicitly avoiding the need for full projected parses. We propose a novel approach that utilizes word-level alignments derived from bitext, along with the output of a source language parser (English in our experiments), to define  constraints  on the space of possible target trees. Our method frames grammar induction as a constrained optimization problem, allowing for partial, approximate transfer through linear expectation constraints on the distributions over trees. Instead of demanding a perfect match between source and target parses, we enforce weaker constraints that reflect fundamental syntactic relationships, such as dependency conservation and language-specific annotation rules. This allows our models to adapt to the unique syntactic peculiarities of the target language while still benefiting from the knowledge encoded in the source language parser. We investigate both generative and discriminative model architectures capable of incorporating these constraints, demonstrating their effectiveness on the Bulgarian and Spanish CoNLL shared task datasets. The results clearly demonstrate that our approach consistently surpasses unsupervised grammar induction methods and, crucially, achieves performance comparable to, or even exceeding, fully supervised learning when limited training data is available in the target language. The burgeoning field of computational argumentation has predominantly focused on tasks such as argument mining – identifying argumentative components within text – and argument ranking – determining which argument is “better” based on a predefined metric. While these tasks represent significant steps forward, they often sidestep a crucial question:  why  one argument is perceived as more persuasive than another. Understanding the qualitative reasons behind argument convincingness is essential for building truly intelligent argumentation systems, capable of not only generating arguments but also evaluating and refining them based on human reasoning. This paper addresses this gap by tackling a novel and challenging task: directly assessing the attributes contributing to the convincingness of arguments in web-based discussions. Current approaches often treat convincingness as a binary outcome, neglecting the nuances of human evaluation. This simplification overlooks the rich constellation of factors that influence persuasion, ranging from the logical soundness of the reasoning to the rhetorical effectiveness of the presentation. To move beyond this limitation, we propose a fully empirical approach, moving away from reliance on pre-defined argumentation schemes or logical fallacies. Instead, we aim to discover, through careful annotation and analysis, the attributes that people naturally attribute to compelling arguments. This work centers around the creation and analysis of a new, meticulously constructed corpus – UKPConvArg2 – designed to capture these subtle aspects of convincingness. The corpus consists of 9,111 argument pairs drawn from online debates surrounding controversial topics. Each pair is accompanied by natural language explanations written by crowd-workers, detailing  why  one argument is more convincing than the other. These explanations are meticulously multilabeled with 17 distinct classes representing diverse attributes, such as “strength of evidence,” “logical flaws,” “use of emotional reasoning,” and "relevance to the topic.” The creation process incorporates strict quality control measures, including multiple annotations per argument pair, rigorous inter-annotator agreement checks, and manual curation to ensure data reliability. The resulting corpus provides a valuable resource for exploring the complex landscape of argument convincingness. We then define two tasks leveraging this new dataset: (1) predicting the full probability distribution of the 17 convincingness attributes for a given argument pair, and (2) classifying the types of flaws present in the less convincing argument. Our experimental results, using both feature-rich Support Vector Machines (SVMs) and sophisticated Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) neural networks incorporating convolutional and attention mechanisms, demonstrate the considerable difficulty of these tasks. While our models achieve reasonable performance, they highlight the need for further research into more advanced techniques capable of capturing the subtle nuances of human reasoning.

Neural sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models have achieved remarkable success across various natural language processing tasks, including machine translation, text summarization, and dialogue generation. A critical, often overlooked aspect of these models is the reliance on accurate and reliable input. In many practical scenarios, the input data is not pristine; instead, it is produced by imperfect upstream systems, such as automatic speech recognition (ASR) or word segmenters. These systems generate hypotheses with varying degrees of confidence, and errors in the input can significantly degrade the performance of the downstream seq2seq model. Traditional approaches typically operate on the 1-best hypothesis generated by the upstream system, effectively discarding valuable information about alternative possibilities and their associated probabilities. This can be particularly problematic when dealing with noisy or ambiguous input, where multiple interpretations are plausible. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach that explicitly models uncertainty in the input using word lattices. A word lattice is a compact representation that encodes multiple possible sequences along with their posterior probabilities, effectively capturing the ambiguity inherent in the upstream system's output. By incorporating lattice information into the seq2seq model, we can leverage these probabilities to guide the decoding process and improve robustness to input errors. This is particularly valuable in scenarios like speech translation, where ASR errors are a primary source of noise. Existing neural network architectures are not inherently designed to handle lattice inputs. While some approaches have explored translating entire lattices without considering posterior probabilities, these methods often suffer from computational inefficiency and fail to fully exploit the information contained within the lattice structure. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a LatticeLSTM, an extension of the TreeLSTM (Tai et al., 2015) architecture that is specifically designed to consume word lattices as input. By modifying the TreeLSTM’s gating mechanisms and incorporating lattice posterior scores into the attention mechanism, we enable the model to effectively integrate uncertainty information during both encoding and decoding. Our work represents a significant step towards building more robust and accurate neural seq2seq models that can handle the inherent uncertainties present in real-world applications. We evaluate our approach on a large-scale speech translation task and demonstrate consistent improvements over baseline methods that rely on either 1-best hypotheses or lattices without posterior score integration, highlighting the effectiveness of our LatticeLSTM architecture. We believe that the ability to explicitly model input uncertainty holds promising potential for enhancing the performance of neural seq2seq models across a wide range of NLP applications.

Topic classification, the task of assigning documents to predefined categories or topics, remains a fundamental challenge in natural language processing. While various approaches leveraging statistical and deep learning techniques have shown considerable success, a persistent issue hinders optimal performance: the significant variability observed within documents belonging to the same topic. This intra-topic variability arises from diverse writing styles, varying levels of detail, and the inherent complexity of natural language expression. Consequently, documents classified as belonging to the same topic can exhibit substantial differences in their feature representations, leading to confusion for classification algorithms. Many existing topic classification methods treat all documents uniformly, failing to account for and mitigate this inherent variability. This can lead to reduced classification accuracy and overall model robustness. Recent research has explored techniques like topic modeling and feature weighting to address this issue, but often at the cost of increased computational complexity or limited applicability across diverse datasets. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel approach centered on intra-topic variability normalization. Our core hypothesis is that much of the variability within a topic can be explained and removed through a linear projection into a lower-dimensional space. We posit that by identifying and suppressing this variability, we can create a more homogeneous representation of intra-topic documents, allowing classifiers to better discern the underlying topic signal. Our method operates in three key stages. First, we formulate an optimization problem aiming to minimize intra-topic variance under the assumption that this variability is linearly removable. This is a crucial assumption that allows us to leverage efficient linear algebraic techniques. Second, we employ Kernel Principal Component Analysis (KPCA) to solve this optimization problem. KPCA provides a powerful framework for dimensionality reduction while implicitly mapping the data into a higher-dimensional space via a kernel function, enabling the capture of non-linear relationships. The solution of the KPCA problem effectively defines a new feature space where intra-topic variability is minimized. Finally, we apply a linear projection to transform the original document representations into this newly discovered feature space. This projection preserves the essential topic-related information while minimizing the impact of the previously dominant variability. We evaluate our proposed variability normalization algorithm using state-of-the-art Support Vector Machines (SVM) and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) classifiers on a challenging free-style conversational corpus. Our experimental results demonstrate a significant and compelling improvement over baseline models without variability normalization.

Language modeling, the task of predicting the probability of a sequence of words, has long been a cornerstone of Natural Language Processing (NLP). Accurate language models are crucial for a wide range of applications, including speech recognition (Voser et al., 2009), machine translation (Papineni et al., 2002), text generation (Bengio et al., 2003), and even tasks like spelling correction (Ng et al., 2002). Over the years, the field has seen the rise of two dominant paradigms for language modeling: count-based n-gram models and neural language models. Count-based n-gram models, rooted in statistical linguistics, are remarkably scalable and offer extremely fast inference speeds. Their reliance on simple frequency counts allows for efficient computation and deployment, especially in resource-constrained environments. However, they often struggle to capture long-range dependencies and exhibit the curse of dimensionality, particularly as the n-gram order increases. Conversely, neural language models, fueled by the deep learning revolution, have achieved state-of-the-art performance on numerous benchmarks. Architectures like recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and transformers (Vaswani et al., 2017) excel at modeling complex sequential dependencies and exhibiting greater generalization capabilities. Yet, neural LMs are computationally expensive to train and deploy, particularly for large vocabularies and extensive datasets. The training process can be time-consuming and requires significant hardware resources. Furthermore, their black-box nature can complicate interpretability and debugging. Historically, these two approaches have largely existed in separate spheres, with researchers often advocating for one over the other based on specific task requirements and computational constraints. However, recent work has explored methods for integrating aspects of both paradigms, albeit in limited ways. For instance, some have used n-gram smoothing techniques to improve the robustness of neural LMs. This paper proposes a novel framework that unifies count-based and neural language models within a single, unified modeling framework. We demonstrate that both types of models can be conceptualized as defining a set of probability distributions over the vocabulary of words. The key innovation lies in our ability to dynamically calculate mixture weights over these distributions during inference, allowing us to seamlessly combine the strengths of each approach. This formulation leads to the creation of novel and surprisingly effective hybrid models, and experimental results across a variety of language modeling tasks demonstrate the clear advantages of this unified approach. By bridging the gap between the traditional count-based methods and the modern neural models, we offer a pathway to more robust, efficient, and versatile language modeling solutions.

Statistical machine translation (SMT) systems have achieved remarkable progress in recent years, facilitating communication across language barriers. A critical preprocessing step for many languages, particularly those lacking explicit word delimiters like Chinese, Japanese, and Thai, is word segmentation (WS). WS involves dividing a continuous character stream into meaningful units (words) that can be subsequently processed by the translation system. While automated WS tools have become increasingly sophisticated, their effectiveness in the context of SMT remains an area of active research. The prevalent approach is to train WS models on manually annotated corpora, such as the Penn Chinese Treebank (CTB) for Chinese. However, the inherent design of these corpora often prioritizes general linguistic annotation rather than optimality for SMT. Consequently, the WS schemes learned from these resources may not perfectly align with the requirements of a robust translation system. The assumption that a WS scheme suitable for general linguistic analysis is also optimal for SMT has not been extensively challenged. We hypothesized that WS schemes learned on general corpora can introduce artificial boundaries that negatively impact word alignment (WA) – a crucial component of phrase-based SMT – and ultimately hinder translation quality. To investigate this, we conducted a detailed analysis using a manually aligned Chinese-English corpus, a resource specifically designed to provide gold-standard WA annotations. Our investigation revealed a surprisingly high degree of conflict: 74.60% of the sentences in our WA corpus, when segmented using an automated WS tool trained on the CTB, exhibited inconsistencies with the manually-provided WA annotations. This highlights a significant discrepancy between general-purpose WS training and the needs of SMT, strongly supporting our initial hypothesis. Motivated by these findings, we propose a novel approach to refine WS specifically for SMT. Rather than simply retraining an existing WS model, we leverage the gold-standard WA annotations to guide targeted word splitting. This "WA-guided splitting" aims to resolve conflicts with the WA by strategically inserting word boundaries that better reflect the alignment patterns. Our experimental results, conducted on the Chinese-English OpenMT corpora, demonstrate the effectiveness of our refinement strategy. We observed a substantial reduction in word alignment error rate (6.82%) – a direct indicator of improved alignment accuracy – and a significant BLEU score improvement (0.63 on average) compared to existing WS techniques. This work underscores the importance of considering the specific needs of SMT when designing and training WS models and demonstrates the potential of incorporating WA information to refine segmentation for improved translation performance.

The burgeoning field of topic modeling has revolutionized the way we analyze and understand large collections of textual data. Initially pioneered by models like Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA), topic models offer a probabilistic framework for uncovering latent semantic structures within documents, moving beyond simple keyword-based approaches. Models like Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) (Blei et al., 2003) have become particularly dominant, finding widespread application in diverse areas ranging from document classification to information retrieval. However, a key limitation of traditional topic models lies in their assumption of document independence – that is, they treat each document as a discrete, unrelated entity. This assumption fails to capture the rich sequential dependencies inherent in many real-world text corpora, particularly those composed of narratives, dialogues, or extended discussions. For example, a novel’s chapters should not be considered independent; rather, they build upon and relate to one another to form a cohesive whole. Ignoring these sequential relationships can lead to a fragmented understanding of the underlying narrative or discourse. This paper addresses this limitation by introducing a novel adaptive topic model specifically designed to capture and leverage sequential information within text. Our core innovation lies in the model's ability to dynamically adapt topics, not only based on the immediately preceding segment of text but also incorporating information gleaned from the overarching parent document. This dual-level adaptation mechanism allows the model to learn topics that evolve gradually over time while simultaneously maintaining consistency with the broader thematic context. This contrasts with existing topic models that typically treat each document or segment in isolation. To facilitate posterior inference within our adaptive topic model, we develop a tailored Gibbs sampling algorithm. Gibbs sampling, a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method, is well-suited for Bayesian inference in probabilistic models and allows us to approximate the posterior distribution of the model parameters. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through comprehensive experimental evaluation on a range of datasets, including a corpus of Herman Melville’s works. Our results show that the adaptive topic modeling framework significantly outperforms existing topic modeling approaches, as measured by perplexity, a standard metric for evaluating language models. Furthermore, our model exhibits a remarkable ability to uncover clear and meaningful sequential structure within the text, reflecting the inherent narrative flow and thematic development. This provides strong evidence that adaptive topic modeling represents a significant advancement in the field, offering a more nuanced and powerful tool for analyzing sequential text.

Machine translation (MT) has traditionally focused on translating from a single source language to a single target language. While this paradigm has yielded significant advancements, it often falls short when dealing with resource-scarce languages - those with limited training data and linguistic resources. The performance of statistical machine translation (SMT) systems, in particular, is heavily reliant on large, high-quality parallel corpora and robust language models. When a target language suffers from data scarcity, translation quality inevitably degrades. A promising approach to mitigate this issue lies in leveraging the potential of multiple target languages. The core idea is that translations into different target languages, even if imperfect, can share underlying semantic structures and linguistic correspondences. By exploiting these shared elements, we can potentially improve the translation quality for weaker target languages by learning from stronger ones. This concept is particularly appealing in scenarios where, for example, we have a strong language model for one target language but a relatively weak one for another. The intuition is that the robust language model in the well-resourced language can help disambiguate translations in the resource-poor language, leading to improved overall translation quality. Several related works have explored the benefits of multilingual MT, including pivot-based translation (Nagata & Duh, 2012) and shared statistical models (Lin et al., 2011). However, these approaches often lack a principled framework for explicitly modeling the cross-lingual relationships between translations. In this paper, we propose a novel method for multi-target machine translation that directly addresses this challenge. Our approach leverages the formalism of synchronous context-free grammars (SCFGs) – a powerful framework for capturing cross-lingual structural correspondences – and extends it to handle multiple target languages simultaneously. SCFGs allow us to model the parallel structure between languages, enabling the transfer of linguistic knowledge across languages. We introduce an extension called Multi-Synchronous Context-Free Grammars (MSCGFs), outlining methods for efficient rule extraction, effective scoring, strategic pruning, and optimized search within this expanded framework. The key contribution of our work is demonstrating how to effectively harness the strength of a well-resourced language to improve the performance of a translation system targeting a resource-scarce language. We present comprehensive experimental results on a range of language pairs, demonstrating that multi-target translation with a strong language model in a related target language can yield substantial gains, achieving improvements of up to 0.8-1.5 BLEU points. This suggests that our MSCGF approach offers a promising avenue for advancing MT, particularly in scenarios involving low-resource languages.

The burgeoning volume of data generated on social media platforms presents unprecedented opportunities for understanding human behavior and societal trends. A critical step in harnessing this data is the ability to infer demographic attributes of users, such as age and gender, based on their linguistic patterns. Such demographic inference has broad implications across a range of disciplines, including social science research seeking to analyze generational differences, economic modeling aimed at consumer behavior analysis, and business applications such as targeted advertising and personalized recommendations. While demographic data is often self-reported, this information can be unreliable or incomplete. Therefore, developing methods to infer demographics from linguistic cues offers a valuable complement to traditional data collection techniques. Traditionally, demographic inference has relied on manually curated lexica – lists of words associated with particular demographic groups. However, these lexica are often created subjectively and lack scalability. The rise of machine learning, particularly in the field of natural language processing, offers a new paradigm for automatically deriving predictive lexica. This paper explores the development of such lexica for age and gender prediction, utilizing large-scale social media datasets – specifically Facebook, blog posts, and Twitter data – that have been augmented with demographic labels. We leverage statistical regression and classification models to identify words and their associated weights that best predict age and gender. These models learn to capture the subtle linguistic nuances that correlate with different demographic groups, reflecting the way individuals express themselves online. Our primary contribution is a set of publicly available predictive lexica for age and gender, built from these social media data sources. Importantly, we demonstrate the effectiveness of these lexica, showing that they achieve state-of-the-art accuracy in language-based age and gender prediction on Facebook and Twitter data. Furthermore, we rigorously evaluate the lexica’s ability to generalize across different social media genres, assessing their robustness and applicability in diverse online contexts. Finally, we investigate their performance in limited message scenarios, exploring how well they function when predicting demographics from short, fragmented pieces of text, as is common in social media communication. Our research provides a valuable resource for the broader research community and paves the way for more accurate and scalable demographic inference from social media data. 1 [Link to Lexica] – Will be provided upon publication.
